II. Software (Chapters 8-14)

Call Recording (Mind Legal Compliance):

Chapter 8: Communication — Texts, Calls, and Social

Communication is the phone's original and core mission. Today it has grown far beyond simple calls and texts into a whole ecosystem of instant messaging, social networks, and email.

1. Advanced features of the Phone app

The Phone app on modern phones is way more than a dialer. It packs in call recording, spam blocking, smart caller ID, and other powerful tools.

Call recording (mind the legal fine print):
  • What it's for: Save important calls for work notes, interviews, customer commitments, or evidence in a dispute.
  • Legal note: In mainland China, a call recording is generally admissible as evidence only with the other party's consent, or when it protects your own lawful rights.
  • One-sided vs. two-sided consent: Legally, a recording made "without the other party's consent" is not automatically invalid. Under relevant Supreme People's Court interpretations, it can still be submitted as evidence as long as the method of recording did not seriously infringe others' lawful rights, violate prohibitive legal rules, or go against public order and good morals. That said, some provincial courts apply stricter standards for "secretly recorded" audio in civil cases; criminal cases usually face even stricter legality review.
  • Regional differences: Courts in places like Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangdong are relatively lenient about one-party recordings as civil evidence. Recordings involving trade secrets or personal privacy need extra care anywhere — they may be excluded for infringing privacy rights.
  • How to do it: Android usually shows a clear "Record" button on the call screen. iOS has no built-in call recording, so you'll need a third-party app or a Bluetooth headset with a recording feature.

Hard rules for using recordings

  • Never use recordings for extortion, spreading them around, or publicly insulting others.
  • Do not casually share content that involves third-party privacy (for example, accidentally catching someone else's conversation).
  • In important situations, say out loud at the start of the call that "this call will be recorded." That keeps things compliant and makes the recording stronger as evidence.
A closer look at spam-call blocking:
  • How it works: The Phone app checks a huge online number database and shows "spam call," "scam call," or a company name when the phone rings.
  • How to turn it on: On Android, open the Phone app > Settings > Spam blocking. On iOS, go to Settings > Phone > Call Blocking & Identification. For brand-by-brand switch paths and recommended options, see the comparison table in Chapter 13, "Useful System Tools."
  • Main labeling platforms: In China, number labeling is mainly handled by three data providers — Tencent Mobile Manager, 360 Mobile Security, and Dianhuabang (Tapir). Carrier features like "caller name" display and "spam blocking" often pull from the same data. Phone makers (Huawei, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo) mostly partner with these providers for their label databases.
  • What to do if you're mislabeled: If your legitimate work number is wrongly tagged as "food delivery," "courier," or "spam," you can appeal through these channels:
  • Dianhuabang (电话邦): visit the number-appeal platform haoma.tk.cn and submit identity verification.
  • 360: Submit via the "Number appeal" feature inside the 360 Mobile Security app.
  • Tencent: Submit on the "Number appeal" page in the "Tencent Mobile Manager" mini program.
  • The big three carriers: China Mobile users can text "KTFSR" to 10086 to enable spam protection. China Telecom users can follow the "Tianyi Anti-Harassment" official account. China Unicom users can set it up in "Unicom Mobile Manager."
  • Next-level spam blocking: Turn on your carrier's "high-frequency call blocking" (such as China Mobile's high-frequency call limit) to automatically block AI robocalls.
  • Common built-in phone blocking features:
  • Blacklist / whitelist: Manually block known spam numbers. Add contacts and courier/delivery numbers to the whitelist so they don't get caught by mistake.
  • SMS keyword filtering: Messages containing words like "prize," "loan," or "click this link" are automatically sent to the blocked box.
  • iOS Silence Unknown Callers: Calls from numbers not in your contacts go quietly to voicemail without interrupting you. Handy if you get lots of spam — just watch out for important calls from new numbers.
  • Do Not Disturb integration: At night or during meetings, allow only contacts through, on a schedule. Your sleep quality will thank you.
  • How apps work together: Prefer the phone's built-in blocking first, then layer on the National Anti-Fraud Center app and carrier spam protection. For cleanup tools, lightweight options like Qingzhuo are fine, but one security/cleanup suite is enough — see Chapter 13.
    • What VoLTE/VoNR are and how to turn them on:
    • VoLTE (Voice over LTE): Voice calls over the 4G network. No more falling back to 2G/3G mid-call, so you can talk and browse at the same time, with clearer audio and faster call setup.
    • VoNR (Voice over NR): Voice over 5G — the next step after VoLTE. Lower latency, better sound, and support for HD video calls. You need a 5G phone, a 5G plan, and local 5G coverage.
    • How to enable: On iOS, go to Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data and turn on "VoLTE." On Android, find the "VoLTE calls" switch under Settings > Mobile network > Mobile data > Advanced. Carriers usually turn it on by default. If your data drops during calls, VoLTE is probably off.

    Quick tip

    If your data suddenly slows or drops during a call, VoLTE/VoNR is probably off and you've fallen back to 2G/3G. Turn it on and you can "talk and scroll" at the same time.

    2. SMS and iMessage/RCS

    Traditional SMS isn't dead. It's still the reliable channel for verification codes, bank alerts, and official notices.

    • iMessage: Messages sent over the internet between Apple devices, shown as blue bubbles. Supports high-quality photos and videos, read receipts, and more — free and end-to-end encrypted.
    • RCS: A next-generation messaging protocol pushed by carriers worldwide and by Google. Features similar to iMessage or WeChat, but based on phone numbers.
    • iMessage and RCS interoperability: Starting with iOS 18, Apple supports the RCS standard. That means iPhones and Android phones can exchange HD photos, read receipts, and typing indicators — goodbye "green bubble" gap. Both carriers need to support RCS, and both phones need a new enough OS.
    RCS rollout in China:
    • China Mobile: An early RCS adopter. Some provinces already support "5G Messages" with rich media and interactive cards. Needs a supported handset and activation at a store.
    • China Telecom: Offers "Telecom 5G Messages." Some plans include it by default; older accounts may need to send a specific SMS command to activate.
    • China Unicom: Rolling out 5G Messages in major cities, but device support is uneven. Many Android models still need "Enhanced messages" or "5G Messages" switched on manually in the Messages app.
    • Real-world experience: RCS has rolled out more slowly than expected in China, mainly because WeChat dominates and device support is inconsistent. Day-to-day chat still runs on WeChat; RCS mostly handles "official push" messages such as bank alerts and government notices.

    Verification-code safety rules

    • Never forward codes: Anyone who asks you to "read out a code" or "forward a text" may be a scammer — including people claiming to be "support," "couriers," or "police, prosecutors, or courts." Your verification code = your money.
    • Phishing SMS: Be wary of links in texts about "ETC expired," "health card frozen," or "lost package compensation." Legitimate organizations never ask for card numbers or passwords via SMS links.
    • Spotting the sender: Official bank texts usually come from short codes starting with 95 or from 1069 + a company signature. A "bank notice" from a normal 11-digit mobile number is almost always a scam.
    • Two-factor backups: Don't casually change the phone number tied to important accounts. If you must, unlink all key accounts first — otherwise the new owner of your old number could reset your passwords via SMS codes.

    3. WeChat/QQ: Managing China's national super-apps

    WeChat and QQ have outgrown simple messaging and become "super-apps" for social, payments, and information.

    Backing up and migrating chat history:
    1. Log into WeChat on your PC or Mac.
    2. Click the menu at the bottom left > [Migrate & Backup] > [Backup & Restore].
    3. Choose "Back up chat history to computer," then pick the chats on your phone.
    4. Migrating to a new phone: On the old phone, open WeChat [Me] > [Settings] > [General] > [Chat Log Migration & Backup] > [Migrate] > [Migrate to Phone/Tablet], then scan the QR code.
    Deep cleaning storage space:
    • Standard path: WeChat [Me] > [Settings] > [General] > [Storage] — clear cache and clean chat history by time or file type.
    • Clean inside a chat: Open a chat > "..." at the top right > [Chat history] > [Manage storage] — delete photos, videos, and files in that chat while keeping the text.
    • Original photos/videos: HD originals from group chats take the most space. In [Manage storage], select "Originals" to delete them in bulk.
    • Turn off auto-download: [Settings] > [General] > [Photos, Videos, Files & Calls] > turn off "Auto-download" so group files don't silently pile up on Wi-Fi.
    • Mini program cache: In [Discover] > [Mini Programs], long-press unused ones to delete and free their local cache.
    • Compressed chat backups: When backing up on desktop WeChat, check "Compress" to shrink multi-GB chat histories to 30–50% of their size.
    Group management tips:
    • Group announcements: Owners/admins post them via "..." at the top right > [Group Announcement]. Everyone gets a strong notification — great for important notices. New members see it automatically.
    • Group to-dos: The owner can turn a pinned message into a "Group To-do." A red badge appears above members' heads and clears when they tap done. Perfect for signups and task collection.
    • Group chains (sign-up lists): Type "#chain" in the input box to start one — great for ordering food or tallying signups. Results auto-summarize at the top without flooding the chat.
    • Group live: "+" at the top right > [Group Live] for a live stream only this group can watch. Good for company training, family gatherings, and product beta tests.
    • Mute a group: Swipe a group name left in the list > [Mute] to tuck unimportant groups into "Muted groups," notifying you only when @mentioned.
    • Only owners/admins can @everyone: In groups of 500+, regular members can't @everyone — less noise for everyone.
    Fine-grained Moments privacy:
    • Group visibility: When posting, tap "Who can see" and choose "Partially visible" or "Hide from," using tag groups you set up earlier (e.g., "Colleagues," "Family," "Clients").
    • How far back friends can look: [Me] > [Settings] > [Friends' Permissions] > [Moments] > [Allow friends to view Moments] — choose "Last 3 days / 1 month / 6 months / All." "6 months" balances privacy and social life nicely.
    • Hide someone's Moments: Long-press a post > [Hide their Moments] or [Unfollow] — they won't know.
    • Moments ads: [Me] > [Settings] > [About WeChat] > [Personal Info & Permissions] > [Personalized Ads Management] to turn off behavior-based recommendations.
    • Strangers see ten posts: [Friends' Permissions] > [Moments] > [Allow strangers to view 10 Moments] — turn this off so strangers can't scroll your history.

    4. Video call comparison

    Each video call tool has its strengths. Picking the right one for the situation makes conversations smoother.

    • WeChat video: Ubiquitous in China, easy for all ages. Great for everyday chats with family and friends. Supports up to 20 people (via the "Group Video" mini program). Downside: quality drops noticeably on poor networks.
    • FaceTime: Apple-only, excellent quality, end-to-end encrypted. Since iOS 15, you can invite Android/Web users via a link, but the host must be on an Apple device. Great for cross-device family calls.
    • Zoom: The go-to for international meetings. Free 40-minute meetings for up to 100 people. Screen sharing, virtual backgrounds, breakout rooms — solid for remote and cross-border work.
    • Tencent Meeting: The office standard in China, deeply integrated with WeChat (scan to join). Up to 300 participants (paid). Cloud recording, live captions, meeting minutes — great for company training and large meetings.
    • Which to pick: Everyday 1-on-1 → WeChat. Apple-to-Apple → FaceTime. Formal business → Zoom or Tencent Meeting (Tencent in China, Zoom across borders).
    Bandwidth and data use reference:
    • WeChat video calls: About 500 Kbps–1 Mbps; roughly 3–5 MB per minute at standard quality, 8–12 MB at HD.
    • FaceTime: About 1 Mbps at SD, 2 Mbps for 720p, and 4+ Mbps for 1080p. Roughly 5–15 MB per minute.
    • Zoom/Tencent Meeting: About 1.5–3 Mbps for 720p, 3–5 Mbps for 1080p. Roughly 300–800 MB per hour; hosts of multi-person meetings use more.
    • Tip: Use Wi-Fi for long video calls. On mobile data, lower the quality yourself (turn off "HD video" in app settings) to save data.
    Video call quality tips:
    • Lighting: Face a light source with a window behind it (natural light is best). Avoid backlighting that turns your face into a silhouette.
    • Angle: Keep the camera slightly above eye level to avoid a double chin. In landscape mode, hold the phone with both hands for stability.
    • Audio: A headset prevents echo and howling. In a quiet room, don't use speakerphone.
    • Network: Prefer Wi-Fi. On 4G/5G, stay near a window for a stronger signal. In group meetings, turn off other videos and keep only the speaker.
    • Background blur: Tencent Meeting and Zoom both support AI blur to hide messy backgrounds. Wear solid colors so you don't "green-screen" into the background.

    Quick tip

    When the connection lags, turn off video and keep audio before hanging up — more polite than dropping the call. Before important meetings, run Tencent Meeting's built-in "Network Test."

    5. Email: Set up and use it on your phone

    • Add an email account: On iOS, Settings > Mail > Accounts > Add Account. On Android, there's usually a built-in "Email" app.
    • Tips: Set different notifications for different accounts. Use swipe gestures to quickly archive, delete, or flag mail.
    IMAP vs POP3 vs Exchange:
    • POP3: Downloads mail and deletes the server copy by default. Good for a single device that needs offline reading. Downside: no history on new devices. No longer recommended.
    • IMAP: Mail stays on the server; local is just a cache. Phones/PCs/tablets stay in sync — read on one, read everywhere. Today's mainstream recommendation.
    • Exchange (including ActiveSync): Microsoft's protocol. Syncs calendar, contacts, and tasks as well as mail. First choice for work email. Supported by Outlook, NetEase Enterprise Mail, and Tencent Enterprise Mail.
    • What to choose: Personal email → IMAP. Work email → Exchange first, IMAP second. Avoid POP3 unless you have a special archiving need.
    Work email setup:
    1. iOS: [Settings] > [Mail] > [Accounts] > [Add Account] > choose "Microsoft Exchange" or "Other."
    2. Android: In the built-in "Email" app or Outlook, choose "Add account" and enter your full address and password.
    3. Server settings (Exchange example): Server is often "mail.yourcompany.com" or "outlook.office365.com"; domain is your company short name.
    4. If you see "Cannot verify server," enter settings manually: Incoming server (IMAP) port 993 with SSL; outgoing server (SMTP) port 465 or 587 with TLS.
    5. After signing in, turn on "Push" in [Account Settings] for real-time mail, and turn off message preview to protect confidential content.

    Heads-up

    Work email usually needs an admin-issued "client authorization password" or "IMAP/SMTP auth code" — not your web login password. If login fails, generate a code in webmail settings first, then enter it on your phone.

    Hands-on: Back up your WeChat chats to a computer

    1. Start the backup on your computer: Open WeChat for desktop > menu at the bottom left > [Migrate & Backup] > [Backup & Restore].
    2. Choose back up to computer: Click "Back up chat history to computer."
    3. Select what to back up on your phone, then wait for the backup to finish.

    Chapter 9: Mobile Office and Learning

    Microsoft 365

    : If your company uses genuine Office, this is the best choice. Format compatibility with the desktop version is nearly perfect, avoiding the slight layout shifts that WPS may have with some complex layouts. Deeply integrated with OneDrive, the document you were halfway through editing on your computer opens as the latest version on your phone.

    Shimo Docs / Tencent Docs

    • : These two represent "online collaboration". They are suitable for multiple people editing the same document simultaneously, with each person's changes shown in real time. I used Shimo Docs to plan a trip with a friend — both of us filling in information into a spreadsheet at the same time was far more efficient than doing it alone.Practical Workflow
    • : My current habit is — important files go to OneDrive, daily editing uses WPS, and team collaboration opens Shimo Docs. Since my files went to the cloud, I've never again had the embarrassment of "forgetting my USB drive".2. Note-Taking Apps: From Quick Notes to a Knowledge System
    • When it comes to taking notes, many people want to build a complex system right from the start, only to give up after three days. My advice is to start light and then go heavy — first build the habit of "recording", then consider the problem of "managing".Quick Notes — The built-in system is enough

    : iOS Notes launches extremely fast and supports document scanning, handwriting, and audio recording. Android's built-in memo apps by various brands are also decent, and can be launched quickly even from the lock screen. These tools are suitable for recording temporary ideas, shopping lists, and meeting key points. The key is fast launch — you can record as soon as you think of something, without waiting for an app to load.Read It Later — Collecting Information

    : WeChat's "Float" feature is actually a hidden gem. When you see a good article but don't have time to read it carefully, tap "Float" in the upper-right corner, and it shrinks into a small dot attached to the edge of the screen, ready to be tapped open to continue reading anytime. It's much more convenient than forwarding to "File Transfer Assistant". In addition, read-later tools like Cubox or Pocket can collect good content you come across anywhere, across platforms.

    Building a System — Notion and Feishu

    • : When you feel that scattered notes are becoming hard to find, it's time to move to Notion. This tool is truly flexible — you can build a "reading notes database" that automatically organizes by book title, author, and rating; or set up a "project board" to visualize the progress of work tasks. Feishu's "Bitable" is similar, and has faster access speeds in China. I use Notion to manage all my writing materials, study notes, and project progress — I've been using it for over three years.A Practical Note-Taking Strategy
    • : My own habit is a "three-piece set" — temporary ideas go to the system memo (instant launch), articles to read go to WeChat's float (handy), and knowledge that needs long-term accumulation goes to Notion (systematized). Don't try to stuff everything into one tool from the start — that makes it easier to give up.3. Scanning and OCR: Bringing the Paper World into Your Phone
    • Phone scanning, when used well, can really save a lot of trips to the print shop. Last time I applied for a visa and needed electronic copies of a bunch of materials, I got them all done with my phone.iPhone users

    : The built-in scanning feature of iOS Notes is already quite good. Open Notes → tap the camera icon → select "Scan Documents", aim at the document and it will automatically recognize the border and correct the perspective. After shooting, you can adjust the color — the "Black & White" mode produces results closest to a scanner, and "Grayscale" is suitable for materials with images.Android users

    : Many brands' cameras have a built-in "Document Scan" mode. If you can't find it, download Microsoft Lens from the app store (free, and integrated with OneDrive).

    OCR Text Recognition

    • : If you need to extract text from scanned documents for editing, you need OCR. WeChat's built-in "Extract Text" feature is the simplest — long-press the image to use it, and the recognition accuracy is decent. For bulk processing, you can use the Baimiao app or CamScanner. For Chinese recognition, Baidu's OCR engine works quite well; WPS's image-to-text feature is also very accurate.Scanning Tips
    • Look Up Tips4. How to Choose a Cloud Drive: There's No Best, Only What's Best for You
    • I thought about choosing a cloud drive for a long time, and finally realized it really depends on what your "primary ecosystem" is.Apple Ecosystem → iCloud
    • : Seamless syncing that makes you barely notice its existence. Photos you take on your phone automatically appear on your computer a few minutes later. And Apple's privacy protection is the strictest. But the drawbacks are also obvious: cross-platform sharing with Android or Windows users is cumbersome, the free tier is only 5GB, and expansion costs money.Windows Primary → OneDrive

    : If you use a Windows PC + Office 365, OneDrive is a natural match. Save a document in Word, and it's automatically stored in the cloud. The 1TB space bundled with the Office subscription is a great deal. The mobile app's auto photo backup feature is also very handy.

    Domestic Sharing → Baidu Netdisk

    • : To be honest, Baidu Netdisk's download speed limit has always been criticized, but its sharing ecosystem is truly unmatched. A large amount of study materials and film/TV resources on the Chinese internet are shared via Baidu Netdisk. If you only occasionally download files shared by others, you can make do without a membership. If you're a heavy resource collector, just pay for the membership — the time saved is worth much more.Aliyun Drive / Quark Drive
    • : These are the rising stars in recent years. Aliyun Drive has no upload/download speed limits (currently), and Quark Drive is deeply integrated with the Quark browser, so you can directly save to the drive when searching for materials, which is very convenient.My Combined Solution
    • : iCloud manages personal photos and daily files (privacy first), Baidu Netdisk stores resources and receives shares (ecosystem first), and OneDrive manages work documents (Office integration first). Three cloud drives, each with its own job, not interfering with each other.5. A Real Mobile Office Scenario
    • Let me share a real experience of my own. Once on a business trip out of town, the client suddenly needed to revise contract terms. My workflow was as follows:At the hotel, I received the client's revision comments via WeChat (text messages + a photo of handwritten annotations).

    Opened OneDrive to find the original contract, opened and edited it with WPS, revising the terms one by one according to the client's WeChat messages.After revisions, used WPS's "Export as PDF" feature, and sent it to the client's WeChat group for confirmation.

    The client raised a second round of comments, so I used WPS's brush tool to directly circle the revision positions on the PDF, with voice annotations explaining the revision approach.

    After confirming everything was correct, used WPS's "Electronic Signature" feature to sign online, and sent it to the other party to sign as well.

    1. Finally, archived the signed contract PDF to both Baidu Netdisk and iCloud, and made a note in my work log in Notion.
    2. The whole process took about forty minutes from start to finish, without turning on a computer at all. To be honest, three years ago I would never have believed a phone could do these things, but now it really can. The key is to familiarize yourself with these tools in advance, so you don't scramble to download and register when you actually need them.
    3. Try it out: Build your mobile office workflow
    4. Choose your primary document app (WPS or Microsoft 365), log in and link it to a cloud drive.
    5. Open Notes or Memo, use the scan feature to scan a document, and export it as a PDF to send to yourself.
    6. Choose a cloud drive app and set it to auto-backup your phone photos (select "Backup only on Wi-Fi" to save data).

    Create a new page in Notion or Feishu, and try building a simple "work log" template.

    Chapter 10: Mobile Payment and Life Services

    1. To be honest, my parents' generation was initially resistant to the idea of "paying with a phone". "If the money is in the phone, what if it gets stolen?" This concern is very normal, but the reality is: the cash in your pocket has a much higher chance of being lost than mobile payment being fraudulently charged. Mobile payment is not about storing money in your phone — it's just a key, a key that opens your bank account.
    2. 1. How Exactly Do You Bind a Bank Card?
    3. Whether you use Alipay or WeChat, the first time you bind a card, you need to go through these steps:
    4. Open the app, find "Me" or "Wallet". Tap "Add Bank Card".

    Chapter 10: Mobile Payment and Life Services

    The bank will send a verification code SMS to your reserved mobile number. Enter it and set a 6-digit payment password.

    This payment password, your bank card password, and your lock screen password should ideally be three different passwords — don't set them the same for convenience.

    A little tip: if you're concerned about security, you can open a Tier II or Tier III electronic account in your bank app specifically for binding to mobile payment. Only keep your everyday spending money in this card, so even if something happens, the loss is limited.

    1. 2. The Payment Code Is "Whoever Sees It, Takes the Money"
    2. Many people are confused about the difference between a payment code and a collection code, and this distinction is very important.
    3. Payment Code
    4. : The barcode + QR code you show to the cashier to scan. This code is equivalent to your "electronic wallet" — whoever scans it can deduct money from your account. So

    absolutely never screenshot it and send it to anyone

    . This code automatically refreshes once per minute precisely to prevent fraudulent use.

    Collection Code

    • : Others scan this code to transfer money to you. This code can be screenshotted, saved, and sent to others — it's safe.Remember this distinction, and you can avoid many fraud traps. Anyone who asks you to "screenshot your payment code and send it over" is 100% a scammer.3. These Security Settings — 5 Minutes to Set Up Can Save You a Lot of WorryFingerprint/Face Payment
    • : In Alipay and WeChat's payment settings, turn on biometric payment. This way, every payment requires your fingerprint or face scan, so even if your phone is lost, the person who finds it can't spend your money.Security Lock

    : Both Alipay and WeChat have a "Security Lock" feature. Once enabled, entering the app's "Wallet" page requires an additional identity verification. Path: Alipay → Me → Settings → Account & Security → Security Center → Security Lock.

    Password-Free Payment Check

    • : Many people have signed up for various password-free payments and forgotten about them. Go to "Payment Settings" in Alipay and WeChat, find "Password-Free Payment / Auto Deduction", and see which services you've signed up for — turn off the ones you don't need.Login Device Management
    • : Regularly check which devices have logged into your account. If you find an unfamiliar device, kick it out immediately. Path: Alipay → Settings → Account & Security → Login Device Management.4. Bus and Subway: Your Phone Is Your Transit Card
    • Nowadays, very few people use physical transit cards when taking the bus or subway. There are two paths for swiping your phone at the turnstile:Virtual Transit Card in Phone Wallet
    • : Open a virtual transit card directly in Apple Wallet, Huawei Wallet, or Xiaomi Wallet. The advantage of this solution is: you don't need to unlock your phone when swiping — just hold it close, the response is fastest, and it works even without a network. Some cities' virtual transit cards also offer the same transfer discounts as physical cards.Alipay/WeChat Ride Code

    : Search for "Ride Code" in the app, and activate the bus or subway ride code for your city. The advantage of this solution is: no need to top up — it deducts directly from your balance or linked bank card. But it requires a network connection, and you need to open the app and find the code before swiping.

    I personally recommend using the virtual transit card in your phone wallet. Although you need to top up 10 or 20 yuan the first time, it's really much more convenient to use, especially when rushing for the subway — you don't have to stop to unlock your phone and find the app.

    • 5. Utility Bills, Food Delivery, Ride-HailingWater/Electricity/Gas Bills
    • : In Alipay or WeChat's "Utility Bills", bind your household water, electricity, and gas account numbers. Then each month when you receive a bill, just tap in to pay. The account number can usually be found on your paper bill, or you can call customer service to ask.Food Delivery Price Comparison

    : The same restaurant often has different prices and promotions on Meituan and Ele.me. Check both before placing an order — sometimes you can save several yuan. Also, Meituan's "Pin Hao Fan" feature lets you order together with friends for a noticeably cheaper price.

    Ride-Hailing Safety

    • : In Didi or Amap Ride-Hailing, remember to set up "Emergency Contact" and "Trip Sharing". When you take a ride, the app automatically shares your trip with your designated contacts. Also, for late-night rides, prioritize "Taxi" over "Express" — taxis have industry regulation and a higher safety level.6. Handle Medical Insurance, Social Security, and Government Affairs on Your Phone
    • Things have changed a lot in recent years — many things that used to require queuing at a service hall can now be done in a few minutes on your phone.Electronic Medical Insurance Certificate
    • : Search for "Electronic Medical Insurance Certificate" in Alipay or WeChat. After activation, you can just swipe your phone when seeing a doctor or buying medicine at a pharmacy — no need to carry your physical medical insurance card. The first time requires facial recognition verification, and afterwards a dynamic code is generated each time you use it.Social Security Inquiry

    : Download the "Palm 12333" app or use "Citizen Center" in Alipay to check social security contribution records, pension account balances, unemployment benefit claims, and more.

    Individual Income Tax

    • : The annual tax reconciliation from March to June each year can be handled on the "Individual Income Tax" app. Remember to check if there are any special additional deductions you can claim (children's education, mortgage interest, supporting the elderly, etc.) — these can all help you pay less tax or get a refund.Remember These to Avoid Scams and Stay Safe
    • Police, prosecutors, banks, and customer service will never ask you to transfer money to a "safe account".Anyone who asks you to screenshot your payment code and send it over is a scammer.
    • Don't click unfamiliar links, especially SMS messages like "ETC expired" or "Social security card suspended".Online shopping refunds are returned via the original payment method — no need to provide your bank card number.

    Do It Now: Give Your Payment Apps a Security Checkup

    • Open Alipay and WeChat, confirm that fingerprint/face payment is enabled.
    • Find the "Security Lock" feature and turn it on.
    • Check the "Password-Free Payment / Auto Deduction" list, and turn off services you no longer need.
    • View the "Login Devices" list, and remove any unfamiliar devices.

    Activate your electronic medical insurance certificate, so next time you visit the hospital you won't need to bring the physical card.

    1. Chapter 11: Photography and Photo Management
    2. To be honest, most people's phone photos fall far short of the phone's actual potential. It's not that your skills are bad — it's that you haven't noticed many small settings and habits. This chapter skips the fluff and only covers things you can use right away.
    3. 1. Have You Made These Mistakes Too?
    4. Let's first talk about the most common problems — see how many you've hit:
    5. The lens is dirty

    Chapter 11: Photography and Image Management

    You never adjust exposure

    : In default mode, tapping the screen focuses, but if you swipe up or down after tapping, you can adjust brightness. Many people's photos come out either too dark or too bright simply because they don't know this operation.

    The flash is always on

    • : The effect of a phone's LED flash is really ugly — the light is harsh and cold, making people look like ghosts. Unless it's truly pitch black, turn it off. In low light, Night Mode works far better than the flash.Zooming by pinching with two fingers
    • : Pinch-to-zoom on the screen is digital zoom, which essentially crops and enlarges the image, noticeably reducing quality. If you want to shoot something far away, use the zoom buttons on the viewfinder (0.5x/1x/2x/3x) — these are optical zoom and don't lose quality.2. A Few Small Tips to Immediately Boost Your Hit Rate
    • These don't require any theoretical knowledge — use them once and you'll see the effect:Rule of Thirds + Grid Lines
    • : Turn on "Grid Lines" (also called reference lines) in camera settings. When shooting, place what you want to highlight at the intersections of the four lines, and the composition will immediately "click". This is the simplest and most effective rule in photography — no mysticism, it just matches the visual habits of the human eye.: Pinch-zooming on the screen is digital zoom — essentially cropping and enlarging the image, which noticeably reduces quality. To zoom in on distant subjects, use the zoom buttons in the viewfinder (0.5x/1x/2x/3x). The 0.5x (ultrawide) and 1x (main camera) are native optical lenses with no quality loss; 2x/3x are typically "lossless quality zoom" — achieved by cropping from high-resolution sensors, with near-optical quality but not a separate lens. Beyond 3x is usually hybrid or digital zoom, with noticeable quality degradation.

    : When shooting landscapes or street scenes, notice whether there are natural lines in the frame — roads, railings, walls, a row of trees — and let these lines extend from the edge of the frame to the subject. Use this technique well, and passersby looking at your photos will think you've studied photography.

    Don't always shoot standing up

    • : Most people always shoot at their own eye level, so their photos all have the same perspective. Try crouching down for a low angle, or finding a high spot to shoot downward — the same place can produce a completely different feel. When shooting kids and pets especially, you need to crouch down — only eye-level shots produce a natural feel.Light is the top priority
    • : Shooting portraits under the bright midday sun produces hard, ugly shadows on the face. The best light is during the "golden hours" of early morning and late evening — the sunlight is angled and warm-toned, making everything look good. Overcast-day light isn't flashy, but it's even and soft, making it actually easier to shoot portraits than under bright sun.Night Mode essentials
    • : After turning on Night Mode, the phone automatically takes multiple shots and composites them. The most critical thing at this point is — your hand absolutely cannot shake. Lean against a wall if you can, rest on a table if you can, or hold your breath if you must. Night Mode requires you to hold steady for 2 to 4 seconds — any shake and the image blurs.3. Portrait Mode and Pro Mode
    • Portrait Mode: It produces the effect of a blurred background with a sharp subject (shallow depth of field). Because phones have small lens sizes, their real bokeh capability is limited, so this relies on AI algorithms — simply put, the AI cuts you out and blurs the background. The best results come at a distance of 1-2 meters; too far or too close and the algorithm easily makes mistakes. Also, when shooting portraits, make sure the background doesn't have overly complex lines, or the AI cutout may "fail" around the hair edges.
    • Pro Mode: If you want full control over the image effect, try Pro Mode. A few key parameters to know: the lower the ISO, the cleaner the image quality, but the darker the image; the slower the shutter, the more light comes in, but hand shake causes blur; white balance controls color temperature — set poorly, photos will look blue or yellow. Most people don't need to use Pro Mode year-round, but understanding these parameters at least lets you know what the camera is doing.

    4. Photo Editing: Don't Overdo It — Just Right Is Enough

    • Many people misunderstand photo editing, thinking that editing makes it "unreal". In fact, photos taken by a camera are already different from what the naked eye sees — appropriate adjustment is to restore the scene you saw at the time, not to fake it.Snapseed
    • : A free editing tool from Google, professional features with no ads. My daily editing flow is: first use "Tune Image" to adjust brightness and contrast → use "Details" to sharpen → use "White Balance" to correct color casts → finally "Crop" to the desired composition. Snapseed's "Selective" feature is very useful — you can adjust only a specific area of the image without affecting the whole thing.Xingtu / Meitu

    : These two are suitable for editing portraits. But I think there's a principle: keep beauty filters under 30% — beyond that it looks fake, with skin like plastic. Natural is more beautiful than perfect.

    Lightroom Mobile

    • : If you're particular about color, this is the most professional. It has advanced features like curve adjustment and HSL per-color adjustment. But for most people, it's overkill.Editing Workflow Suggestion
    • : My own habit is to shoot the original photo first, then edit slowly on a computer screen or iPad at home — the phone screen is too small and the color isn't quite accurate. If you must edit on the phone, remember to set the screen brightness to medium-high, and don't edit in power-saving mode.5. Too Many Photos? Organization Strategies
    • Thousands of photos piled up in the phone album, taking forever to find a specific one — everyone has had this experience. Here are a few practical organization methods:Make good use of search
    • : Now both iPhone and most Android phone albums support smart search. You can search for keywords like "cat", "seaside", "ID card", "flowers", and the system will use AI to identify image content and find them for you. You can also search by date and location, like "last May" or "Beijing". Not many people know about this feature, but it's really useful.Regularly clean up junk

    : Screenshots, duplicate photos, blurry failed shots — these are the real culprits taking up space. The iOS album has an automatic "Duplicates" merge feature; on Android, you can search for the "screenshots" folder in the file manager and batch-delete unneeded screenshots. I spend five minutes a month cleaning up and free up several gigabytes.

    Create albums — don't rely solely on default sorting

    • : The system sorting by time is fine, but for cross-time content like "child's growth photos", "travel photos", and "important documents", you should manually create albums to categorize them. Apple's "Shared Albums" can even let family members add photos together — one person creates it, and the whole family can view it.Backup is the bottom line
    • : Photos are the most irreplaceable data — files can be recreated, chat histories can be lost and that's that, but a child's photos or an elderly person's videos, once lost, are truly gone. You must enable cloud backup. iCloud Photos is the most worry-free; on Android, each brand has its own cloud service, or you can use Baidu Netdisk / Aliyun Drive for auto backup. The principle is: have at least one cloud backup — don't put all your eggs in one basket.6. Screenshots and Screen Recording
    • Screenshots: Press the power button + volume up button simultaneously — a universal method for all phones. Many Android phones also support three-finger swipe down screenshots and knuckle double-tap screenshots. Long screenshots (scrolling screenshots) are well-established on Android — after taking one shot, tap the "Scroll" button, and the phone automatically scrolls down and stitches together a long image, suitable for capturing chat histories and web pages.
    • Screen Recording: Add "Screen Recording" from the Control Center, tap once to start recording, tap again to stop. Before recording, long-press the record button to choose whether to record microphone sound — turn on the mic if you're making a tutorial with narration, turn it off if you're just recording operations. The recorded video is automatically saved to the album.

    Practice: Complete a Full Shoot + Edit + Organize on Your Phone

    • Turn on "Grid Lines" in camera settings, find a spot with natural light, and take three photos (remember to wipe the lens and adjust exposure).Select the best one, and use Snapseed for basic adjustments (brightness, contrast, cropping).
    • Create a dedicated album for this photo, named "My Works".Check whether cloud backup is enabled, to ensure the photo has a copy in the cloud.

    Chapter 11 Supplement: Professional Imaging Techniques

    To truly understand the mysteries of phone photography and video, you need to know some professional imaging technology. This knowledge not only helps you better use your phone's camera, but also makes you more discerning when choosing devices.

    1. Resolution, Frame Rate, and Bitrate: The Three Elements of Video Quality

    Resolution:

    Resolution determines image clarity, expressed in pixel count.

    • 720P (HD): 1280×720 pixels, entry-level clarity.
    • 1080P (Full HD): 1920×1080 pixels, currently the most mainstream resolution.
    • 2K (QHD): 2560×1440 pixels, clearer than 1080P.
    • 4K (UHD): 3840×2160 pixels, ultra HD with rich detail.
    • 8K: 7680×4320 pixels, the future standard, currently with limited device support.

    The higher the resolution, the clearer the image, but the larger the file and the higher the demands on storage and processing power.

    Frame Rate:

    Frame rate determines image smoothness, expressed in frames per second (fps).

    • 24fps: The standard cinema frame rate, with a unique "cinematic feel".
    • 30fps: Commonly used for TV and web video, smooth and natural.
    • 60fps: High frame rate, suitable for sports scenes and game recording, very smooth.
    • 120fps/240fps: Ultra-high frame rate, can be used for slow-motion video.

    The higher the frame rate, the smoother the image and the better the slow-motion effect, but the larger the file.

    Bitrate:

    Bitrate determines the data density of video, expressed in data per second (Mbps).

    • The higher the bitrate, the better the image quality and the more detail preserved, but the larger the file.
    • Too low a bitrate causes compression artifacts like mosaic blocks and color banding in the image.
    • Professional video shooting usually requires high bitrate to preserve more room for post-processing.

    2. Video Coding Formats: H.264, H.265, and ProRes

    H.264 (AVC):
    • Characteristics: The most widely used coding format, with excellent compatibility.
    • Pros: Almost all devices can play it, with moderate compression efficiency.
    • Cons: Compared with newer formats, lower compression efficiency and larger files.
    • Applicable scenarios: Web video sharing and everyday shooting for ordinary users.
    H.265 (HEVC):
    • Characteristics: An upgrade to H.264, with about 50% better compression efficiency.
    • Pros: Smaller files at the same quality, supports higher resolutions and frame rates.
    • Cons: Encoding and decoding require a more powerful processor; some older devices are incompatible.
    • Applicable scenarios: 4K video shooting and scenarios with limited storage space.
    Apple ProRes:
    • Characteristics: A professional video codec developed by Apple, with nearly lossless compression.
    • Pros: Extremely high image quality, large room for post-processing, accurate color.
    • Cons: Extremely large files, requiring substantial storage and professional hardware to process.
    • Applicable scenarios: Professional video production and cinema-grade shooting.
    ProRes RAW:
    • Characteristics: Combines the advantages of ProRes and RAW formats.
    • What is RAW: Unprocessed raw sensor data, preserving maximum information.
    • Pros: Huge room for post adjustment—exposure, white balance, and other parameters can be changed without any quality loss.
    • Cons: Extremely huge files, requiring professional post-production software to process.
    • Applicable scenarios: High-end professional production. iPhone 15 Pro series and later support Apple ProRes video recording (up to 4K 60fps), and iPhone 17 Pro further supports ProRes RAW direct in-device recording.

    3. HDR: High Dynamic Range Technology

    HDR (High Dynamic Range) technology preserves detail in both the brightest and darkest parts of the image at the same time.

    • HDR10: The most basic HDR standard, with good compatibility.
    • HDR10+: A standard promoted by Samsung, supporting dynamic metadata.
    • Dolby Vision: The top-tier HDR standard developed by Dolby, with the best image quality, but requires licensing.
    • HLG: Broadcast-grade HDR standard, compatible with ordinary displays.

    When shooting HDR video, you need an HDR-capable display to see the full effect.

    4. Color Space and Color Depth

    Color Space:
    • sRGB: The standard color space, with the best compatibility.
    • Display P3: A wide-gamut standard promoted by Apple, with richer colors.
    • Rec.2020: The standard color space for HDR video, with the widest gamut.
    Color Depth:
    • 8-bit: 16.7 million colors, the standard for ordinary video.
    • 10-bit: 1.07 billion colors, the standard for professional video, with smoother color transitions.
    • 12-bit: 68 billion colors, a high-end professional standard.

    Practical Advice

    • Everyday shooting: 1080P/4K + 30fps + H.265 encoding, balancing quality and file size.
    • Sports shooting: 1080P/4K + 60fps, to ensure smoothness.
    • Professional creation: 4K + ProRes (if supported), to preserve maximum post-production room.
    • Storage advice: High-bitrate video takes up a lot of space — back up to your computer or cloud drive regularly.

    Explore: Your Phone's Video Settings

    1. Open the Camera app and switch to video mode.
    2. View the resolution and frame rate options, and try different combinations.
    3. If supported, check whether there are advanced options like HDR and ProRes.
    4. Shoot a few video clips with different settings, and compare the image quality and file size.

    V. RAW vs HEIF vs JPEG Comparison

    What Is RAW Format:

    RAW format is the "raw data" recorded by the camera sensor — pure, unprocessed original information without any compression. It's like raw ingredients that need post-processing "cooking" to become a finished product. Phones, due to storage and processing limitations, default to "pre-cooked" JPEG or HEIF. RAW must be explicitly enabled.

    RAW vs HEIF vs JPEG Comparison:
    • JPEG: The oldest format, best compatibility (any device can open it). 8-bit color depth, lossy compression, smallest files (2-5MB per photo). Limited post-processing room — forcing detail out of shadows produces banding artifacts.
    • HEIF/HEIC: Apple's newer format, files are half the size of JPEG at the same quality (1-3MB per photo). Supports 10-bit color depth and transparency channel. Drawback: some older devices and Windows require plugins to open.
    • RAW: Uncompressed raw data, largest files (20-100MB per photo). Color depth typically 12-16 bit, maximum post-processing room. Drawback: requires professional software (Lightroom, Snapseed, etc.) to open and process — cannot be shared directly.
    Why Professional Photographers Shoot RAW:
    • Lossless White Balance Adjustment in Post: If white balance is wrong in JPEG (e.g., yellow under tungsten lighting), correcting it in post degrades quality; RAW lets you reset color temperature with zero loss.
    • Greater Exposure Tolerance: In JPEG, shadows underexposed by 2 stops are basically dead black — brightening produces noise. RAW can recover usable detail from shadows underexposed by 3-4 stops. Same applies to overexposure.
    • Richer Shadow and Highlight Detail: RAW's dynamic range far exceeds JPEG — much more latitude for preserving highlights without blowing out and shadows without crushing.
    • Sharpening, Noise Reduction, and Lens Correction All Controllable in Post: In-camera processing is a "one-shot deal." RAW can be adjusted repeatedly, always starting from the original data.
    How to Enable RAW on Phones:
    • iPhone ProRAW: Only iPhone 12 Pro and later Pro models. Go to "Settings → Camera → Formats" and enable "Apple ProRAW." A "RAW" button appears at the top of the camera interface — tap to enable. Files are about 25MB each — enable only when needed.
    • Android Motion Raw / Ultra RAW: Naming varies by brand. Xiaomi/OPPO/vivo flagships have RAW toggle in camera "Pro Mode" or "More"; Huawei enables RAW in "Pro Mode"; Samsung Galaxy S series has RAW option in "Pro" mode. Files are typically 20-50MB.
    • General Advice: No need to enable RAW for casual daily shooting — files are too large and waste space. Only enable for important scenes (landscape, portrait, post-processing needed).

    VI. Computational Photography Principles

    Modern phone photography is inseparable from "computational photography" — using algorithms, not just lenses and sensors, to generate photos. Understanding these core principles helps you understand what your phone does the moment you press the shutter.

    Multi-Frame Fusion:

    When you press the shutter once, the phone actually takes multiple photos. The algorithm aligns and fuses the frames to produce one high-quality image.

    • Night Mode: Takes multiple underexposed photos within 1-3 seconds, aligns and stacks them — noise cancels out, brightness accumulates. The result: clean images even in low light.
    • HDR (High Dynamic Range): Shoots underexposed, normal, and overexposed frames (or more), then composites them into one photo with detail in both highlights and shadows. Especially effective for backlit scenes.
    • Deep Fusion (Apple) / Photonic Engine: For medium-to-low light scenes, analyzes and fuses multiple frames pixel by pixel, focusing on improving texture and detail — sweaters, hair, and similar details become noticeably clearer.
    Semantic Segmentation:

    AI doesn't process the entire image uniformly — it first "understands" what's in the scene — sky, faces, grass, buildings, clothing — then applies different processing strategies to each region.

    • Sky: Selectively enhance blue, reduce brightness to prevent overexposure.
    • Faces: Identifies skin tone areas, selectively brightens and smooths skin, leaving facial features and hair untouched.
    • Grass/Leaves: Enhance green saturation, boost detail sharpening.
    • Background Blur: In Portrait mode, AI identifies the subject's outline, blurring the background while keeping the subject sharp.
    Deep Learning Applications:
    • AI Scene Recognition: The camera automatically recognizes scenes like "food," "pets," "night," "document" and optimizes parameters accordingly. For example, food mode enhances warm tones and saturation to make food look more appetizing.
    • AI Portrait Bokeh: Phone lenses physically can't achieve DSLR-level shallow depth of field. Deep learning models predict subject edges, then blur the background. Latest algorithms correctly handle details like hair strands and glass edges.
    • AI Eraser/AI Outpainting: Select passersby or objects in the frame, and AI "fills in" the occluded areas based on context. This is generative AI applied to imaging.
    Computational vs Optical Photography:
    • Computational Photography Advantages: Good image quality in a small form factor, usable shots in extreme scenes like low light and backlight, and ordinary users can take "good-looking" photos without photography knowledge.
    • Computational Photography Disadvantages: Images can be "over-processed" — excessive sharpening, color distortion, unnatural sky colors; multi-frame fusion creates ghosting when subjects move; detail is "computed" rather than truly recorded.
    • Optical Photography Advantages: Large sensor + wide-aperture lens truly captures light, natural image quality, large post-processing room; no artifacts from algorithmic "hallucination."
    • Trend: Modern flagship phones combine "optical + computational" — large sensors capture real data, algorithms optimize the result. The two aren't opposed.

    VII. Lens Types and Focal Lengths

    Modern flagship phones typically have three to four lenses, each corresponding to a different focal length. Understanding focal lengths helps you choose the right lens for each scenario.

    Common Lenses and Equivalent Focal Lengths:
    • Ultrawide (13-24mm equivalent): Widest field of view, suitable for landscapes, architecture, and interior spaces. Captures expansive scenes, but edges have distortion (straight lines curve), and faces stretch in portraits. Good for "big scenes," not for "close-ups."
    • Main Camera (24-28mm equivalent): The most commonly used lens, best image quality, widest aperture. Balances field of view and quality — works for both people and scenery. The "1x" on most phones is the main camera.
    • Telephoto (70-200mm equivalent): For distant subjects and portrait close-ups. Telephoto compresses spatial perception (distant mountains and nearby people appear closer together), producing more natural facial proportions and background blur in portraits.
    • Periscope Telephoto (200mm+ equivalent): Uses a folded reflective optical path to achieve longer focal lengths within the phone's thickness. Captures clear detail at great distances — suitable for concerts, sports, wildlife. Only on flagship models.
    Sensor Size vs Pixel Size Trade-off:

    The sensor is the "foundation," determining how much light can be captured. The industry says "a bigger sensor crushes the competition" — at the same pixel count, a larger sensor means larger individual pixels, more light intake, and better image quality.

    • Large Sensor: More light intake, better night image quality, wider dynamic range. Disadvantages: phone must be thicker (camera bump), higher cost.
    • High Pixel Count, Small Sensor: In sufficient daylight, high pixel count produces sharper photos, convenient for post-cropping. But in low light, each pixel receives insufficient light, producing more noise.
    • Mainstream Flagship Choices: Main cameras are typically 1/1.3-inch to 1-inch (some models already use 1-inch sensors), around 50MP — the balance point between image quality and size.
    Pixel Binning Technology:

    To balance high pixel count in daylight and large pixels at night, manufacturers use "pixel binning" — merging multiple small pixels into one large pixel for output.

    • Quad Bayer (4-in-1): 50MP sensor outputs 12.5MP photos. Each output pixel is synthesized from 4 adjacent pixels, increasing light intake 4x for cleaner images.
    • Nonacell (9-in-1): Used for 100MP+ sensors, outputs approximately 11-12MP. Same principle, even greater light intake.
    • Practical effect: In default shooting mode, you get the binned low-pixel photo — good quality, small file. When you need maximum detail (e.g., documents, distant subjects), manually switch to "high-resolution mode" for full-resolution output.

    VIII. Special Shooting Modes

    Beyond everyday photography, your phone has several special modes that, when used correctly, can capture shots you normally can't get.

    Panorama Mode:
    • Move the phone slowly and steadily in the direction of the arrow — don't go fast, or stitching misalignment will occur.
    • Keep the phone vertically stable and only pan horizontally. If it bobs up and down, the horizon will become wavy.
    • Use with caution when there are moving people or cars — stitching may produce "half bodies" or "ghosts."
    • Panorama can also be shot vertically — vertical shooting with horizontal stitching, suitable for tall buildings or waterfalls.
    Slow Motion and Time-Lapse:
    • Slow Motion: Shot at 120fps or 240fps high frame rates, played back as slow motion. Great for capturing water droplets, sports moments, and pets jumping. Requires ample light — slow motion mode has shorter exposure time, resulting in poor low-light quality.
    • Time-Lapse: Takes photos at intervals and combines them into a fast-forward video. Great for traffic, cloud movement, sunsets, and flower blooming. Shooting can take minutes to hours — always use a tripod to secure the phone; handheld shots will be blurry.
    • Tip: For time-lapse cloud photography, set up the phone and shoot for 15-30 minutes. The result is about 10 seconds of stunning time-lapse footage.
    Starry Sky / Astronomy Mode:
    • You need to get away from urban light pollution — find a rural area or mountain with no streetlight interference at all. You can't capture the Milky Way in the city.
    • A tripod is mandatory — handheld shots will be blurry. The phone must be held steady for several seconds to tens of seconds.
    • Weather should be clear and cloudless, with the moon not too large (a full moon will overwhelm starlight). Dark nights around the beginning or end of the lunar month are best.
    • iPhone's "Night Mode" automatically detects starry skies and extends exposure time (up to 30 seconds); Android flagships' "Star Mode" or "Astronomy Mode" works similarly. Be patient — don't move the phone after pressing the shutter.
    Macro Mode:
    • Used for photographing flowers, insects, jewelry, text close-ups, and other small objects. Can focus as close as 1-2 centimeters.
    • Some phones have a dedicated macro lens (usually a 2MP or 5MP small-sensor lens) with average quality; flagship phones use the ultra-wide lens to double as macro, producing better quality.
    • When shooting up close, the lens is very near the subject and may block light — use a desk lamp or flashlight to supplement lighting if needed.
    • The focus distance is extremely close, creating a very shallow depth of field — moving the subject a few millimeters forward or back can cause focus loss. Keep your hands steady and ideally have the subject stay still.

    Practical Tips for Still Photography

    • Daily shooting: HEIF/JPEG default is fine — small file size and adequate quality.
    • Important scenes (landscape, portrait, post-processing needed): Enable RAW to preserve maximum post-processing flexibility.
    • Choose the right lens: ultra-wide for landscapes, telephoto for portraits, main camera for everyday use.
    • Night scenes and starry skies: Always secure the phone and enable Night Mode or Astronomy Mode.
    • Phones with large sensors (e.g., 1-inch sensor models) have higher quality ceilings, but shooting technique remains the key.

    Try It Yourself: Understand Your Camera's Capabilities

    1. Check if your phone supports RAW shooting (Settings → Camera → Format). Try enabling it and take a shot, then compare the JPEG and RAW file sizes of the same scene.
    2. Switch between the ultrawide, main camera, and telephoto focal lengths and shoot the same distant scene with each, to feel the differences in perspective and quality.
    3. Find a scene with Night Mode or Starry Sky Mode, secure the phone, and take a night photo.
    4. Try shooting a wide scene in Panorama Mode, keeping the phone moving smoothly and steadily.

    QQ Music

If you care about "being able to find every song you want to listen to", QQ Music is the most reliable choice.

    Apple Music

    • : The first choice for Apple users. Clean interface, no ads, good sound quality, and supports lossless and Dolby Atmos.     • : If you use Bluetooth headphones, check the music app settings for "Sound Effects" or "Equalizer" — slightly adjust the bass and treble for a noticeable improvement. Also, streaming music uses a lot of data — remember to turn on "Play lossless only on Wi-Fi" in settings, or download your favorite playlists in advance for offline listening.2. Podcasts: The "Ear Companion" on Your Commute
    • Podcasts — people who haven't listened think they have nothing to do with them, but once they start, there's no going back. Essentially, it's "the Netflix version of radio shows" — some talk tech, some discuss history, some read stories — whatever type you want, it's there.Xiaoyuzhou App

    Listening tips

    • : Most podcast apps support 1.2x or 1.5x playback speed — once you're used to it, you can save a lot of time. I usually listen to Chinese at 1.2x and English at 1.5x. Also, definitely turn on "Auto-download new episodes" and "Auto-delete after playing", so your phone won't pile up with audio files you've already heard.3. Watching Video: The Right Way to Open Players and Streaming
    • Many people don't know that the formats a phone can play are far more than what streaming apps offer. A good local player can solve many problems.VLC Player
    • : Open source and free, can play almost any format — MKV, AVI, FLAC, even ISO disc images. If you downloaded a video that plays on your computer but not on your phone, it's most likely a format issue — install VLC and it's solved. It also supports external subtitles — put the .srt subtitle file and the video in the same folder, and VLC will auto-load it.nPlayer

    : If you want a more refined experience, this paid app is worth buying.     Bilibili (B Site)

    • : No longer just an ACG site — the learning resources on it are now absurdly abundant. Postgraduate exam prep, programming, photography, cooking — tutorials on everything. However, when watching educational videos, it's recommended to turn off danmaku, otherwise it's easy to get distracted.Casting to TV
    • : No matter how big your phone screen is, it's not as comfortable as a TV. On the same Wi-Fi, open the "TV" cast button in the upper-right corner of the video app to cast the image to your TV. Most smart TVs and projectors support it — the experience of watching shows and movies is so much better. iPhone users can also use AirPlay to directly mirror the entire screen.4. E-Book Reading: You Can Read Well on a Phone Too
    • Some say reading on a phone hurts the eyes and is distracting — these points are indeed valid. But the advantages of phone reading are also obvious — anytime, anywhere, maximizing the use of fragmented time. I've read quite a few books on my phone — on the subway, while queuing, before bed.WeChat Reading
    • : Currently the best reading app experience in China. The library is very comprehensive, with both published books and web novels. It uses a "reading time for book coins" model — the more you read, the more free books you can exchange for, which is very friendly to students. Its "Underline" feature lets you see which passages others have marked — sometimes seeing good sentences highlighted by others really resonates. However, the "Reading Leaderboard" thing is a bit competitive, easily turning into "reading just to rack up hours" — I suggest turning it off.Kindle App

    : If you have a Kindle device, the phone Kindle app can sync your reading progress. Genuine Kindle e-books have much better layout quality than pirated PDFs, but the Kindle China store has closed, so you need to switch to an overseas region.

    Apple Books

    • : Built into iPhone, suitable for reading EPUB and PDF. Minimalist interface, very comfortable page-turning animation. If you download an e-book file from the internet, just "Share to Books" to import it.Reading Settings Advice
    • : No matter which app you use, be sure to set the background to a warm yellow tone (eye-care mode), increase the font size, and widen the line spacing. When reading at night, turn on "Dark Mode" — white text on black is much easier on the eyes. Never read with white background, black text, and small fonts in low light for too long — eye fatigue accumulates.5. Mobile Gaming: Play Well, Without Harming Your Phone
    • My attitude toward mobile gaming is: playing is fine, but don't let it control you in return. Use gaming tools wisely to play more comfortably without delaying your real business.Game Mode / Game Space
    • : Mainstream phones now all have this feature. When turned on, the phone automatically clears background apps, blocks notifications, and prevents accidental touches — if you're in the middle of a team battle and a phone call suddenly pops up, Game Mode can block it for you. Some phones also support Performance Mode / E-sports Mode, forcing the processor to run at full speed, but at the cost of faster heating and battery drain.How to adjust image quality and frame rate

    : Don't just max everything out. First ensure frame rate (smoothness), then pursue image quality. 60 fps is much smoother than 30 fps, but 120 fps puts a lot of pressure on the phone — mid-range phones shouldn't force it. If you play competitive games (like Honor of Kings or PUBG Mobile), frame rate priority is far more important than image quality — smooth control feel is a hundred times more important than pretty grass textures.

    What to do when your phone heats up while gaming

    • : This is normal, but prolonged high temperatures will damage battery life. A few cooling methods: remove the phone case for better heat dissipation; lower screen brightness to around 70% (brightness is a major heat source); don't charge and play games at the same time (compounded heating kills the battery fast). If the phone gets too hot to hold, exit the game immediately and let it rest for a while.Anti-addiction tools
    • : iOS "Screen Time" and Android "Digital Wellbeing" both let you set daily time limits for game apps. I set myself a maximum of one hour on weekdays and two hours on weekends. When the time is up, the app icon turns gray and can't be opened. This limit is genuinely useful, not just for show.Cloud Gaming
    • : If your phone isn't powerful enough but you want to play big titles, you can try cloud gaming platforms (like Tencent START Cloud Gaming or NetEase Cloud Gaming). The game runs on a remote server, and the image is streamed to your phone as video. It demands a lot from your network but almost nothing from your phone's performance. The downside is that latency is unavoidable — suitable for strategy and RPG games, not for FPS shooters.Get Hands-On: Build Your Mobile Entertainment System
    • In your music app, download your 3 favorite albums or playlists to ensure offline listening.Subscribe to 3 channels of interest on Xiaoyuzhou or Apple Podcasts, and download an episode to try.
    • Install VLC Player, and try using it to play a video file copied from your computer.Find a book you want to read in WeChat Reading, set a warm background and eye-care mode, and adjust the font to a comfortable size.

    If you play games, open Game Mode and see what settings you can optimize (do-not-disturb, frame rate priority, etc.).
