    1. Productivity: Manage your time and attention

    Productivity apps are the "backbone" of digital life. They help you organize scattered ideas, tasks, and files. Picks by scenario below.

    1. To-do lists (task management)
    • TickTick. Best for: People who want work, life, and study tasks plus a calendar in one place. A top pick in this section. Highlights: Sync across phone/PC/tablet/web; to-dos + calendar + Pomodoro in one; natural language like "meeting tomorrow at 3pm" or "weekly report every Monday" auto-parses times and repeats; supports subtasks, tags, priorities, attachments, and shared lists. Great for "schedule + daily check-ins + review" in one flow.
    • Getting more out of TickTick:
    • Calendar view: Drag meetings and deadlines onto the calendar to spot conflicts at a glance — more intuitive than a plain list.
    • Recurring tasks: Set meds, bills, and workouts as repeating rules instead of retyping every time.
    • Pomodoro: Start focus sessions on a task and see how much you actually finished this week.
    • Phone integration: Say "remind me…" to your voice assistant to create system reminders. Double up important deadlines in the system calendar too.
  • Todoist. Best for: Minimalists who work across platforms. Highlights: Clean, restrained interface; clear hierarchy (task → subtask → sub-subtask); karma points that nudge good habits.
  • Microsoft To Do. Best for: Office workers and Outlook users. Highlights: Completely free, no ads; "My Day" clears each morning and eases mental load; deep Microsoft ecosystem integration.
  • System Notes/Reminders. Best for: Light users who'd rather not install third-party apps. Highlights: Native experience, zero lag, add via Siri/Xiao AI, works with system widgets.
    • 2. Pomodoro (focus training)
    • Forest. Best for: People who can't keep their hands off their phone. Highlights: Grow a tree while you focus; leave the app early and the tree dies. Virtual life as positive feedback; plant together with friends.
    • Tide. Best for: People who need white noise to focus or fall asleep. Highlights: Nature sounds (rain, waves, forest) + Pomodoro + meditation in one. Calm, healing, minimal interface.
    • The rule of thumb: Classic 25 minutes focus + 5 minutes break. Adjust to 50/10 or 90/20 to match your energy.
    3. Calendars (visualize your time)
    • System calendar. Best for: Everyone. Highlights: Most reliable native alerts, very low battery use, add via Siri/Xiao AI.
    • Google Calendar. Best for: Multi-device users and shared schedules. Highlights: "Goals" auto-schedules fitness/study time; Gmail smartly pulls events from email.
    4. Notes (capture knowledge)
    • Notion. Best for: People who want notes, tasks, databases, and wikis in one place — students, freelancers, teams. Highlights: All-in-one knowledge base with block editing; build homepages, reading lists, project boards; rich template ecosystem.
    • Obsidian. Best for: Serious knowledge workers, researchers, writers. Highlights: Local Markdown storage, backlinks + graph view — let your notes form a "second brain." Your data is fully yours.
    • flomo. Best for: Capturing quick ideas without writing long essays. Highlights: Card-style notes, as easy as posting a social update; # tags for grouping; browse by timeline.
    • Apple Notes. Best for: iPhone/Mac users with light note-taking needs. Highlights: Fast launch; scans documents, sketches, checklists; iCloud sync. Free and deeply integrated.
    • Evernote. Best for: Power users who clip lots of web pages and archive materials. Highlights: Powerful web clipper, OCR for text in images; long-standing and stable — but Premium is paid.
    5. PDF tools
    • PDF Expert. Best for: iPad/iPhone users, professionals annotating contracts, students. Highlights: Widely considered the best PDF editor on iOS — smooth markup, signing, merge/split, form filling.
    • WPS. Best for: Office users juggling Word/Excel/PPT/PDF. Highlights: One-stop office suite, plays well with Chinese cloud drives and WeChat files; free tier is plenty for daily use.
    • Adobe Acrobat. Best for: People who need strict PDF compliance (legal, design, publishing). Highlights: Official standard, reliable PDF/A conversion, professional cross-device sync and e-signatures.
    6. Scanning (digitize paper)

    Paper contracts, receipts, homework, whiteboard notes, ID copies… your phone camera can replace most scanners. Core flow: Shoot clearly → auto crop & perspective fix → export PDF/image → optional OCR.

    • CamScanner. Best for: Business people and students who often scan contracts, receipts, and IDs. Highlights: Auto edge detection, perspective correction, OCR; multi-page PDFs with cloud sync.
    • Microsoft Lens. Best for: Students who need whiteboards/pages as Word docs. Highlights: Free, no ads, one-tap export to OneNote/Word, accurate text recognition.
    • Apple Notes scanning. Best for: iPhone users with light scanning needs. Highlights: No extra app — tap the camera icon in Notes; auto shadow removal, sign and markup. Free and solid.
    • Baimiao / CamScanner web / brand camera "Document Scan": Huawei, Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo cameras mostly include a Documents/Scan mode. Android can also use Google Camera or the system scanner. Handy for snapping a one-page contract in a hurry.
    • Shooting tips: Even lighting, keep the phone parallel to the page, aim at all four corners. For multi-page docs, shoot in order then merge to PDF. Watermark sensitive IDs and watch where you store them; clear them from "Recently Deleted" when done.

    2. Health and fitness

    Health apps are the phone's most underrated "personal assistant." They track sleep, heart rate, and activity continuously — reflecting long-term trends better than the occasional hospital visit.

    1. Workouts
    • Keep. Best for: Home workouts, total beginners, fat loss and toning. Highlights: Huge free course library from HIIT to yoga; AI builds your training plan; lively community.
    • Nike Training Club (NTC). Best for: People who want professional coaching and structured training. Highlights: Official Nike app, all courses free, demos by real coaches, organized by muscle group/equipment.
    • Apple Fitness. Best for: Apple Watch users who want ring-based motivation. Highlights: Three daily activity rings (Move/Exercise/Stand), visual goals, seamless heart-rate data from the watch.
    2. Sleep tracking
    • AutoSleep. Best for: Apple Watch users who want deep/light sleep breakdowns. Highlights: Tracks automatically while you sleep with the watch on — no start/stop; quality score and bedtime tips.
    • Sleep Cycle. Best for: People who sleep without a watch and want phone-based tracking. Highlights: Uses the mic to analyze movement and snoring; smart alarm in light sleep so waking up hurts less.
    • Mi Fitness. Best for: Xiaomi Band/watch users. Highlights: Free and tightly integrated with Xiaomi bands; heart rate, SpO2, and sleep in one; great value.
    3. Meditation and relaxation
    • Calm. Best for: Stressed professionals and people who struggle to fall asleep. Highlights: "Daily Calm" guided meditations + Sleep Stories (celebrity narrators); beautiful interface; rich English content.
    • Tide. Best for: Chinese-speaking users who need white noise to focus or sleep. Highlights: Polished domestic app — nature sounds + meditation courses + Pomodoro; friendly Chinese guidance.
    • Little Sleep. Best for: People who need sleep sounds and want to record sleep talk/snoring. Highlights: Stackable white noise (rain + fan + campfire), sleep timer; sleep-talk recordings that are fun and useful.
    4. Women's health
    • Flo. Best for: Cycle tracking, trying to conceive, and women's health. Highlights: Accurate AI predictions for periods/ovulation; anonymous community Q&A; polished design.
    • Meiyou. Best for: Users in China who want Chinese community content and education. Highlights: Rich local content tailored by stage — period/TTC/pregnancy/parenting.
    5. Medication reminders
    • Medication Assistant. Best for: People on long-term meds and adult children managing parents' medicine. Highlights: Scan to ID drugs, auto-build a med list, pop-up reminders, share adherence logs with family.
    6. Data hubs
    • Apple Health / Google Fit. Best for: All smartphone users. Highlights: Aggregates data from your phone, band, and third-party health apps (steps, heart rate, sleep, cycles) into one "health record center."

    3. Travel and getting around

    On the road, a few good apps save you from countless headaches. Picks by stage of the trip below.

    1. Flights and trains
    • Umetrip. Best for: Frequent flyers. Highlights: Official CAAC data — most authoritative flight status, gate changes, delay alerts; aircraft type and seat maps.
    • 12306. Best for: Anyone taking trains in China. Highlights: The only official ticket channel; waitlist purchases (auto-buys when someone refunds); easy student/group tickets.
    • VariFlight. Best for: People sensitive to delays and those doing airport pickups. Highlights: Accurate delay predictions; share your trip so family can watch your location and ETA.
    2. Maps and navigation
    • Amap (Gaode). Best for: City users in China, drivers and ride-hailing. Highlights: Accurate live traffic, great at avoiding jams; ride-hailing one-stop; rich transit transfer options.
    • Baidu Maps. Best for: People who need detailed POIs and indoor navigation. Highlights: Street View/AR navigation; detailed indoor maps for malls and attractions; fun voice packs.
    • Google Maps. Best for: International travelers. Highlights: Best global coverage, honest local reviews; Street View and offline maps are lifesavers abroad.
    3. Translation
    • Google Translate. Best for: Travelers and cross-language learners. Highlights: "Conversation" real-time two-way translation and camera instant lookup — travel essentials; offline language packs supported.
    4. Currency conversion
    • Minimalist Currency. Best for: Travel, overseas shopping, cross-border buys. Highlights: Ultra-clean interface, 160+ currencies, live rates, multi-currency compare; long-press a number to convert quickly.
    5. Weather
    • System Weather / China Weather. Best for: Everyone — the first stop for forecasts and official alerts. Highlights: OEM weather apps and official channels like "China Weather" push rainstorm, typhoon, and heat alerts as banners/notifications. Authoritative.
    • Caiyun Weather. Best for: People who need minute-level rain forecasts. Highlights: Industry-leading "will it rain in the next two hours" accuracy; animated rain map; proactive alerts before rain starts.
    • Carrot Weather. Best for: Weather fans who want fun and rich widgets. Highlights: Snarky AI voice reports, tons of custom widgets, pro radar. Paid version unlocks more.
    • Alert essentials: Weather apps need notification permission to deliver alerts. Alerts come in blue, yellow, orange, and red; red means the highest risk of severe weather — adjust your plans. See Section 7 of this chapter for more setup tips ("Weather alerts / disaster alerts / earthquake alerts").
    6. Travel guides
    • Mafengwo. Best for: Detailed planners, road trips, deep travel. Highlights: Rich user trip reports; thorough destination tips/routes/what to avoid; downloadable offline guides.
    • Xiaohongshu (RED). Best for: Young travelers hunting real experiences, hidden spots, and food. Highlights: Visual posts and short videos; fast-updating "3 days in XX city" guides; great search.

    4. Automation for beginners

    Automation is leverage: configure once, save effort for a long time — compressing dozens of daily taps to zero. This section is just a concept intro; see Chapter 23, "Computational Thinking and Automation," for details.

    • iOS Shortcuts: Apple's official automation tool. No coding needed — chain actions like "when I get home: turn on Wi-Fi + dim the screen + read the weather" with one tap.
    • Android automation: Built-in scene tools (like Xiaomi "Automations" or Huawei "Smart Scene") are the easiest to start with. Tasker is powerful but has a steep learning curve — better for tinkerers.
    • Core idea: First spot the things you repeat every day, then ask "can one trigger + several actions replace this?" For detailed examples and advanced tricks, see Chapter 23.

    5. Browsers and search engines: Your gateway to information

    A browser is your window to the internet; a search engine is your compass in the sea of information. Use them well and you'll avoid a lot of detours.

    How a browser works:

    When you type a web address, the browser: ① asks a DNS server for the IP behind the domain; ② sends an HTTP/HTTPS request to that server; ③ the server returns page code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript); ④ the browser parses and renders it into the page you see.

    Recommended browsers:
    • Microsoft Edge: Chromium-based, fast and compatible. Built-in Copilot AI can summarize pages, translate, and chat. Cross-device sync. Strong personal recommendation as a main browser.
    • Safari: Apple's default browser, deeply integrated and power-efficient. Good privacy, but fewer extensions.
    • Chrome: Most widely used worldwide, with a huge extension library. But it's memory-hungry and drains phone batteries faster.
    Choosing a search engine:
    • Bing: Microsoft's search engine, tightly integrated with Edge. AI summaries give answers, not just links — very efficient. Image search is solid too.
    • Yandex: Russia's largest search engine, strong at image search and reverse image search. Great for finding similar images or identifying objects.
    • Baidu: The main option for searching in China, but it shows a lot of ads — you need a critical eye.
    • Google: The most precise search engine globally, but it needs special network access inside China.
    Guide to efficient research:
    • Use AI search: Bing's AI summaries and Edge's Copilot can answer questions directly and pull key facts out of huge result lists — much faster than clicking link after link.
    • Spot ads and false info: Results marked "Ad" or "Sponsored" are paid placements, not organic. Check the source's authority and prefer official sites and known media.
    • Download apps safely: Search "app name + official site," like "WeChat official site," and click results with the official domain. Avoid third-party download sites — they often bundle junkware.
    • Spotting the real official site: For Windows 11 go to microsoft.com; for Chrome go to google.com. Matching the domain to the brand is the most basic check.
    Website domain basics:

    A domain is a site's "street address." Reading it helps you judge what a site is and where it comes from:

    • Common suffixes:
    • .cn — China's country domain
    • .org — Nonprofit organizations
    • .net — Network service providers
    • .edu — Educational institutions
    • .gov — Government agencies
    • .xyz/.tech/.info — Newer generic domains, cheap to get, use caution
  • Country/region domains:
  • .kr — Korea
  • .uk — United Kingdom
  • .de — Germany
  • .tw — Taiwan
  • .hk — Hong Kong
  • Safety tip: .gov and .edu sites are usually more trustworthy because registration is strict. Cheap domains like .xyz and .top are easy for phishing sites to grab — stay alert.
    • Ad blocking:
    • AdGuard. Best for: Anyone annoyed by pop-ups, banner ads, and in-app ads. Highlights: System-wide ad blocking (not just the browser), filters in-app banners and splash tracking, saves data, speeds up pages. Paid version covers all devices.
    Privacy browsers:
    • Brave. Best for: Everyday browsers who care about privacy and hate ad tracking. Highlights: Chromium-based, blocks ads and trackers out of the box, built-in Tor private windows, faster and lighter than Chrome.
    • DuckDuckGo. Best for: People who don't want one search to follow them everywhere with ads. Highlights: Built-in search engine (no search history), one-tap "Fire Button" clears all traces, consistent cross-platform experience.
    Browser comparison:
    Browser Highlights Best for
    Microsoft Edge Chromium + built-in Copilot AI: summarize pages, translate, chat Productivity-focused office users, heavy AI users (recommended main browser)
    Safari Deep Apple integration, power-efficient, strong privacy iPhone/Mac users who care about battery and system integration
    Chrome Most widely used globally, richest extension ecosystem Power users who need many extensions, cross-device sync fans
    Brave Blocks ads and trackers out of the box, faster Privacy-minded users who want ad blocking without installing add-ons
    DuckDuckGo Search engine keeps no history; one tap clears traces Privacy-sensitive users who don't want personalized tracking

    Try building a "wind down before bed" automation

    1. Create a trigger: a set time (say 22:30).
    2. Add actions: lower volume > turn on Do Not Disturb > play a chill playlist > dim the screen.
    3. Save and test.

    6. Useful system tools: Cleanup, spam blocking, and safety

    Beyond productivity and health apps, daily life often comes down to three things: fewer interruptions, enough storage, and keeping scammers out. This section first covers handy utilities, then zooms in on built-in phone spam blocking — many people own a phone for years and never flip these switches on.

    1. System cleanup and storage
    • Qingzhuo. Best for: Android users who want a lightweight way to clear cache, leftover files, and empty folders without a bloated "phone manager" suite. Highlights: Tiny, no ads; deep scan for leftovers, large-file finder, storage breakdown. More restrained than commercial "one-tap boosters" — good for hands-on users doing regular maintenance. Note: Check paths before cleaning. Don't blindly select WeChat, gallery, or document folders. Prefer the brand's built-in storage cleaner for system caches; treat third-party tools as supplements.
    • Built-in storage cleaner. Best for: Everyone, especially older users and people who want zero hassle. Highlights: Android [Settings] > [Storage] > [Clean up]; iOS [Settings] > [General] > [iPhone Storage]. The system knows its own app cache structure best and is least likely to delete something important. Make this your first choice.
    • WeChat/QQ built-in storage tools. Best for: Heavy chatters. Highlights: WeChat [Me] > [Settings] > [General] > [Storage] — clean by chat or file type. Safer than outside "WeChat cleaner" apps.
    • Rule of thumb: If the system or app has a built-in option, use that instead of a third party. If you can select by path or type, avoid "clean everything." The goal is freeing space — not wiping important data along with it.
    2. Anti-spam and safety utilities
    • National Anti-Fraud Center. Best for: Everyone — especially parents, finance-related jobs, and people who shop online or take unknown calls often. Highlights: Official app; call warnings, SMS risk tips, suspicious URL checks. Linked to police anti-fraud databases — the most official layer of the "three lines of defense."
    • Brand security centers / phone managers. Best for: Users of that brand. Highlights: Huawei Phone Manager, Xiaomi Security Center, OPPO Phone Manager, vivo Phone Manager, and so on. Bundle spam blocking, virus scans, permission management, and payment protection. Usually free and better integrated with the system — don't install a second commercial security suite on top and cause permission clashes.
    • Carrier spam blocking. Best for: People bombed by robocalls and AI voice calls. Highlights: China Mobile: text KTFSR to 10086. China Telecom: follow "Tianyi Anti-Harassment." China Unicom: set up in "Unicom Mobile Manager." Blocking happens on the carrier side, so calls never ring — a batch of spam numbers gets stopped before they reach you.
    • AdGuard. Best for: Anyone annoyed by pop-ups, banner ads, and in-app ads. Highlights: System-wide ad blocking (not just the browser), filters in-app banners and splash tracking, saves data, speeds up pages. Paid version covers all devices.
    • Be careful with "cleaner / spam blocker" all-in-one suites: Some third-party managers sit in the background and keep asking for contacts and SMS permissions. Their blocking may be no better than the system's, and they burn battery and raise privacy risks. Prefer built-in features first, then the official anti-fraud app.

    How to pick utility apps

    • System first: For blocking, cleanup, and permissions, turn on the phone's built-in switches first.
    • Official extras: The National Anti-Fraud Center and carrier spam blocking are official channels you can layer on.
    • Go easy on third parties: One app per job is enough. Avoid permission fights and background resource grabs.
    • Less is more: The more tools you install, the bigger the notification and permission surface — and the more "the tools themselves" interrupt you.
    3. Built-in spam blocking: How to turn it on by brand

    Entries by brand below. Names may vary slightly by system version — search Settings for "spam," "block," or "unknown callers." This pairs with Chapter 8 on spam calls: that chapter covers number labeling and mislabel appeals; this one focuses on where the switches live.

    Platform Where to find it Recommended switches
    iPhone / iOS [Settings] > [Phone] / [Messages] Silence Unknown Callers; Blocked Contacts; "Filter Unknown Senders" in Messages
    Xiaomi / Redmi Phone app > Settings > Spam blocking; or Security app Smart blocking, block one-ring hangs, SMS keyword filter
    Huawei / Honor Phone > Spam blocking; Phone Manager > Spam blocking Caller ID, blacklist, smart SMS blocking
    OPPO / realme / OnePlus Phone app > Spam blocking; or This phone > Spam blocking Call blocking, scam call detection, SMS filter rules
    vivo / iQOO Phone > Spam call blocking; i Manager Spam blocking, scam call warnings, message filtering
    Samsung Phone > Settings > Block numbers / Caller ID and spam protection Block unknown numbers, spam call ID (varies by region)

    Layering three lines of defense

    Everyday setup: "system blocking + carrier spam blocking + National Anti-Fraud Center." The system handles labels and blacklists; the carrier stops robocalls on the network; the anti-fraud app adds official warnings. You don't need max settings on all three — or you'll block couriers, food delivery, and your doctor. Whitelist contacts and recent calls.

    Hands-on: Turn on spam blocking today

    1. Open Phone app settings, find "Spam blocking / Silence Unknown Callers," and turn on smart blocking.
    2. Do the same on your parents' phones: same path + enable carrier spam blocking (China Mobile: text KTFSR to 10086).
    3. Install "National Anti-Fraud Center" from the app store, sign up, and turn on call warnings.
    4. Call a known spam test number (or check the block log) to confirm it works.

    7. Weather alerts, disaster warnings, and earthquake early warnings

    Spam blocking stops phone scams; early warnings stop natural disasters and extreme weather. Many people install a weather app just for the temperature, but never turn on notifications or earthquake warnings. In the seconds to tens of seconds before a red rainstorm alert, typhoon, or quake, your phone could buy you precious time to get to safety.

    1. Weather alerts: Rainstorms, typhoons, heat
    • Official channels first: Alerts from the China Meteorological Administration, National Meteorological Center, and provincial bureaus are the most authoritative. Follow the "China Weather" WeChat account and Weibo, or install official apps like "China Weather."
    • System weather apps: Huawei Weather, Mi Weather, OPPO Weather, vivo Weather, Apple Weather, and others usually push local observatory alerts. Open the weather app settings and make sure "Severe weather alerts" notifications are on.
    • Minute-level rain apps like Caiyun Weather: Handy before commuting or school pickup to decide "umbrella or not in the next 30 minutes." For official warnings, still rely on the meteorological authority.
    • Alert colors (general):
    • Yellow: Be extra careful; cut unnecessary outdoor activity.
    • Orange: Serious. Stay indoors if you can and keep away from danger zones.
    • Red: Extremely serious. Follow closures and evacuation guidance. Don't push through flooded roads, flash-flood areas, or high-wind zones.
  • Common alert types: rainstorm, blizzard, typhoon, heat wave, cold snap, gale, lightning, hail, icy roads, fog, drought, geological hazard risk.
    • 2. Natural disaster warnings: Not just "rain"
    • Who issues them: Weather bureaus handle meteorological alerts. Geological hazards and flash floods are often issued jointly by natural resources, water resources, and emergency management departments. Local governments also push via emergency radio, SMS, and 12379.
    • Get warnings on multiple channels:
    • Follow local "Emergency Management" and "Weather Bureau" accounts on WeChat.
    • 12379 national alert channels (SMS/services, depending on your region).
    • TV, emergency radio, village/community loudspeakers — in mountains or flood season, don't rely on your phone alone.
  • Outdoors and travel tips: In a typhoon, stay away from billboards and trees. In heavy rain, avoid underground garages, tunnels, and underpasses. In mountain areas, if a "geological hazard weather risk" alert is issued, leave steep slopes and valleys immediately.
  • Pair with the emergency handbook: For post-disaster contact loss, dead phones, or location-based rescue calls, see Chapter 32 (earthquake/disaster scenarios) and Chapter 7 (satellite messaging without a network).
    • 3. Earthquake early warning: Not the same as "earthquake prediction"

    Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) pushes an alert seconds to tens of seconds before damaging waves (especially S-waves) reach you. It uses the fact that radio waves beat seismic waves and stations detect P-waves first. It cannot predict whether a quake will happen, but it can buy time to "take cover nearby, cut fire sources, get out of elevators." Closer to the epicenter, the warning window shrinks — sometimes to nothing.

    • Official and industry options: In mainland China, common sources include capabilities tied to the China Earthquake Networks Center and services promoted by groups like the Institute of Care-Life (Chengdu). Some phones ship with or can receive these warnings online.
    • Third-party apps: Search the app store for "earthquake warning" apps from official or research bodies. Check the developer before installing — avoid fake "quake predictor" apps that demand a pile of unrelated permissions.
    • What to do when an alert sounds: Indoors, take cover nearby (under a table, inside corners of load-bearing walls, next to sturdy furniture) and protect your head and neck. Stay away from windows, exterior walls, and tall furniture. Don't blindly rush the stairs or jump. If you're in a lift, get off at the nearest floor. Outdoors, move to open ground away from power lines, billboards, and unstable buildings. After the shaking, check gas and wiring and watch for aftershocks.
    • Don't silence it: Earthquake alerts should be allowed to break through silent/Do Not Disturb. Keep your phone within reach at night, and don't set the ringer to zero.
    4. Built-in earthquake warnings: How to enable by brand

    Entries below may vary by system version. Search Settings for "earthquake," "early warning," or "safety alert." iOS has limited built-in support for warnings in China — you'll usually need a reliable third-party app with location and notification permissions.

    Platform Common path Notes
    Xiaomi / Redmi Phone Manager / Security > Earthquake warning; or search "earthquake" in Settings Some versions include a built-in warning service; needs internet and location
    Huawei / Honor Settings > Safety > Emergency alerts / Earthquake warning May be named "Emergency alerts" and cover earthquakes among others
    OPPO / realme / OnePlus Settings > Safety (SOS emergency) > Earthquake warning Depends on model and regional service coverage
    vivo / iQOO Weather app or Settings > Safety/More > Earthquake warning Follow the menus on your actual system version
    iPhone / iOS Often no full built-in switch; install a reliable earthquake warning app and allow notifications App needs background run and location; don't block its alerts in Do Not Disturb
    Samsung, etc. Settings > Safety and emergency / Wireless emergency alerts "Emergency alerts" coverage varies by region and carrier

    Common myths about earthquake early warning

    • Warning ≠ prediction: It can't tell you "will there be a quake tomorrow." It only alerts after a quake starts and before the waves arrive.
    • You don't always get many seconds: Near the epicenter you may get only a few seconds — or none. Warnings mainly help surrounding areas.
    • Mute it and it's useless: Even the best warning fails if it's silenced, killed in the background, or denied location.
    • Bogus apps: Be wary of "earthquake predictor" apps that want contacts and SMS. Prefer built-in system options or reputable institutional apps.

    Putting warnings together

    Daily setup: "system weather alerts + official weather/emergency channels + earthquake warning (system or trusted app)." Like spam blocking, you don't need a pile of similar apps. What matters: notifications on, location allowed, and alerts that can break through Do Not Disturb. After you finish spam blocking on your parents' phones, check their weather and earthquake alerts too.

    Hands-on: 10-minute warning settings check

    1. Open the system weather app, go to settings, and turn on "Severe weather alerts" notifications.
    2. Search Settings for "earthquake" or "warning" and enable earthquake/emergency alerts (Android). On iPhone, install a trusted earthquake warning app and allow notifications.
    3. Follow your local weather bureau or emergency management account on WeChat and allow its pushes.
    4. Confirm alerts can still sound with Do Not Disturb on. Repeat the check on your parents' phones.

    8. Cross-device teamwork: Remote control, fast transfer, account safety

    A phone feels smooth when it teams up with your computer and tablet. This section adds high-frequency tools: remote-control your PC from a phone, AI office work and remote collaboration, live wallpapers, LAN file transfer, cross-device clipboard, authenticator 2FA, and linking paper scanning with schedules. For systematic multi-device setups, see Chapter 17.

    1. Control your computer from a phone: Sunlogin / ToDesk
    • Sunlogin Remote Control. Best for: People who need to operate a home/office Windows or Mac while out — also popular for helping parents fix phones remotely (see Chapter 27). Highlights: Mature domestic ecosystem; phone app controls the desktop, transfers files, and can power on/off (some features need hardware). Free tier is enough for light personal use.
    • ToDesk. Best for: People who want stable, low-latency remote work/ops. Highlights: Device ID + password connection; phone controls PC (and sometimes PC controls phone, depending on version); file transfer and multi-monitor switching feel smooth. Domestic nodes usually perform well.
    • Basic setup: Install the client on the computer and sign in / stay online → install the app on the phone → connect with device ID + access password (or the same account) → use the phone as a trackpad/gestures for the desktop.
    • Safety rules (memorize these):
    • For personal use: Turn on two-step verification, change default passwords, sign out or disable unattended access when done. On work computers, follow company security policy.
    • In public, remote work carefully — watch for people peeking at your screen and passwords.
    2. AI office apps: Trae / WorkBuddy / Dumate
    • Trae. Best for: Coding and document collaboration, friendly in Chinese environments. Highlights: ByteDance's AI IDE/assistant; SOLO mode can spin up a project from one sentence. Efficient for daily coding and document edits. If it runs on a computer, you can pair it with remote control or official companion features on mobile to check/follow tasks (check the latest product form). See Chapter 41 for the AI coding tools landscape.
    • WorkBuddy. Best for: Office users who want AI help with meeting notes, email, reports, and work docs. Highlights: An AI assistant aimed at office scenarios — great for draft → polish → summarize flows. Start some workflows on the phone; leave heavy lifting to the computer.
    • Dumate. Best for: Teams/individuals who want multi-person collaboration with docs and knowledge management in one place. Highlights: AI collaboration office tool focused on gathering materials and co-editing. View and lightly edit on the phone; do complex layout on a bigger computer screen.
    • What "phone remote-controls computer" means here: Many AI office features run on desktop/web. From your phone, connect back via Sunlogin/ToDesk or use the product's own mobile app/webpage to "remote" AI tasks on the computer during your commute. Rule: heavy compute and long docs on the computer; check progress and tweak a few lines on the phone.
    • Privacy note: Before uploading contracts, ID cards, or customer data, read the product's privacy terms and company compliance rules. For work materials, prefer tools your organization specifies.
    3. Live wallpapers: miHoYo Desktop Mate (phone + PC)
    • Desktop Mate. Best for: Fans of miHoYo characters who want free live wallpapers. Highlights: Free live wallpaper app from miHoYo on phone and PC. Character Live2D/animated performances can sit on your desktop; some devices/systems allow lock screen or home wallpaper use.
    • Battery and performance: Live wallpapers use more power and GPU than static images. On low battery or older phones, use them only while charging, or lower the frame rate if the app offers it.
    • Install source: Prefer the official site or a trusted app store. Avoid third-party "cracked" builds with bundled malware. On PC, watch the install path and whether auto-start is needed.
    4. Fast LAN file transfer: LocalSend / Feige / AirDrop
    • LocalSend. Best for: Mixed Android/Windows/iOS/Mac/Linux setups that want cross-platform transfers without public cloud. Highlights: Open source, direct LAN connection. Send photos, videos, and docs on the same Wi-Fi — no cable, no vendor servers. Speed depends on your router.
    • Feige (IPMsg). Best for: Office Windows PCs and older LAN office setups. Highlights: A classic LAN transfer/chat tool, good for big files on an intranet. Download from a trusted source; on company networks follow IT policy.
    • AirDrop. Best for: iPhone, iPad, and Mac users. Highlights: One-tap sharing in the Apple ecosystem. Bluetooth discovery + Wi-Fi Direct, no mobile data. Set "Contacts Only" to reduce strangers pinging you.
    • Also worth knowing: Mi Share, Huawei Share, vivo Share, and similar brand tools are very fast within the same brand. WeChat "File Transfer Helper" is convenient but limited by file size and signed-in devices. For big files, prefer LocalSend/AirDrop.
    • Tips: Both devices on the same Wi-Fi. Public Wi-Fi is risky for sensitive files — prefer a personal hotspot. After transfer, confirm the file opens completely on the receiving side.
    5. Cross-device clipboard: KDE Connect / brand phone-PC link
    • Apple Universal Clipboard. Best for: iPhone + Mac users. Highlights: Sign in with the same Apple ID and enable Handoff — copy on the phone, paste on the Mac (and vice versa). Works for text and some files.
    • KDE Connect. Best for: Android + Windows/Linux/Mac users who want open-source clipboard sync, notification mirroring, and remote input. Highlights: Pair on the LAN to sync clipboards, push phone notifications to the PC, use the phone as a slide clicker/trackpad. Data doesn't go through third-party accounts.
    • Brand phone-PC links: Huawei Multi-Screen Collaboration / Super Device, Mi Continuity, vivo Share, OPPO Connect, Honor Connect, and others often include cross-screen clipboard and drag-and-drop. Best experience within the same brand.
    • Windows + Android official path: "Phone Link / Link to Windows" (evolved from Your Phone) lets you see phone notifications and photos on the PC and copy/paste in supported cases. Deeper on Samsung and some other models.
    • Safety note: Clipboards can retain passwords and codes. On shared computers, be careful with global sync. After pasting into a password field, avoid a second paste that leaks it. Some keyboards also read the clipboard — check permissions.
    6. Authenticator 2FA: Aegis / Microsoft Authenticator
    • Why an authenticator instead of SMS: SMS codes can be hijacked via SIM swap. TOTP codes are generated locally on a time algorithm, don't need phone signal, and resist phishing/interception better (still protect against malware and screenshots).
    • Aegis Authenticator. Best for: Android users who prefer open source and local control. Highlights: Free and open source, encrypted backup and import/export, clean UI, unlock token list with fingerprint/face.
    • Microsoft Authenticator. Best for: Microsoft account, Office 365, and work account users; works on iOS/Android. Highlights: Push approval for sign-ins, password monitoring, and account backup (depending on version). Tightly integrated with Windows and enterprise identity.
    • Google Authenticator / 2FAS, etc.: Common in their ecosystems too. What matters is encrypted backup so you don't lose tokens when you switch phones.
    • Must-do when switching phones: Transfer from the old device, or use the service's "backup codes / recovery key." Print backup codes and store them in two places — not just on the same phone.
    • Password managers: Some password vaults can store TOTP too. Convenient, but risk is concentrated. For high-value accounts, split the job: "password manager + separate authenticator." See Chapter 14.
    7. Suggested combo: How a day fits together

    Example workflow

    • Morning: Check today's schedule in TickTick → glance at weather/alerts → open Trae/docs on the computer, phone aside.
    • Daytime: Scan paper materials to PDF with a scanning app, send to the computer via LocalSend/AirDrop; draft long docs on the computer with AI office tools.
    • Out and about: Connect back to the computer with ToDesk/Sunlogin to continue tasks; sign in to important accounts with Aegis/Microsoft Authenticator codes.
    • Evening: Check off done items in TickTick; if you like, change the wallpaper with Desktop Mate to unwind.

    Remote control and account safety rules

    • If a stranger asks you to install remote-control software → hang up and find official support yourself.
    • Never tell anyone your verification codes or authenticator codes — not even "couriers" or "support."
    • Before remote-controlling a work computer or installing AI software on it, ask IT first.
    • Be extra careful transferring files or logging in remotely on public networks.

    Hands-on: Run the cross-device chain once

    1. Put phone and computer on the same Wi-Fi and send a photo with LocalSend (or AirDrop).
    2. Create a TickTick task "Tonight 8pm: organize scans" and confirm it shows on both phone and computer.
    3. Turn on 2FA for your email or WeChat (if supported), bind it to Aegis or Microsoft Authenticator, and save backup codes.
    4. Install Sunlogin or ToDesk on your own computer, connect once from your own phone, then sign out or strengthen the password — learn the flow without leaving a back door.

    Chapter 14: Password Managers

    In the digital age, your passwords are the keys to your front door. But with too many keys, all too complex—what then? A password manager is your "universal key butler".

    I. Why Do You Need a Password Manager?

    Modern people have dozens or even hundreds of online accounts on average. If every account uses the same password, one hacked website puts all accounts at risk. If every account uses a different complex password, they are impossible to remember.

    A password manager solves this dilemma: you only need to remember one master password, and it remembers all the others for you.

    2. How Password Managers Work

    1. Encrypted Storage: All passwords are stored with high-strength encryption, and only you can decrypt them.
    2. Master Password: You set a master password to unlock the password vault. The master password itself is not stored on the server.
    3. Auto-Fill: On website or app login pages, the password manager automatically fills in your account and password.
    4. Password Generation: Can generate random, complex passwords to improve security.

    III. Introduction to Encryption Principles

    Understanding the encryption principles behind password managers helps you judge whether a service provider is trustworthy. Below are several core concepts explained in plain language.

    1. AES-256 Encryption

    AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption algorithm certified by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), widely used by banks, military, and government. "256" refers to the 256-bit key length — it would theoretically take longer than the age of the universe to brute-force. Mainstream password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, KeePass, etc.) all use AES-256 to encrypt your password vault.

    2. Zero-Knowledge Architecture

    "Zero-knowledge" doesn't mean the service provider stores nothing — it means thatencryption and decryption are both done locally on your device, and the server only stores encrypted ciphertext. The specific process:

    1. You enter your master password in the client.
    2. The client derives an encryption key from the master password (this happens on your phone/computer).
    3. Only the encrypted ciphertext is uploaded to the server.
    4. On next login, the server sends back the ciphertext, and the client decrypts it again using your master password.

    Key Point:The master password itself never leaves your device, and the server doesn't have it either. So even if the service provider is hacked, the attacker only gets a pile of unbreakable ciphertext — unless they can guess your master password.

    Why does "zero-knowledge" mean the service provider can't see your passwords either?

    Because the decryption key is derived from your master password, which exists only in your mind and is used only on your local device. The service provider's server has neither the master password nor the decryption key — only ciphertext. That's why legitimate providers like Bitwarden and 1Password explicitly state "we cannot see your passwords either" — it's not that they don't want to, it's that they technically can't.

    3. Key Derivation Functions: PBKDF2 and Argon2

    The master password can't be used directly as an encryption key — it needs to be processed by a "key derivation function." The purpose of this function is todeliberately slow down computation, making the cost of brute-force attacks prohibitively high.

    • PBKDF2: A well-established standard, widely used by iCloud Keychain, Bitwarden, LastPass, and others. Slows down cracking through repeated iteration (typically 100,000+ times) of hashing.
    • Argon2: The winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition, more modern than PBKDF2. In addition to "computational cost," it introduces "memory cost" — making it difficult for specialized hardware like GPUs/ASICs to accelerate cracking. Already supported by Bitwarden, KeePassXC, and others.

    Higher iteration counts are more secure but also slower to unlock. Legitimate providers publicly disclose their derivation algorithm and iteration counts for security community auditing.

    4. Case Study: The LastPass 2022 Data Breach

    In August 2022, the veteran password manager LastPass announced that its development environment was breached; in November of the same year, it further disclosed that hackers had taken backups of users' password vaults (encrypted ciphertext). Key lessons from the incident:

    • Zero-Knowledge Architecture Held the Line: Since the password vault was encrypted, hackers got the ciphertext but couldn't decrypt it — provided the user's master password was strong enough.
    • Users with Weak Master Passwords Are Most at Risk: Hackers can brute-force weak master passwords offline, so users with weak or reused master passwords face real risk.
    • Metadata Was Also Leaked: Although password contents were encrypted, metadata like site URLs and notes may not have been, revealing which services the user used.

    Lessons Learned from LastPass

    First, your master password must be long and unique (16+ characters recommended, with upper/lower case, digits, and symbols); second, prioritize providers that support Argon2id with high iteration counts; third, always enable independent two-factor authentication for high-value accounts (bank, email) — don't rely solely on a password manager.

    IV. Mainstream Password Manager Recommendations

    System Built-in:
    • iCloud Keychain: The first choice for Apple ecosystem users. Seamlessly integrated with Safari and apps, free, secure. The downside is that cross-platform use is inconvenient.
    • Google Password Manager: Convenient for Android users. Integrates with Chrome and the Android system, free.
    • Huawei Password Vault: Built into HarmonyOS, suitable for Huawei users.
    Third-Party Professional Tools:
    • Bitwarden: Open source and free, powerful, supports all platforms. Highly recommended for privacy-conscious users.
    • 1Password: Beautiful interface, rich features, suitable for families and teams. Paid.
    • LastPass: A long-established password manager, with limited features in the free version.
    • KeePass: Completely local storage, open source and free. Suitable for geek users.

    V. Real Password Strength Assessment

    Password managers generally display a "password strength" indicator bar (red/yellow/green), but this assessment often only considers length and character variety, which isn't comprehensive. To truly judge whether a password is secure, you need to consider "entropy" and "whether it has been leaked."

    1. Entropy: The Scientific Measure of Password Strength

    "Entropy" measures the uncertainty of a password, measured in bits. The higher the entropy, the more attempts are needed for brute-force cracking.

    • "123456": Extremely low entropy, cracked instantly.
    • "P@ssw0rd": Appears complex, but appears in all dictionary attack lists, so entropy is still low.
    • "correct horse battery staple": Four random words, approximately 44 bits of entropy, far harder to crack than "P@ssw0rd."
    • 16 random characters (including upper/lower case + digits + symbols): Approximately 100 bits of entropy, uncrackable by brute force with current computing power.

    Conclusion:"Length + randomness" is more important than "complex symbols". This is why the random long passwords generated by password managers are truly secure.

    2. HaveIBeenPwned: Check If Your Password Has Been Leaked

    Maintained by security researcher Troy Hunt, haveibeenpwned.com it collects accounts and passwords leaked in major data breaches. You can:

    1. Enter your email to check if your account was exposed in a breach.
    2. Use the Pwned Passwords feature to check if a password is in the known leaked database (password managers and browsers have this built in).

    If a password appears in the leaked database,no matter how complex it looks, you must change it immediately— because dictionary attacks prioritize these known passwords.

    k-Anonymity Query Principle

    Worried that entering your password on HaveIBeenPwned will cause another leak? No need to worry. Modern queries use the "k-anonymity" protocol: the browser only sends the first 5 characters of the password hash to the server, the server returns all hashes starting with those 5 characters, and the comparison is done locally. In other words, the server never sees your complete password hash. 1Password and Bitwarden's "leaked password detection" both work this way.

    3. Built-in Monitoring Features in Password Managers
    • 1Password Watchtower: Real-time monitoring of weak passwords, reused passwords, leaked passwords, expired passwords, and sites not using 2FA, displayed with red/orange/yellow severity levels.
    • Bitwarden Vault Health: Free version shows weak and reused passwords; paid version can detect leaked passwords (based on HaveIBeenPwned).
    • iCloud Keychain "Security Recommendations": iOS Settings → Passwords → Security Recommendations, alerts you which passwords appear in known leaks and which are reused.
    • Google Password Manager "Password Checkup": Built into Chrome, can one-tap check for leaked, weak, and reused passwords.

    Check Now: Are Your Passwords Safe?

    1. Go to haveibeenpwned.com, enter your commonly used email, and see which breach events it appeared in.
    2. iPhone users: Settings → Passwords → Security Recommendations, address each red warning one by one.
    3. Chrome users: Settings → Passwords → Check Passwords, follow prompts to change.
    4. 1Password/Bitwarden users: Open Watchtower/Health Reports, prioritize "leaked" and "reused" items.

    VI. Passkey: The Future of Passwordless Login

    In 2024-2026, password technology is undergoing a revolution —Passkeyis poised to completely replace traditional passwords. Jointly promoted by Apple, Google, and Microsoft, endorsed by the FIDO Alliance and the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), this is the biggest change in login methods in decades.

    1. What Is Passkey?

    Passkey is based on the FIDO2 / WebAuthn standard, usingon-device key pairsto replace passwords. The principle can be simplified as:

    • Your phone generates a key pair:Public key(registered with the website) + Private key(permanently stored in your device's secure chip).
    • When logging in, the website sends a "challenge," your phone signs it with the private key, and the website verifies it with the public key.
    • Before signing, you need to confirm your identity via biometrics (Face ID / fingerprint) or device PIN.
    • Throughout this process,no password is transmitted over the network.
    2. Passkey vs. Traditional Passwords
    Dimension Traditional Password Passkey
    Phishing Resistance Poor, phishing sites can steal passwords Naturally phishing-resistant, private key only signs for real domains
    Server Breach Impact Password hashes may be cracked Server only stores public key, no impact from breach
    Convenience Requires memorization/entry/management Face ID/fingerprint login in one second
    Replay Attack May be intercepted and replayed by man-in-the-middle Each signature is one-time, cannot be replayed
    3. Platform Support Status
    • Apple iCloud Keychain Passkey: Native support on iOS 16+ / macOS Ventura+, Passkeys sync across all devices signed in with the same Apple ID, no need to recreate on new devices.
    • Google Password Manager Passkey: Native support on Android + Chrome, Passkeys stored in Google Account, sync across Android devices; since 2023, Google personal accounts support Passkey login.
    • Microsoft: Windows 11 / Edge already supports Passkey; Microsoft Account, Outlook, Office and other services are gradually opening up Passkey login, manageable in Microsoft Authenticator.
    • 1Password / Bitwarden: Already supports Passkey creation, storage, and cross-platform sync, freeing you from being locked into a single ecosystem.

    Cross-Device Sync Is the Key Breakthrough

    The biggest pain point of early Passkey was being "bound to a single device" — you had to recreate it when switching phones. Starting in 2023, Apple, Google, and Microsoft implemented cloud sync for Passkeys: iCloud Keychain syncs across Apple devices, Google Password Manager syncs across Android devices. Third parties like 1Password have enabled cross-ecosystem sync. This means Passkey is now practical enough to replace passwords.

    4. How to Create and Use Passkey on Your Phone

    iOS (iPhone) Path:

    1. On the account security page of a Passkey-supporting website (such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon, eBay, PayPal), select "Add passkey."
    2. The system shows a Face ID / Touch ID verification window. Once verified, the Passkey is automatically generated and saved to iCloud Keychain.
    3. Next time you log in to this website, enter your username and select "Sign in with iPhone" — just a Face ID scan and you're in.
    4. Management: Settings → Passwords → find the corresponding website to see the Passkey entry.

    Android Path:

    1. On the account security page of a Passkey-supporting website, select "Add passkey."
    2. Google Password Manager popup → select your Google account → screen lock verification (fingerprint/pattern/PIN).
    3. Passkey is automatically saved to Google Password Manager and synced across Android devices with the same account.
    4. Next time you log in, select "Use Passkey" — just unlock your screen and you're in.
    5. Management: Android Settings → Passwords, passkeys & autofill → Password Manager → google.com.
    5. Cross-Device Passkey Login

    If you're on a Windows PC logging into a website that only has a Passkey on your iPhone, you can authorize via QR code scan:

    1. On the website login page, select "Use Passkey."
    2. Select "Use another device."
    3. The PC displays a QR code — scan it with your iPhone.
    4. iPhone shows a Face ID verification, and upon confirmation, the website login is completed on the PC.

    This process uses dual encrypted communication via Bluetooth + internet — the Passkey private key never leaves your iPhone.

    Try It Now: Experience Passwordless Login

    1. Sign in to your Google Account → Security → Passkeys → Add a passkey, experience Face ID/fingerprint login.
    2. Sign in to your Microsoft account → Security → Advanced Security Options → Add a passkey.
    3. Try it on services that already support Passkey, such as Taobao, JD.com, eBay, and PayPal.
    4. Keep traditional passwords as backup, gradually migrate high-value accounts to Passkey.

    Transition Period Recommendations

    Passkey hasn't completely replaced passwords — many websites are still in a "Passkey + password" coexistence phase. Recommendation: prioritize enabling Passkey for high-value accounts, butdon't immediately delete traditional passwords, keep them as backup; continue using your password manager, since not all websites support Passkey. Treat Passkey as a "powerful supplement to password managers" rather than an "immediate replacement."

    VII. Hardware Security Keys

    If your security requirements exceed those of ordinary users — for example, if you hold significant cryptocurrency, are an executive/journalist/activist, or protect enterprise core accounts — hardware security keys are a more reliable choice than SMS verification codes.

    1. What Is a Hardware Security Key?

    A hardware key is a physical device (shaped like a USB drive) with an internal security chip that stores your private key, requiring physical contact or NFC to complete authentication. Representative products:

    • YubiKey(Yubico): The most mainstream, supports FIDO2/WebAuthn, U2F, OTP, PIV, OpenPGP, with USB-C / USB-A / NFC and other interfaces. Series 5 costs $50-70.
    • Google Titan: Made by Google, USB-C + NFC / Bluetooth, about $30-40.
    • OnlyKey: Open-source alternative, supports multiple protocols.
    • Domestic Alternatives: Such as Feitian ePasskey, more affordable.
    2. Why Are Hardware Keys Safer Than SMS Verification Codes?
    • Phishing Resistance: Like Passkey, hardware keys only respond to the real domain, so phishing sites can't trick them into providing verification codes.
    • SIM-Swap Resistance: SMS verification codes can be intercepted via SIM-swap attacks, while hardware keys don't need a phone number.
    • Man-in-the-Middle Resistance: The FIDO2 protocol includes a challenge value in each signature, preventing replay.
    • Physical Isolation: The private key remains inside the hardware chip forever — even if malware compromises your computer, it can't read it.
    3. Applicable Scenarios
    • Cryptocurrency exchange accounts, wallet recovery.
    • Enterprise SSO, remote work VPN, SSH server login.
    • Email, GitHub, social media and other "master accounts" — once compromised, all other accounts can be reset.
    • Journalists, lawyers, executives, and other high-sensitivity individuals.
    4. How to Configure a Hardware Key as Two-Factor Authentication

    Using a Google Account + YubiKey as an example:

    1. Purchase a YubiKey (recommended to buy two at once — one for daily use and one as backup, stored in different locations).
    2. Sign in to myaccount.google.com → Security → 2-Step Verification.
    3. Select "Add security key" → insert the YubiKey into the USB-C port or tap it against your phone's NFC sensor.
    4. Follow the prompt to touch the YubiKey's metal contact to complete registration.
    5. It's recommended to register a second backup key.
    6. In the "2-Step Verification" settings, set the hardware key as the preferred verification method, with SMS as backup.

    Websites with mainstream support: Google, GitHub, Microsoft, Apple ID, Facebook, Twitter, Dropbox, GitLab, AWS, Coinbase, Binance, and more.

    Dual-Key Strategy

    The biggest risk of hardware keys is "loss." Recommendations: ① Register two different keys simultaneously; ② Carry one with you (on a keychain) and store one in a home safe or bank deposit box; ③ Some websites allow printing "backup recovery codes" for offline storage. This way, even if the primary key is lost, you won't be permanently locked out of your accounts.

    Be Careful with Purchase Channels

    Always purchase from official stores or authorized dealers — don't buy used or keys from unknown sources, as pre-configured hardware could theoretically have been implanted with a backdoor. YubiKey firmware cannot be updated after manufacturing, but Yubico continuously publishes security advisories — follow their official website.

    VIII. Family/Team Password Sharing

    In family scenarios, Netflix, home Wi-Fi, router admin, and smart lock passwords need to be shared among the whole family; in team scenarios, servers, databases, and social media accounts require multi-person collaboration.Sending passwords via WeChat or writing them in shared documents are high-risk practices— once chat history or document permissions are leaked, the passwords are leaked too.

    1. 1Password's "Shared Vaults"

    1Password is the benchmark product for family and team sharing. Its core mechanism ismultiple vaults:

    • Personal Vault: Only you can see it, for private accounts like banks and email.
    • Shared Vault: Family or team members can all see it, for shared items like Netflix, home Wi-Fi, and shared credit cards.
    • Permission Tiers: The team version can set certain members to "view only" or "view but not edit."

    Family or team members don't need to share a master password — each logs in with their own account and can see the shared vault content they're authorized for. Password changes sync in real-time to all members.

    2. Bitwarden's "Organizations" Feature

    Bitwarden's free version supports individual password sharing (via the "Send" feature for time-limited sharing of a single password); the paid version can create "Organizations" to share entries with family or team colleagues with fine-grained permissions. Bitwarden also offers a self-hosted option, suitable for enterprises with high data sovereignty requirements.

    3. Family Scenarios: Secure Ways to Share Netflix, Wi-Fi, and Other Passwords
    • Netflix / Streaming Sites: Store login passwords in 1Password Families' "Shared Vault" — family members log in individually without sharing in a group chat.
    • Home Wi-Fi Password: iOS devices can share Wi-Fi passwords directly via AirDrop to visiting guests without reading it aloud; Android 12+ also has a "Nearby Share Wi-Fi" feature.
    • Smart Locks, Smart Appliances: Use the manufacturer app's "Family Members" feature to create individual accounts for each person, rather than sharing one admin account.
    • Home Router Admin: Store the admin password in a 1Password Shared Vault, and set up a separate SSID for guest Wi-Fi.

    1Password Families Value for Money

    1Password Families costs about $4.99/month, supporting up to 5 family members, each with an independent personal vault + 4 shared vaults. That's less than $1/person/month — currently the best family sharing experience. Bitwarden's family plan at $10/year supports 6 people, offering better value but with a slightly less polished interface.

    4. Team Scenarios: Server/Database Password Sharing
    • 1Password Teams / Business: Can create multiple vaults by department and project team, with fine-grained permission control and auditable access logs.
    • Bitwarden Teams / Enterprise: Open-source solution, self-hostable, enterprise version supports SSO integration and directory sync.
    • Separation of Duties Principle: Admin passwords should not be held by only one person — designate 2-3 "emergency contacts" to ensure business continuity when key personnel leave or take vacation.
    • Offboarding Process: Immediately revoke departing employees' password manager access, and rotate all high-sensitivity passwords they had access to if necessary.
    5. Emergency Access: In Case Something Happens to You

    Imagine a scenario: you alone manage all the family's important accounts, but you're unexpectedly hospitalized or pass away, and your family can't log into the bank, email, or insurance accounts.The "Emergency Access" featureis designed exactly for this — authorize a trusted family member/friend to access your password vault when you can't respond.

    Bitwarden Emergency Access Setup:

    1. Log in to Bitwarden Web Vault → Settings → Emergency Access.
    2. Add the trusted contact's email and invite them to accept.
    3. Set a "wait period" (7-14 days recommended): the time window from when they make a request to when you confirm.
    4. If you don't respond during the wait period (decline or take no action), the other person automatically gains access after it expires.
    5. You can manually reject requests or revoke emergency access permissions at any time.

    1Password Emergency Access:

    1. 1Password doesn't call it "Emergency Access" directly, but it can be achieved through the "Family/Team Organization" feature — after adding family members to the family plan, place some entries in a "Shared Vault."
    2. For individual plan users, it's recommended to tell one highly trusted family member your master password, or write it in a sealed envelope stored in a safe.
    3. 1Password also provides a "Recovery Code" — be sure to print and save it when enabling two-factor authentication.

    Set Up Now: Leave a "Spare Key" for Your Family

    1. Choose a trusted family member as your "emergency contact."
    2. Set up emergency access in your password manager (Bitwarden) or add them to a family shared vault (1Password).
    3. Write the master password + recovery code on paper, seal in an envelope, store in a home safe or inform a trusted family member.
    4. Review every six months to confirm the emergency contact is still appropriate.

    IX. Password Manager Best Practices

    • Set a Strong Master Password: The master password is the last line of defense — make sure to set a long, complex password and memorize it firmly.
    • Enable Two-Factor Authentication: Turn on 2FA for your password manager account to add a layer of protection.
    • Regularly Check for Weak Passwords: Most password managers have a "security audit" feature that helps you find weak and duplicate passwords.
    • Don't Forget the Master Password: The master password cannot be recovered — forgetting it means losing all passwords. It's recommended to write it down on paper and keep it in a safe place.
    • Emergency Access: Set up an emergency contact, so if you can't access your account, a trusted person can obtain your passwords.

    Important Reminder

    Password managers are convenient but come with risks: if your master password leaks, all your passwords are exposed. So your master password must never reuse any other password, nor be written somewhere easily found. Also, choose a provider with a good security track record.

    Try It Now: Get Started with a Password Manager

    1. Pick a password manager (Bitwarden or your system’s built-in one is recommended).
    2. Register an account and set a strong master password.
    3. Import existing passwords (if any) or start adding new passwords.
    4. Install the browser extension or mobile app, and experience the auto-fill feature.
    5. Check the security audit report to find passwords that need improvement.

    III. Advanced (Chapters 15-20)

    Charge as you use

    Chapter 15: Battery Science and Battery Life Optimization

    Afraid of heat

    : High temperature is the number one killer of batteries.

    Aging

    • : Over time, the maximum capacity will decrease—this is normal.Core Metrics: Cycle Count and Battery Health
    • One cycle is not one charge. For example, if you use 60% today and recharge to full, then use 40% tomorrow and recharge to full, the total 100% consumed counts as one cycle.Battery health is the current maximum capacity as a percentage of brand-new. Below 80%, you'll noticeably feel the battery life shorten.
    • How to check?iPhone: Settings > Battery > Battery Health & Charging; Android: usually search "battery health" in Settings.
    2. Charging Mysticism? Fast Charging, Wireless Charging, and the Golden Rule
    • Does fast charging damage the battery?
    • Using original or certified fast-charging accessories causes minimal harm. The phone and charger have temperature control and will automatically reduce power if overheated.
    • Wireless charging : Convenient but less efficient, with more noticeable heat. Suitable for overnight charging.

    Golden maintenance rule

    • : Try to keep the battery level between 20%-80%. Don't keep it starving (0%) or stuffed (100%). 3. Complete Guide to Fast Charging Protocols: Why Won't Your Charger Charge Fast?
    • Wireless charging1. Basic Principles of Fast Charging
    • Charging power = voltage × current (P = U × I). To increase power, you either raise the voltage, raise the current, or both. Different protocols choose different technical approaches.Fast charging workflow:

    iPhone "80% Charge Limit" Feature — Turning the Golden Rule into a System Setting

    The iPhone 15/16 series (iOS 17+) has turned the "20%-80% rule" into a system feature. When enabled, the phone automatically stops charging at 80%, significantly slowing battery aging. Settings path:

    Settings > Battery > Battery Health & Charging > Charging Optimization > 80% Limit

    The three options mean: ①No Limit— charges to 100%; ②Optimized Battery Charging— learns your routine, only delays to 100% during the last portion of overnight charging; ③80% Limit— stops at 80% directly, best for battery longevity. For people who are always at home/office with charging available, the 80% Limit is strongly recommended; for frequent travelers who need a full charge on the go, Optimized Battery Charging is a good choice.

    GaN Chargers — A Traveler's Best Companion

    You may have noticed that fast chargers are getting smaller and smaller — the hero behind this isGaN (Gallium Nitride)this new semiconductor material. Compared to traditional silicon-based chargers, GaN chargers have several clear advantages:

    • Compact Size: At the same power output, GaN chargers can be 1/2 or even 1/3 the size of traditional silicon ones. A 65W GaN charger is smaller than Apple's old 5W charger.
    • High Efficiency, Low Heat: Gallium nitride's switching loss is far lower than silicon, with energy conversion efficiency reaching 95%+, so it doesn't get hot during charging.
    • Travel-Friendly: A single 65W or 100W multi-port GaN charger can simultaneously charge a phone, tablet, and laptop — much lighter than carrying three "bricks."
    • Buying Advice: Look for GaN chargers that support the PD protocol (65W+ can charge laptops). Well-known brands like Baseus, Anker, Nubia, and Xiaomi are all good choices. Make sure to check that the cable is compatible (high-power charging requires a Type-C cable with an E-Marker chip).

    Handshake phase

    : The phone and charger communicate through the data cable, exchanging their supported protocols and power information.

    Negotiation phase

    : Both parties determine a commonly supported maximum power level.

    Charging phase

    1. : The charger outputs voltage and current according to the negotiated values, and the phone manages the power.Adjustment phase
    2. : As the battery level increases, the phone gradually reduces the charging power to protect the battery.2. Mainstream Fast Charging Protocols in Detail
