    • 1,500-3,500 yuan is the best value-for-money sweet spot
    • Last year's flagship is a better deal than this year's mid-range
    • Five pitfalls: multi-camera scam, high-megapixel trap, carrier-customized phones, curved screen myth, AI gimmicks
    • 618 and Double 11 are the two best time windows for buying phones each year

    Chapter 29: Digital Wellbeing — Building a Healthy Relationship with Your Phone

    Have you ever experienced this: you only meant to scroll short videos for 5 minutes, then looked up and realized two hours had passed? Or lying in bed at night scrolling your phone, getting more and more awake, and finally falling asleep at 2 AM? Phones have changed our lives, but they're also quietly consuming our time and health. This chapter isn't about "quitting phones" — it's about helping you take back control.

    I. Check Your "Screen Time" — Numbers Are a Wake-Up Call

    Before making changes, understand the current situation. Your phone has a feature many people have never opened called "Screen Time" (iPhone) or "Digital Wellbeing" (Android). It tells you exactly how much time you spend on your phone each day and which apps that time goes to.

    • iPhone: Settings > Screen Time > See All Activity. You'll see daily unlock counts, pickup counts, and time spent in each app.
    • Android: Settings > Digital Wellbeing & Parental Controls. Huawei calls it "Healthy Phone Usage," Xiaomi calls it "Screen Time Management." Similar features, all showing daily usage data.

    80% of people who see this data for the first time are shocked. A friend of mine discovered after checking that they spent over 4 hours a day on Douyin — that's 28 hours a week, equivalent to a part-time job. This kind of "digital shock" is the first step toward change.

    II. Set App Time Limits — Install a Speed Limiter for Yourself

    Once you know where the problem is, you can set targeted limits. No need to delete apps outright — just set a "daily allowance":

    1. iPhone: Settings > Screen Time > App Limits > Add Limit. Select the app you want to restrict (e.g., Douyin) and set 30 minutes per day. When the time's up, the app icon grays out, and opening it requires an additional password entry.
    2. Android: Settings > Digital Wellbeing > App Timers. Select an app and set a daily usage limit; when time's up, the app icon grays out.
    3. Tip: Set the limit password to something you don't use often and is hard to remember. If it's too easy to enter, you'll be tempted to "extend" every time, making the limit useless.

    III. The Right Way to Use "Do Not Disturb" — Not Muting Notifications, But Muting Anxiety

    Many people's phones buzz with notifications dozens of times a day, and each buzz interrupts their attention. You think you're just "glancing at a notification," but it actually takes 15-20 minutes to refocus after each interruption. Do Not Disturb isn't about "going offline" — it's about helping you regain control of your attention.

    • Schedule It: Set Do Not Disturb to automatically turn on from 10 PM to 7 AM. This way, your sleep won't be interrupted by a spam text message.
    • Allow Important Contacts Through: In Do Not Disturb settings, set "Allow Calls From" to "Favorites" or enable "Repeated Calls" (a second call within 3 minutes will ring normally). This way you won't miss emergency calls from family, but won't be bothered by sales calls.
    • Work Focus Mode: iPhone's "Focus" mode lets you set custom scenarios — for example, a "Work" focus only allows work-related app notifications, while a "Reading" focus silences all notifications.

    IV. Eye Protection Relies on Habits, Not Apps — The 20-20-20 Rule

    Prolonged screen time inevitably causes dry, sore eyes. Eye protection mode (blue light filter) helps somewhat, but what really works is changing your eye usage habits:

    The 20-20-20 Rule

    Every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something 20 feet (about 6 meters) away for 20 seconds. This simple action effectively relieves ciliary muscle fatigue.

    • Enable Eye Protection Mode: Settings > Display > Eye Protection (or Night Shift). When enabled, the screen's color temperature warms up, reducing blue light. Recommended to set it to auto-enable from sunset to sunrise.
    • Adjust Screen Brightness: When the environment is dark, the screen should be dim too. Many people keep their screen too bright in the dark — this is the most damaging behavior for your eyes. Enable "Auto-Brightness" and make sure it works properly.
    • Maintain Distance: Keep the phone at least 30 cm from your eyes. Many people hold their phones very close, which keeps the ciliary muscle in a state of tension, accelerating nearsightedness.

    V. Neck Rescue Guide for "Phone Benders"

    When looking down at your phone, your neck bears 5-6 times the pressure of normal standing. Long-term neck bending can straighten the cervical curve, cause bone spurs, dizziness, and hand numbness. Here are some simple improvement methods:

    • Raise Your Phone: When looking at your phone, try to hold it at eye level rather than looking down at your lap. Your arms may get tired, but your neck will thank you.
    • Move Your Neck Every 30 Minutes: Slowly turn your head left to the limit, hold for 3 seconds, return to center; then turn right, hold for 3 seconds. Repeat 5 times. Then do the "rice character exercise" — trace the character 米 ("rice") in the air with your chin.
    • Wall Standing for 3 Minutes: Press the back of your head, shoulder blades, buttocks, and heels against a wall. Stand for 3 minutes daily to effectively correct the hunched, head-down posture.

    VI. Sleep and Phone — The Bedroom Habit Most Worth Changing

    Blue light from your phone screen suppresses melatonin production, making you "more awake the more you look." Many people feel "I'll get sleepy as I scroll," but they're actually being tricked by blue light — when they finally put the phone down, they can't fall asleep. Here are improvement suggestions:

    • No Phone for 1 Hour Before Bed: This is the most effective yet hardest to follow. If you can't manage it, at least turn on "Night Shift/Eye Protection Mode" to minimize blue light.
    • Put the Phone Out of Reach: Put the charger at the other end of the bedroom, not on the nightstand. This way you won't be tempted to pick it up and scroll, and when the alarm goes off, you have to get up to turn it off — killing two birds with one stone.
    • Enable "Sleep Mode": iPhone's "Sleep" Focus can automatically lock the screen and simplify the lock screen during sleep hours; Android brands have similar features.
    • Use an Alarm Clock Instead of Your Phone: Buy a cheap physical alarm clock for a dozen or so yuan. Stop using your phone as an alarm, and you'll escape the trap of "just checking the time, then can't help scrolling."

    VII. Information Anxiety — Learn "Selective Blindness"

    The amount of information we receive daily equals what people in ancient times received in a lifetime. But the human brain wasn't designed to process this much information — overload leads to anxiety, scattered attention, and decision fatigue. The solution isn't "getting more information" but "actively filtering":

    • Unfollow: Open your list of followed accounts, bloggers, and creators, and ask yourself one question: "Did I get any real value from this in the past month?" If not, unfollow. Quality over quantity for information sources.
    • Turn Off Non-Essential App Notifications: Turn off notifications for all apps except WeChat, phone, SMS, and calendar. News doesn't need push notifications — you'll see it when you actively look.
    • Set an "Information Fast Day": Pick one day a week (e.g., Sunday) to completely avoid phone news and short videos. You'll find the sky doesn't fall, and you'll feel noticeably better on Monday.

    Hands-On: One-Week Digital Health Challenge

    1. Today: Open Screen Time / Digital Wellbeing and review last week's usage data.
    2. Tomorrow: Set daily limits for your most time-consuming entertainment apps (recommend 30-60 minutes).
    3. Day after: Schedule Do Not Disturb (22:00-07:00), allowing calls from favorites.
    4. Day 4: No phone for 1 hour before bed; move charger to the other end of the bedroom.
    5. Day 5: Unfollow 5 accounts or bloggers you no longer watch.
    6. Day 6: Try a full day of "information fast" — no news, no short videos.
    7. Day 7: Review this week's Screen Time report and compare with last week.

    Chapter Summary

    • First check your screen time data — understanding the current state is the first step to change
    • Set limits for entertainment apps, schedule Do Not Disturb — regain control of your attention
    • The 20-20-20 rule is the simplest and most effective eye care habit
    • Looking down at your phone puts 5-6x pressure on your neck — raise your phone and stretch regularly
    • No phone 1 hour before bed, charger out of reach
    • The antidote to information anxiety is "active filtering," not "getting more"

    Chapter 30: Screen Mirroring, Presentations, and Car Connectivity

    Your phone screen is at most 7 inches, but your TV is 55 inches and your projector is 100 inches. Casting your phone screen to a larger display is a completely different experience. This chapter covers three high-frequency scenarios: screen casting, presentations, and car connectivity — helping you extend your phone's capabilities to bigger screens.

    I. Three Wireless Casting Camps — Don't Mix Them Up

    Wireless casting all looks like "phone screen to TV," but there are three underlying technologies that are mutually incompatible:

    Technology Who Uses It Protocol
    AirPlayiPhone/iPad/MacApple ecosystem, smoothest experience. Requires Apple TV or AirPlay-enabled TV
    MiracastAndroid phonesWi-Fi Direct connection, no router needed. Android phones' "wireless casting" uses this by default
    DLNAAll platformsOnly pushes media files (video/music/photos), doesn't mirror screen. Good for pushing video to TV for playback
    Operation methods for each platform:
    • iPhone: Control Center > Screen Mirroring > Select your TV/Apple TV. If the TV doesn't support AirPlay, you can buy an Apple TV box or an AirPlay-enabled TV stick.
    • Android: Swipe down the notification panel > Find "Wireless Cast" / "Smart Cast" / "Multi-Screen Interaction" button > Select TV. Phone and TV must be on the same Wi-Fi.
    • Universal Solution: If the TV is too old to support any wireless casting, plug a Chromecast or Xiaomi Box / Huawei Box into the TV's HDMI port to receive casts.

    II. Wired Casting — More Stable, Zero Latency

    Wireless casting is convenient but has latency, making gaming and presentations unpleasant. Wired casting solves this:

    • iPhone: Requires a Lightning/USB-C to HDMI adapter cable (about 100-200 yuan). Plug in, and the phone screen outputs directly to the TV/projector's HDMI port.
    • Android: Some phones support USB-C to HDMI direct connection (requires DP Alt Mode support; most flagships support it). Just buy a USB-C to HDMI cable.
    • Meeting Room Scenario: If you frequently use your phone for presentations, keep an HDMI adapter cable in your bag. Meeting room TVs/projectors almost all have HDMI ports — just plug in and go, far more reliable than fiddling with wireless casting.

    III. Phone Becomes Computer — Desktop Mode

    Some Android phones support "Desktop Mode" — when connected to a monitor, the phone outputs a computer-like desktop interface that can be operated with mouse and keyboard:

    • Samsung DeX: Samsung flagship's signature feature. Connecting a monitor brings up a desktop interface with multi-window support, the closest experience to a real computer. With Bluetooth keyboard and mouse, you can travel without a laptop.
    • Huawei Desktop Mode: Huawei Mate series / Pura series also has similar functionality when connected to a monitor. Supports multi-window, file management, and office apps.
    • Motorola Ready For: Moto flagships also support it, with features similar to DeX.
    • What is RAW: Light office work (email, document editing), PPT presentations, watching videos on big screen. Not suitable for heavy Excel work or professional design.

    IV. Car Connectivity — The Right Way to Use Your Phone While Driving

    Operating your phone while driving is illegal, but navigation, music, and calls are essential. Car connectivity systems let you use your phone's core features on the car's infotainment screen, so the phone can be set aside:

    • Apple CarPlay: Top choice for iPhone users. Connect to the car system via USB or wirelessly, and the car screen shows a streamlined iPhone interface — navigation (Amap/Baidu Maps), music, phone, messages, podcasts. Siri voice control is entirely hands-free.
    • Android Auto: Android users' counterpart. Features similar to CarPlay, supporting Google Maps, Spotify, etc. Some features are unavailable in China due to Google service restrictions.
    • Huawei HiCar: Huawei's proprietary solution, widely supported by domestic car models. Beyond navigation and music, it also supports Huawei video calls, parking camera fusion, and other unique features.
    • Baidu CarLife: Cross-platform solution, works with both iOS and Android. Fewer features but broad compatibility — many older car models only support CarLife.

    Security Reminder

    Regardless of which car connectivity solution you use, always rely on voice control while driving. Set your navigation destination and music playlist before starting to drive — never operate the car screen while in motion.

    V. Meeting Room Casting in Practice — No More Panic

    Meetings are the most frequent casting scenario and also the most prone to problems. Here are practical tips:

    • Arrive Early to Test: Never wait until the meeting starts to connect casting. Arrive 10 minutes early and test your connection method. Wi-Fi casting fails more often than you'd think.
    • Prepare a Wired Plan B: Keep an HDMI adapter cable in your bag. When wireless casting won't connect, a wired connection is your lifesaver.
    • Disable Notification Preview: When casting, your WeChat messages appear on the meeting room big screen. Before casting, turn off "Lock Screen Notification Content Preview" in settings, or enable "Presentation Mode" (some phones support this — automatically hides notifications during casting).
    • "Present Documents" Rather Than "Operate Your Phone": If you're presenting a PPT, store the file on your phone and open it in WPS for fullscreen playback, rather than casting your entire phone screen. This is more professional and smoother.

    Hands-On: Complete a Phone-to-TV Cast

    1. Chapter 18: Data Backup and Migration
    2. Open a photo or video on your phone.
    3. Try wireless casting (iPhone uses Screen Mirroring, Android uses the wireless cast button).
    4. If it fails, check whether the TV supports the corresponding protocol, or try DLNA push (tap the "Cast" button in the Gallery/Video app).
    5. After successful casting, try doing other operations on your phone to see if the big screen mirrors them.

    Chapter Summary

    • Three wireless casting camps: AirPlay (Apple), Miracast (Android), DLNA (cross-platform media push)
    • Wired casting is more stable with zero latency — an HDMI adapter cable is essential for meeting rooms
    • Samsung DeX / Huawei Desktop Mode turns your phone into a light office computer
    • Car connectivity: Four major solutions — CarPlay / Android Auto / HiCar / CarLife
    • Meeting room casting golden rules: test early, prepare a Plan B, disable notification preview

    Chapter 31: Getting Started with Short Video Shooting and Content Creation

    In 2026, short videos are no longer "toys for young people" — they've become the fundamental way everyone gets information and expresses themselves. Whether you want to document your life, share knowledge, or start a side business, your phone is your best creative tool — no need to buy a camera or learn Premiere. A single phone is enough to get started. This chapter helps you start from scratch.

    I. Think Before You Shoot: Who's Your Audience?

    The first mistake many people make is "picking up the phone and shooting immediately" without knowing who the audience is. Before you start, answer three questions:

    1. Who is my audience?— Content for kids, peers, or elderly viewers requires completely different styles.
    2. What value can I provide?— Make people laugh (entertainment), learn (knowledge), crave (food), or feel warm (emotion). You need at least one.
    3. Which platform can I consistently post on?— Douyin/Kuaishou (general entertainment), Xiaohongshu (lifestyle), Bilibili (in-depth content), WeChat Channels (social circle). Choose one main platform to focus on — don't distribute across all platforms from the start.

    II. Phone Camera Basic Settings — 5 Things to Do Before Shooting

    1. Set Resolution to 1080P, Frame Rate to 30fps: This is the standard for short video platforms. 4K files are too large and upload slowly. 60fps has no advantage on social platforms and just creates bigger files.
    2. Clean the Lens: The first and most important tip. Wipe the lens with your clothes before shooting — the image immediately becomes noticeably clearer.
    3. Lock Focus and Exposure: Long-press the subject in the viewfinder for 2 seconds until "AE/AF Lock" appears. This prevents brightness fluctuations while moving during the shot.
    4. Horizontal or Vertical?— For Douyin/Kuaishou/WeChat Channels/Xiaohongshushoot vertically (9:16). For Bilibili/YouTubeshoot horizontally (16:9). Decide the platform first, then the orientation.
    5. Enable Grid Lines: Settings > Camera > Grid. The foundation of rule-of-thirds composition, helping you quickly find the visual center.

    III. Five Camera Movement Techniques — Make Your Footage Come Alive

    The biggest problem for beginner videographers is footage that's too "static" — standing still the entire time. Learn these five basic camera movements, and your footage will instantly feel more professional:

    • Push: The phone slowly moves toward the subject. Creates tension or intimacy of "approaching."
    • Pull: The phone slowly moves away from the subject. Pulls from detail to wide shot, establishing the environment.
    • Pan: The phone stays in place, rotating left or right. Good for landscapes and showing space.
    • Track: The phone moves parallel, following the subject. Requires steady hands, best with a smartphone gimbal.
    • Follow: The phone follows behind or in front of the subject. The most commonly used movement in vlogs.

    Stability Is the Top Priority: Shaky footage looks very unprofessional. Two-handed grip is more stable than one-handed; when walking, bend your knees slightly and use a "ninja walk" to reduce up-and-down bouncing; if you have budget, buy a smartphone gimbal (DJI OM series about 500-800 yuan) — it's a game-changer.

    IV. Editing Basics — CapCut Is Enough

    JianYing (the domestic version of CapCut) is currently the most beginner-friendly mobile editing tool — free, feature-rich, and template-heavy. Here's the basic workflow:

    1. Import Footage: Open CapCut > New Project > Select and import your video clips.
    2. Trim: Drag the timeline to trim the wasted footage at the beginning and end of each clip. Principle: keep only the parts with information — shorter is better than longer.
    3. Add Transitions: Tap the "Transition" button between two clips and choose a simple transition effect. Beginners should use "Dissolve" or "Fade to Black" — avoid flashy 3D transitions.
    4. Add Subtitles: CapCut has an "Auto Captions" feature that generates subtitles with one tap. Accuracy is about 90% — just manually proofread once.
    5. Add Music: CapCut's music library has many royalty-free tracks. Choose a BGM that matches the rhythm and content, and set the volume to about 1/3 of the original video audio.
    6. Export: Export at 1080P, 30fps, bitrate set to "Recommended."

    V. The Importance of Thumbnails — 70% of People Decide Whether to Watch Based on the Cover

    A short video's thumbnail is its "storefront" — it determines whether people click. Key points for making thumbnails:

    • Thumbnail Should Have One Sentence: Write the core content of the video in large text, e.g., "Learn Phone Photo Editing in 3 Minutes." Font should be large, colors bright, with contrast against the background.
    • Thumbnail Must Match Content: Don't be a "clickbaiter" — if the thumbnail says one thing but the video shows another, viewers will swipe away immediately, and the algorithm will penalize you.
    • Facial Expressions Should Be Vivid: If the thumbnail has a person, pick a moment with a vivid or exaggerated expression. Human faces attract more clicks than text.
    • Making Thumbnails in CapCut: In CapCut, select the best frame, add text overlay, and export as an image for the thumbnail.

    VI. Three Content Creation Principles

    • First 3 Seconds Determine Life or Death: On short video platforms, viewers decide within 3 seconds whether to swipe or keep watching. The first 3 seconds must have a "hook" — a question, a suspense, or a surprising visual.
    • One Video, One Topic: The most common mistake beginners make is cramming too much into one video. One video should solve one problem — thoroughness beats comprehensiveness.
    • Persistence Beats Talent: Algorithmic recommendation requires "warming up the account." The first 20 videos will get almost no views — this is normal. Keep updating 2-3 per week, let the algorithm learn your content direction, and traffic will gradually grow.

    Hands-On: Shoot a 30-Second Short Video

    1. Pick a small topic you know well (e.g., "How to make phone fonts larger").
    2. Shoot 3-5 vertical clips, each 5-10 seconds.
    3. Use CapCut to splice, trim, add subtitles, and add BGM.
    4. Create a thumbnail with large text.
    5. Export and send to a friend first for feedback before publishing.

    Chapter Summary

    • Think before shooting: who's the audience, what value you provide, which platform to post on
    • 5 things before shooting: 1080P/30fps, clean lens, lock focus/exposure, decide orientation, enable grid
    • Five camera movements: Push, Pull, Pan, Track, Follow — stability is priority #1
    • Edit with CapCut: trim → transitions → subtitles → BGM → export — six steps
    • First 3 seconds are make-or-break, one video one topic, persistence beats talent

    Chapter 32: Phone Safety Emergency Handbook

    This chapter is an emergency plan. We hope you never need it — but if your phone is lost, stolen, or used in a scam, it will help you cut the damage. In earthquakes, rainstorms, and other disasters, a phone is also how you get warnings, share your location, and stay in touch. Read it through now, screenshot the key steps or print it and keep it at home — because in an emergency your phone may already be gone, and in a disaster it may be dead or offline.

    Scenario 0: Earthquake / extreme weather — how your phone helps you stay alive

    This is about personal safety, not accounts and money. For warning setup, see Chapter 13, "Weather alerts, disaster warnings, and earthquake early warnings." Here we only cover what to do after the alarm sounds.

    Earthquake alarm: Drop, cover, hold — don't just film it

    1. Take cover nearby: Drop, cover, hold on (under a table, inside corners of load-bearing walls, next to sturdy furniture). Protect head and neck. Stay away from glass, exterior walls, and hanging lights.
    2. Don't blindly rush downstairs: The main shock often lasts only seconds to tens of seconds; stairwells can be more dangerous. Never use elevators.
    3. Evacuate in order after shaking stops: Use the stairs, watch for aftershocks and falling objects. Reach open ground away from poles, billboards, and unstable buildings.
    4. Use your phone wisely: Short messages to emergency contacts ("I'm at XX, safe/hurt, need help") save more battery than long calls. Prefer text/SMS/WeChat when you can.
    5. No signal? See Chapter 7 on satellite SOS / satellite messaging (on supported models), or try higher/open ground. In some cases, network-free Bluetooth walkie-talkie apps help too.
    6. Turn off non-essential features: In an emergency, toggle airplane mode on a timer, turn off Bluetooth scanning, lower brightness — stretch battery life by hours. Save the last bar for "I'm safe" and rescue messages.

    Rainstorm / typhoon / flash flood: Act during the warning stage

    • On a red alert: Stay indoors as much as possible. Avoid underground spaces, underpasses, riverbanks, and steep slopes.
    • Trapped outdoors: Move to higher floors of sturdy buildings. Don't wade through floodwater (missing manhole covers and live wires). When calling 119/110, give landmarks and water level.
    • Before traveling: Check weather apps and local alert accounts. On long drives, avoid mountain roads along water and cliffs.
    • Family plan: Agree that "if we lose contact, use the last WeChat/SMS location" so nobody burns battery on endless calls.

    Four things to do before you need them

    1. Turn on system earthquake warnings / a trusted warning app, and let it break through silent mode.
    2. Pin 2–3 emergency contacts at the top of Contacts and show them on the lock screen (iOS/Android Medical ID or lock-screen message).
    3. Keep power banks at home and in your bag. Charge up and pack a cable before long trips.
    4. Memorize at least one number you can dial without Contacts (a family mobile). Write it on paper in your wallet.

    Scenario 1: Phone lost or stolen — the golden 30 minutes

    The first 30 minutes after losing a phone are "golden time." Handle them right and you protect your money and privacy. Follow this order and skip nothing:

    Standard 30-minute playbook

    1. Borrow a phone and call your own number (minute 1): It may just be nearby; a kind stranger can return it.
    2. Lock the phone remotely (minutes 2–5): On another phone or computer, sign in to Find My:
    3. Android brands: Huawei cloud.huawei.com / Xiaomi i.mi.com / OPPO cloud.oppo.com, etc.
    4. Suspend the SIM (minutes 5–10): Call your carrier (China Mobile 10086 / Unicom 10010 / Telecom 10000) and report the phone lost to suspend the SIM. This is the most critical step — if scammers get your SIM, they receive your codes and can reset every password.
    5. Freeze payment accounts (minutes 10–20):
    6. WeChat: Report to police at 110, then contact WeChat support, or WeChat Security Center > Freeze account
    7. Banking apps: Call the number on the back of your bank card and ask to freeze online banking
    8. Tell family and friends (minutes 20–25): Post on Moments or have family spread the word that your phone is lost, so scammers can't use your identity to trick others.
    9. Report to police (minutes 25–30): Call 110 or go to the nearest station and get a report receipt. You'll need it for insurance and bank disputes later.

    Scenario 2: You got scammed — the 72-hour window

    If you realize you've been scammed, staying calm is critical. Panic leads to bad decisions and more losses. Do this:

    1. Stop all transfers immediately: No matter what they say, don't send another cent. "Send one more deposit and we'll refund everything" is the classic second-round scam.
    2. Keep every piece of evidence: Don't delete chats! Don't delete call logs! Screenshot chats, transfers, and the other party's account details. These are key for reports and getting money back.
    3. Call 96110 right away: China's national anti-fraud hotline. Operators guide emergency stop-payment — if the transfer was recent (usually within 24 hours), the bank may freeze the other account and intercept funds.
    4. Call 110: Bring your phone, ID, and transfer receipts to the nearest station for a statement.
    5. Contact your bank/payment platform: Report the scam and ask to freeze the accounts involved. For credit-card fraud, ask the bank to start a chargeback.
    6. Change every password: On another safe device, change passwords for Apple ID/brand account, WeChat, Alipay, and banking apps, and turn on two-factor authentication.

    Scenario 3: Phone infected with malware — what now?

    If your phone shows strange pop-ups, installs weird apps on its own, or your bill/data spikes — it's likely malware:

    • Step 1: Enter safe mode — on Android, power off with the power button, then power on and hold volume-down after the vibration until "Safe mode" appears. Third-party apps are disabled in safe mode, making cleanup easier.
    • Step 2: Uninstall suspicious apps — in safe mode, Settings > Apps, sort by date, remove unknown recent installs.
    • Step 3: Scan with a security app — install "Tencent Mobile Manager" or "360 Mobile Security" and run a full scan.
    • Step 4: Factory reset (last resort) — if nothing works, back up important data and factory reset. Warning: A factory reset erases everything. Back up photos, contacts, and key files first.
    • iPhones almost never "get viruses" — iOS's sandbox makes malware hard to survive. If your iPhone acts up, it's usually an app bug or a settings issue. A factory reset fixes 99% of problems.

    Scenario 4: Account hijacked — take back control fast

    1. Change your password now: If you can still sign in, change it immediately. Make it completely different from the old one.
    2. Kick other devices: In account security settings, find "Login devices" and sign out anything you don't recognize.
    3. Check login history: Review the last 7 days. Strange locations mean the account really was taken.
    4. Turn on two-factor authentication: If you haven't, do it now. It's the most effective way to prevent another hijack.
    5. Check linked info: Verify the phone number and email on the account weren't changed. If they were, use account recovery to take it back.
    6. Check payment settings: If WeChat/Alipay was hit, look for altered password-free payments or auto-debits, and bank cards added to unfamiliar accounts.

    Scenario 5: Blackmail message — don't panic, don't pay

    Two common scripts: ① "I have your private video/photos; pay or I'll send them to everyone in your contacts"; ② "Your phone is hacked; pay or I'll lock it." If this happens:

    • 99.9% is a scam: They don't have anything on you. They send the same message to tens of thousands of people and wait for someone to pay.
    • Don't reply, don't pay: Replying tells them "this number is live" and marks you as a target for more harassment.
    • Screenshot the evidence, then block them.
    • Change passwords: If it eases your mind, change passwords on your main accounts.
    • If there's a real privacy leak risk: Report to police. They have experience with these cases.

    Scenario 6: Deepfake video / voice cloning scams — seeing is no longer believing

    Since 2024, deepface and voice cloning let scammers "become" your family, boss, or friends on video calls. "Mom, I'm in trouble, send money" — the person looks and sounds exactly like your son, but it's fake. This is one of the hardest and most dangerous scams right now.

    Step 1: Spot the tells — four common giveaways in AI fakes

    • Abnormal blinking: Real people blink 15–20 times a minute; AI faces often blink too little or with stiff rhythm.
    • Lips out of sync: Watch the mouth against the audio — there's often a fraction-of-a-second lag.
    • Blurry face edges: Hairlines, ears, and hair edges may show "fuzzy" fringes or flicker.
    • Inconsistent lighting: Highlights and shadows on the face don't match the background light, or features "slide" wrong when the head turns.

    Step 2: Three ways to check if they're real

    • Ask for a specific action: Turn the head, cover the face, block the mouth then open and close it. Deepfakes break on occlusion and big head turns — faces warp or lag behind motion.
    • Ask only they would know: Invent a fake question like "which clinic did we take the dog to last time?" Scammers can't answer or will stall.
    • Call back on a known number: Hang up and dial the number saved in your contacts. Scammers can't control the real phone number — the truth comes out immediately.

    Step 3: If you already lost money — report it

    1. Stop transfers now: No matter how "urgent," pause. Anyone pushing "transfer fast, don't hang up" is almost certainly a scammer.
    2. Keep every piece of evidence: Screen-record and screenshot video call frames, chats, their account, transfer receipts — key material for technical investigation.
    3. Call 96110: Say it's a "deepfake voice/video" scam; operators can start emergency stop-payment.
    4. Call 110: Bring all evidence to the station and explain AI forgery was used — this helps police classify the case.
    5. Warn family and friends: Scammers may use your fake video on others. Post a heads-up in Moments or the family group chat.

    Scenario 7: SIM swap — your number gets "stolen"

    Many people haven't heard of this attack, but it's devastating. A SIM swap means an attacker fakes your identity and gets a replacement SIM at a store. Once that succeeds, your phone suddenly loses service, while their phone with the new SIM receives every SMS code — Alipay, banks, WeChat all wide open.

    How to notice: Three warning signs of a SIM swap

    • Phone suddenly shows "No service" / "No SIM" even though you didn't touch the card and restarting doesn't help — often the moment of the swap.
    • Carrier texts say "SIM replacement successful" or "service change successful" — but you never requested it.
    • You suddenly stop getting verification codes — and other texts too, because SMS has been hijacked to their card.

    Protection — put a lock on your SIM too

    • Set a SIM PIN: Path Settings > Phone > SIM PIN. After enabling, every restart or SIM swap needs the PIN. Even if they get the card, they can't use it.
    • Enable carrier two-step verification: In China Mobile/Unicom/Telecom apps, find "Security Center" or "Service verification," turn on replacement-SIM alerts and a second password for service changes. Then staff will demand extra ID checks if someone tries to replace your SIM.
    • Don't rely on SMS for important accounts: For banks, Apple ID, and other high-value accounts, prefer authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator) or hardware keys over SMS codes.
    • Watermark ID copies: When a business needs a copy, write "For XX use only" — attackers often impersonate you with leaked ID info.

    If it already happened — speed is everything

    1. Call your carrier immediately to suspend: Mobile 10086 / Unicom 10010 / Telecom 10000. Freeze SIM replacement and stop the attacker from using your number.
    2. Sign in to key accounts from another device: On a computer or family phone, change passwords for banks, Alipay, WeChat, Apple ID and kick unknown devices.
    3. Freeze payment accounts: Alipay 95188 report loss, WeChat Security Center freeze, bank support freeze online banking.
    4. Go to a carrier store with your ID: Get a new SIM in person and restore your number.
    5. Report to police: SIM swap counts as "infringing citizens' personal information." Bring evidence (suspension time records, financial loss, replacement SIM records).
    6. Full audit: After getting your number back, check recent logins and transactions for misuse.

    Prevention beats cure — five daily habits

    1. Lock screen passcode + two-factor authentication — both on
    2. "Find My Phone" confirmed on
    3. SIM PIN set (Settings > Phone > SIM PIN) so a lost phone can't use your card
    4. Don't install shady apps; don't tap unknown links
    5. Back up important data regularly (photos, contacts, chat history)

    Hands-on: Make your own emergency contact card

    1. On a piece of paper, write: carrier support (Mobile 10086 / Unicom 10010 / Telecom 10000), bank support, 96110 anti-fraud hotline, 110 police, family numbers.
    2. Write the registration email and backup contact for your Apple ID / brand account.
    3. Keep that paper in your wallet or on the fridge — not only on your phone, because in an emergency your phone may be gone.
    4. Check now: Is "Find My Phone" on? Is the SIM PIN set?

    Chapter recap

    • Lost phone golden 30 minutes: Borrow a phone → lock remotely → suspend SIM → freeze payments → warn contacts → report to police
    • Scammed 72-hour window: Stop transfers → keep evidence → call 96110 → report → contact bank → change passwords
    • Malware: Safe mode → uninstall suspicious apps → security scan → factory reset (last resort)
    • Hijacked account: Change password → kick devices → check logins → enable 2FA → check linked info → check payments
    • Blackmail messages are 99.9% scams — don't reply, don't pay, screenshot and block
    • Deepfake voice/video scams: Watch blinking, lips, edges, lighting; ask them to turn their head and cover their face; ask private questions; call back on a known number
    • SIM swap: Treat sudden "No service" as a red flag. Set a SIM PIN, enable carrier two-step verification, use authenticator apps for important accounts
    • Five daily habits: Lock screen + 2FA, Find My Phone, SIM PIN, no shady apps, regular backups

    Part VI: Outlook and Car Connectivity (Chapters 33-34)

    We've covered practical tools and emergency plans. Now let's look at the storms brewing on the horizon. This chapter is short, but it points at the next 5–20 years: Will phones disappear? What will replace them? How will our relationship with the digital world change?

    Chapter 33: Future Outlook — The Next Journey of Smartphones

    Phones won't disappear overnight, but their "monopoly" may be eroded by a new generation of devices. This chapter covers three things: what next-gen devices look like, how the phone may "disappear" to become a new identity foundation, and the ethical issues we must consider ahead of time.

    I. AR/VR and Spatial Computing: The "Second Desktop" Beyond Phones

    The competition for next-gen devices has begun. The most likely candidates to divert time from phones are AR/VR and spatial computing devices:

    • Vision Pro Successor: The launch of Apple Vision Pro marked the official arrival of the "spatial computing" concept, but the first generation's price (starting at 29,999 yuan) and weight remain barriers. A lighter, cheaper Vision is expected in 2026-2027, bringing spatial computing from "developer toy" to "early majority." At that point, iPhone may become the computing companion and data hub for Vision glasses.
    • Another future evolution direction for phones may be "invisibility." It will transform into an omnipresent "behind-the-scenes promoter," becoming the sole cornerstone of your digital identity.: Open a "second desktop" in front of your eyes, making digital information as ubiquitous as air. Meta and Ray-Ban's smart glasses have sold millions of pairs, and domestic brands like Rokid, XREAL, and INMO are also releasing consumer AR glasses. By 2025-2026, AR glasses can do real-time translation, navigation HUD, and AI assistant conversations, but they're still limited by waveguide display and battery life — 3-5 years from "replacing phones."
    • Smart Rings and Wearables: Samsung Galaxy Ring, Oura Ring, and other smart rings are gaining popularity, serving as "body-worn sensors" that complement the phone's health monitoring. The phone's role is shifting from "all-in-one terminal" to "hub + multiple lightweight accessories."

    II. Brain-Computer Interface: Thought as Interaction Medium

    Thought itself will become an interaction medium, but this path is longer than imagined:

    • Neuralink Latest Progress: Musk's Neuralink completed its first human implant in 2024 — the first subject, Noland Arbaugh, controlled a computer mouse with his thoughts to play chess. Currently, implantable BCIs (brain-computer interfaces) primarily target assistive scenarios for paralyzed patients, aiming to help them "operate" the digital world again.
    • Non-invasive BCI: Multiple companies are developing non-invasive headbands (such as Kernel, OpenBCI) that can read brain signals without surgery, but with far lower precision than invasive ones. We're still quite far from "typing with thoughts."
    • Consumer Outlook: BCI is 10-20 years from consumer-level phone interaction, but may first be used in accessibility assistance and focus monitoring. Ethical and privacy issues ("Whose privacy do my brain waves belong to?") will become debate focal points before the technology matures.

    III. The Phone's "Disappearance" and New Identity Foundation

    Another future evolution direction for the phone may be "disappearing" — becoming an omnipresent "behind-the-scenes enabler" and the sole foundation of your digital identity:

    • : Your cloud personal data vault is the center.: Instantly complete "prove you are you" authentication — no need to manually enter verification codes when logging into any service.
    • An ultimate question always exists: Are we "gods" empowered by technology, or "brains in vats" fed by algorithms?: Pre-set digital asset inheritance plans during new device activation, making "digital afterlife" a factory default.
    • When you unconsciously light up the screen every few minutes, is this your habit or a designed "addictive behavior"?: Your cloud-based personal data vault is the center; hardware is just an access point. Change phones or devices — your identity and data always follow you.

    IV. Ethical Reflection: Are We Still the Masters of Our Phones?

    Let automation be your faithful "co-pilot."

    • AI Ethics: When on-device AI understands your preferences better than you do, is your "choice" an expression of free will or a guided outcome? When AI Agents place orders and reply to messages on your behalf, where do responsibility and boundaries lie?
    • Data Sovereignty: Does your health data, brain wave data, and biometric data belong to you, the device manufacturer, or the cloud service provider? The Personal Information Protection Law and EU GDPR are just starting points — the true implementation of "data portability rights" and "the right to be forgotten" still has a long way to go.
    • Digital Divide: AI phones, foldable screens, and satellite communications are widening the gap between those who "can afford" and those who "can't." Equitable access to digital infrastructure will become a new social issue — just as critical as "knowing how to use the internet" was 20 years ago.
    • Build your stable "digital rear base."
    • Regularly perform "digital decluttering" and "social fasting."

    V. Stay Connected, Stay Independent — Your Digital Life Philosophy

    No matter how technology evolves, these digital life philosophies will still apply 10 years from now:

    1. Try It: Draft Your "Personal Digital Device Terms of Service"
    2. Write a simple "terms of service" for you and your phone to define your relationship. For example:
    3. Article 1: My attention time belongs to me. You should proactively enter "Do Not Disturb" mode when I am working/spending time with family.
    4. Article 2: My personal data is my property. Your primary responsibility is secure encryption and convenient syncing.
    5. Article 3: Our common goal is to improve life efficiency and experience. If you make me addicted through manipulative design, I have the right to uninstall you.

    V. Appendices

    Write a simple "terms of service" for yourself and your phone (and future AR glasses and AI assistants) to define your relationship. For example:

    • Appendix A: New Phone Unboxing "Step-by-Step" Guide
    • 1. Unboxing Inspection "Three-Step Process":
    • Check Appearance

    Chapter Summary

    • Vision Pro and AR glasses are new computing entry points beyond phones, but won't replace phones in the short term
    • BCI is 10-20 years from consumer use; ethical issues will mature before the technology does
    • The phone is evolving toward "disappearing" — from device-centric to identity-centric
    • AI ethics, data sovereignty, and the digital divide are core issues for the next 10 years
    • Staying connected while staying independent is the timeless philosophy of digital life

    Chapter 34: In-Depth Guide to Car-Phone Connectivity — The Fusion of Phone and Automobile

    Cars are evolving from "four wheels plus a sofa" to "four wheels plus a smartphone." Whether you drive a gas car or an EV, the relationship between your phone and car infotainment system determines your driving experience. This chapter clarifies the three routes for car-phone connectivity, the characteristics of each camp's system, and tips that make driving easier.

    I. Three Routes for Car-Phone Connectivity

    There are currently three approaches to connecting phones with cars. Understanding them means understanding the entire ecosystem:

    • Phone Casting to Car Screen: The car screen acts as just a "monitor" and "speaker" — computing and map data come from the phone. Representative solutions: Apple CarPlay, Google Android Auto, Huawei HiCar, Baidu CarLife. The advantage is that the phone ecosystem is directly brought to the car without reinstalling apps; the disadvantage is that the car's own hardware capabilities go unused.
    • Deep Integration of Phone and Car System: The car system is independent but shares accounts, apps, and data with the phone, and can even "hand off" tasks. Representative solutions: HarmonyOS Cockpit (AITO/Luxeed), BYD DiLink, NIO OS, Li Auto system. The advantage is an integrated experience; the disadvantage is being locked into one brand ecosystem.
    • CarPlay 2.0 Deep Integration: The next-generation CarPlay released by Apple in 2025 no longer just "casts" — it takes over core functions like the instrument cluster, climate control, and seat adjustment. Ferrari, Aston Martin, and Porsche are among the first to adopt it, marking a new era where "phone manufacturers drive the car infotainment system."

    II. CarPlay / Android Auto / HiCar Comparison

    The three mainstream casting solutions each have their strengths. Use this table when choosing a car or phone:

    Solution Supported Phone OS Supported Car Models Feature Richness China Availability
    Apple CarPlay iPhone only Very wide, most car models support it High — maps/music/phone/messages all work Good, works natively
    Android Auto Android (domestic phones need service framework) Fairly wide, mainly joint venture/imported cars High, comparable to CarPlay Average, requires VPN to activate
    Huawei HiCar Mainly Huawei phones, some support other Android Domestic cars and some joint venture models Fairly high, can integrate with HarmonyOS Cockpit Excellent, local ecosystem
    Baidu CarLife Both iOS and Android Fairly wide, common retrofit for older cars Medium, updates are slow Excellent, local ecosystem

    III. HarmonyOS Cockpit: Seamless Flow Between Phone and Car

    If CarPlay is "casting phone to car," HarmonyOS Cockpit is "phone and car are already family." The collaboration between Huawei phones and AITO/Luxeed car systems represents the highest level of domestic car-phone connectivity:

    • Super Desktop: The car system directly accesses apps on the phone — no need to reinstall on the car. Music playing on the phone and navigation routes automatically continue on the car screen when you get in, and return to the phone when you get out — seamless throughout.
    • App Handoff: Navigation set on the phone is automatically taken over by the car system when you close the door; when you arrive at the parking lot, the phone continues walking navigation to the final destination. The "last mile" is no longer a gap.
    • Shared Account Between Phone and Car: Log into your Huawei account once, and the car system automatically syncs your music membership, map favorites, schedule, and contacts. The car and phone are different terminals of the same identity, not two independent systems.

    IV. Car Systems from New Automakers

    Domestic EV infotainment systems have evolved from "navigation + music" to mobile smart terminals, each with distinctive approaches:

    • NIO OS: The NOMI voice assistant is an industry benchmark — it can recognize multiple commands and contextual continuous dialogue, with emotional expressions. The NIO Phone turns the phone into a "car key + second screen," deeply integrated with the NIO ecosystem.
    • Li Auto System: Multi-screen interaction is the highlight — the front passenger screen can independently play shows, and the rear screen can play cartoons. "Task Master" lets you customize scenarios, like "auto-pause music when door opens, resume when closed."
    • Xiaomi HyperOS Car System: Deeply integrated with Xiaomi phones, watches, and home appliances. Alarms set on the phone remind you on the car system; when navigating home, the home AC turns on in advance. HyperOS connects the "person-car-home ecosystem."
    • BYD DiLink: The signature rotating screen — vertical for short videos, horizontal for maps, adapting to app orientation. Built-in app store leads in ecosystem richness among traditional automakers.

    V. Phone as Car System — Can It Work?

    If your car system is too old or too hard to use, can you just use your phone instead? The answer: yes, but it depends on the scenario.

    • Motorola Ready For / Desktop Mode: Some Motorola, Samsung, and Huawei phones support "Desktop Mode" — connect a monitor and it becomes a simple computer. In theory, it could connect to a car screen, but real-world compatibility varies, and it lacks car-specific interactions (like steering wheel buttons).
    • Phone Mount vs. Built-in Car System: If the built-in car system lags or maps are outdated, a sturdy phone mount + phone navigation is a practical choice. But note: ① small phone screen is hard to see while driving; ② summer heat can cause the phone to thermal-throttle or shut down; ③ long navigation drains battery fast — you need a car charger.
    • Recommendation: For short trips or temporary use, a phone mount is fine; for daily commuting and long trips, upgrading to a CarPlay/HiCar-enabled system or installing an aftermarket unit is better for both experience and safety.

    Security Reminder

    Regardless of which solution you use, operating your phone while driving violates traffic rules. A phone mount is only for "viewing navigation" — not for "operating the phone." Set destinations, switch songs, etc. only after pulling over, or use voice control.

    VI. Practical Tips

    • Unstable Wireless CarPlay Connection: ① Turn off car Bluetooth and re-pair; ② Delete paired device records on the car side and reconnect; ③ Check if your phone is connected to multiple Bluetooth devices causing conflicts; ④ Update car firmware and phone system to the latest version; ⑤ If all else fails, switch to wired CarPlay — more stable.
    • Car Data Plan Used Up: ① Turn on phone hotspot and connect the car system to it; ② In car settings, switch "high data consumption" apps (like video and streaming music) to Wi-Fi; ③ Regularly clear the car's offline map cache.
    • Driving Mode Auto-Trigger: ① iOS "Focus" set to "auto-enable when connected to car Bluetooth," automatically blocking non-urgent notifications; ② Android "Driving Mode" or third-party apps (like Tasker) can auto-mute and auto-reply to messages when connected to Bluetooth; ③ Huawei phones can set "smart payment" to auto-switch music to the car system when you get in.

    Tips When Choosing a Car

    If you care about the infotainment experience, be sure to test at the dealership: ① Bring your phone and test CarPlay/HiCar connection stability; ② Test voice assistant response speed and command recognition; ③ Check if the app store has your frequently used apps; ④ Pay attention to OTA update frequency — good car systems are built through software iteration.

    Hands-On: Optimize Your Car Connectivity Experience

    1. Confirm which connectivity solution your phone and car support (CarPlay / HiCar / Android Auto / CarLife).
    2. Clear the car's Bluetooth pairing list once, keeping only your commonly used phones to reduce connection conflicts.
    3. Set up a "Driving Focus" that auto-activates when connected to car Bluetooth.
    4. Download the car brand app (e.g., HarmonyOS Smart Driving, Li Auto, NIO App) to see if you can remotely control AC and check vehicle status.

    Chapter Summary

    • Three connectivity routes: casting (CarPlay etc.), deep integration (HarmonyOS Cockpit etc.), CarPlay 2.0 deep integration
    • CarPlay has the widest ecosystem; HiCar has the best domestic experience; Android Auto requires workarounds in China; CarLife suits older cars
    • HarmonyOS Cockpit's Super Desktop, App Handoff, and shared accounts represent the deep integration direction
    • NIO NOMI, Li Auto multi-screen, Xiaomi person-car-home, BYD rotating screen — each has its own style
    • Using a phone as car system is only suitable for temporary scenarios — upgrade or install aftermarket for long-term use
    • Practical tips: CarPlay reconnection, phone hotspot for data, Bluetooth-triggered driving mode

    Children and Phones Special Topic (Chapter 35)

    The relationship between children and phones is one of the biggest headaches for this generation of parents. Give it too early, fear addiction; too late, fear falling behind. Control too much, fear rebellion; too little, fear losing control. This chapter doesn't take sides or lecture — it breaks down "when to give, how to manage, how to teach, how to protect" into actionable steps, helping you be a confident parent in the digital age.

    Chapter 35: Children and Phones — An Educational Guide for the Digital Age

    This chapter doesn't paint phones as "monsters," nor does it advocate "the earlier the smarter." We'll go step by step by age: giving devices, setting rules, teaching literacy, and protecting health.

    I. At What Age Should Kids Get a Phone?

    There's no standard answer, but there are age baselines. Giving a phone too early — the child's prefrontal cortex isn't fully developed, so self-control can't keep up with algorithms' "temptation design." Too late — the child may become "socially disconnected" from peers. Here are age-based recommendations:

    • Ages 3-6: Try to avoid phones entirely. If needed, no more than 15 minutes per session, with parent-selected educational cartoons, and must beco-viewed with a parent. Screen time has the greatest impact on vision and attention development at this stage.
    • Ages 7-9: Can "borrow" a parent's device for online classes, audiobooks, and research. Start establishing "request before use, return after" rules. No dedicated phone.
    • Ages 10-12: Consider a "feature phone" or kids' smartwatch for school commute communication. If a smartphone is truly needed, enable strict parental controls.
    • Ages 13+: Entering middle school, social needs increase. A smartphone can be given, but with a "usage agreement" and regular reviews.

    The "Good Enough" Principle

    A child's first phone doesn't need to be a flagship. "Excess performance" processors often end up running games. Choose a mid-range phone with adequate battery, eye-friendly screen, or an official refurbished model — easier to manage. Budget reference: 1,500-2,500 yuan covers most students' needs.

    Smartwatch as a Transition

    If you just want to solve the "can I reach them after school" problem, a kids' smartwatch is better than a phone. It can only make calls, send voice messages, and track location — no browser or short videos, naturally limiting "addiction gateways":

    • XiaoTianCai (Little Genius) Phone Watch: Most complete ecosystem, peer social "tap to add friend" is its core selling point, but the proprietary app ecosystem is relatively closed.
    • Huawei Kids' Watch: Good integration with Huawei phones, accurate positioning, supports video calls, high value for money.
    • Xiaomi Kids' Watch: Affordable, complete basic features, suitable for budget-conscious families.

    When buying a watch, note: choose one that supports4G full network compatibilitymodels (2G/3G are being phased out), and check carrier kids' plan rates.

    II. Complete Parental Control Guide

    Before giving the device to the child, the first thing isn't turning it on — it's setting up parental controls. Both platforms have native solutions:

    iOS: Screen Time
    • App Limits: Settings > Screen Time > App Limits — set daily time limits per app category (e.g., games 30 minutes).
    • Downtime: Set a daily "lights out" period (e.g., 22:00-7:00) — all apps gray out, only phone calls available.
    • Content Restrictions: Filter movies, web content, and app installs by age, and disable in-app purchases.
    • Family Sharing: Use the parent's iPhone to remotely manage the child's device, approve download requests, and view usage reports.
    Android: Google Family Link / Brand Parental Controls
    • Google Family Link: Google's official solution — remotely manage device usage time, lock devices, view activity reports. Availability on domestic Android varies by model.
    • Xiaomi Kids Space: Settings > Kids Space — set usage time, whitelist apps, requires parent password to exit.
    • Huawei Student Mode: Settings > Healthy Phone Usage > Student Mode — restrict usage times and apps, supports remote management.
    • OPPO/vivo Kids Mode: Enable in "Settings" or the dedicated "Kids Space" app — similar principle.
    Feature iOS Screen Time Android Family Link / Brand Solutions
    App LimitsSupported, by categorySupported, per app
    DowntimeSupportedSupported (brand solutions vary slightly)
    Content FilteringSystem-level, more thoroughDepends on brand, varies
    Remote ManagementFamily SharingFamily Link / Brand Cloud
    App Install ApprovalRequires parent approvalFamily Link supports it

    Parental Controls Aren't "Once and Done"

    Kids can always find ways to bypass them (search "how to crack Screen Time" online — tons of tutorials). Technical measures are just the baseline — the real defense is parent-child communication and trust. I recommend reviewing usage reports together with your child monthly, rather than unilaterally monitoring.

    III. Youth Mode

    Major content platforms have built-in "Youth Mode" — when enabled, it limits usage time, filters inappropriate content, and disables in-app purchases and tipping. This is a legally mandated feature, butparents must actively enable it and set a password:

    • Douyin/Kuaishou Youth Mode: 40 minutes daily (disabled 22:00-6:00), only curated science and educational videos shown — no livestreaming, no tipping, no recharging.
    • WeChat Youth Mode: Limits WeChat Pay (requires parent-authorized amount), restricts Official Account and Channels content, Shake and Nearby features are disabled by default.
    • Game Anti-Addiction System: National-level real-name authentication + time limits. Minors can only log into games on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and public holidays from 20:00-21:00, for 1 hour per day.

    Don't Use Parents' IDs for Real-Name Authentication to "Borrow Accounts"

    Many kids use parents' IDs to register game accounts and bypass anti-addiction. This violates user agreements and removes protections. Parents should safeguard their payment passwords and identity information — don't "lend accounts" to children for convenience.

    IV. Digital Literacy Education

    Technology can block 90% of risks — the remaining 10% depends on the child's judgment. Rather than "no internet," it's more important to teach them "how to use the internet":

    • Privacy protection: Don't share real name, school, or home address with strangers. Don't send personal photos, ID cards, or family group photos. Keep location services off by default, only enable when needed.
    • Cyberbullying Recognition and Response: Being insulted, ostracized, or having photos maliciously edited are all forms of bullying. Tell your child: don't retaliate, don't delete evidence, tell a parent immediately. On WeChat, long-press the message to report — the platform will handle the bully's account.
    • Content Criticism: Teach children to distinguish "facts" from "opinions," recognize clickbait and sensationalism. Understand that algorithms only push what you want to see, not the whole picture. Treat "too good to be true" ads as always fake.
    • Cybersecurity: Don't click unfamiliar links, don't scan QR codes from unknown sources, don't download apps from non-official stores. Don't share passwords with anyone (including "best friends"). Anyone asking for verification codes is a scammer.

    Hands-On: Sign a "Phone Usage Agreement" with Your Child

    Writing rules down, both parties signing, and posting them prominently is far more effective than verbal agreements. Recommended contents:

    • Usage times: e.g., "Available 19:30-20:30 after homework is done."
    • No-phone zones: at the dinner table, in the bedroom before sleep, in class — phone put away.
    • Content boundaries: don't install apps without telling parents, don't private chat with strangers.
    • Violation consequences: e.g., "One violation halves next day's usage time."
    • Parent commitment: don't "scroll" on the phone in front of the child beyond agreed time — lead by example.

    V. Healthy Usage Habits

    Children's eyes, neck, and sleep are still developing — phone damage is greater than for adults:

    • Screen Time Recommendations: Ages 3-6: no more than 1 hour daily; ages 6-12: no limit for educational content, no more than 1 hour for entertainment; ages 12+: negotiate with the child, but entertainment no more than 2 hours.
    • Eye Protection Habits: Follow the "20-20-20 rule" — every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something 20 feet (about 6 meters) away for 20 seconds. No phone 1 hour before bed — blue light suppresses melatonin and affects sleep.
    • Posture Management: Keep the phone screen at eye level, don't hunch over. Get up and move after every 30 minutes of continuous use.
    • Family Shared Rules: Set "no-phone zones" at the dining table, bedroom, and study. During family movie time and outdoor activities, everyone puts their phone away — making "putting down the phone" a family culture, not a punishment for the child.

    Parents Are the Best "Firewall"

    Research shows a strong positive correlation between parents' phone usage time and children's. Demanding that children stay off their phones while scrolling short videos until late at night yourself makes the rules ineffective. To change your child, start by putting down your own phone.

    VI. Digital Legacy and Children

    This section is easily overlooked but very important. Children's digital assets (accounts, photos, stored value, game items) also face inheritance and privacy issues:

    • Inheritance of Children's Digital Assets: When a child unfortunately passes away, the inheritance process for social accounts, game accounts, and cloud photos is the same as for adults — requires death certificate and proof of kinship. Parents should set up "legacy contacts" or "emergency contacts" for children's important accounts in advance (e.g., Apple Legacy Contact, WeChat account inheritance).
    • Digital Privacy of Minors: The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that processing personal information of minors under 14 requires guardian consent, with dedicated privacy rules. Parents should regularly review the privacy policies of apps their children use frequently, and turn off "personalized recommendations" and "data sharing" toggles.
    • Account Registration Recommendations: Accounts registered for children should use parent-controlled email/phone numbers for unified management during the minor stage; account transfer can be done when the child reaches adulthood.

    The Other Side of "Children's Digital Legacy"

    Children are being "recorded" from birth — growth photos posted by parents, videos from kindergarten, health data from smartwatches. Once uploaded, this data is hard to completely delete. Before posting, think: Will the child feel embarrassed by this photo in ten years? Respecting your child's digital identity starts with restraining from "sharenting."

    Chapter Summary

    • There's no standard age to give a phone, but ages 3-6 should avoid it, and before 13 use a kids' watch or feature phone as transition
    • "Good enough": choose a budget phone, not a flagship — excess performance equals excess temptation
    • iOS Screen Time and Android Family Link/brand parental controls are two technical defense lines — use them together for better protection
    • Youth Mode and game anti-addiction are legally required, but parents must actively enable them and guard the passwords
    • Digital literacy is more important than technical blocking: teach kids to recognize bullying, protect privacy, and critically evaluate content
    • Healthy habits start with parents — when you put down your phone, your child will too
    • Children's digital legacy and privacy are emerging issues — set up "legacy contacts" and restrain from sharenting

    Chapter 36: Phones and Smart Home — Make Your House Think

    Your phone can do one more increasingly important job: be the remote for your whole home. From a light bulb or plug to a door lock, smart home gear is moving from "geek toy" to everyday setup. This chapter sorts out protocols, ecosystems, hubs, and starter kits, then closes with a safety checklist so "smart" doesn't backfire.

    1. Smart home protocols: Pick the right one

    Before buying a smart device, check which protocols it supports — that decides whether your phone and ecosystem can control it. Four mainstream options and their personalities:

    • Matter: Released in 2022 by the CSA (Connectivity Standards Alliance), backed by Apple, Google, Amazon, Samsung, and others. One goal: make every brand speak the same language. Rapidly becoming the unified standard from 2023–2026. Matter devices can join Apple HomeKit, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Mi Home at once — no more single-ecosystem lock-in.
    • Thread: Matter's underlying network "plumbing." Low power, self-healing mesh (if a node drops, signals reroute), fast and smooth. Devices with a Thread border router (HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, Xiaomi central hub) feel noticeably more stable.
    • Wi-Fi: Big bandwidth, connects directly to the router, but power-hungry and can clog channels with many devices. Good for cameras and robot vacuums that move lots of data.
    • Bluetooth (BLE): Easy setup, power-efficient, but short range and no mesh. Good for locks and temp/humidity sensors with tiny payloads.
    • Zigbee: Classic low-power mesh protocol; needs a dedicated hub. Devices are cheap and stable, but cross-brand interop is weak. Gradually replaced by Matter + Thread.

    Rule of thumb

    Buying smart gear in 2026? Prefer the "Matter over Thread" label — the most future-proof choice today. Older Wi-Fi or Bluetooth devices don't need to be tossed; keep using them and move to Matter on new purchases.

    2. The big three ecosystems

    Protocols are the "language"; ecosystems are the "club." Even with Matter, you'll still pick one main ecosystem for automations and voice. Quick comparison:

    Ecosystem Strengths Weaknesses Best for
    Apple HomeKit Strongest privacy (mostly local), smooth iPhone/Siri/Shortcuts integration Fewer, pricier devices; needs HomePod or Apple TV as hub Apple households that value privacy and polish
    Mi Home (Xiaomi) Widest device range, best value, solid Xiao AI More closed ecosystem, more cloud data, more ads Budget buyers who want one-stop whole-home setup
    Huawei HiLink (HarmonyOS) Seamless with HarmonyOS phone/tablet/watch; device range growing fast Fewer overseas devices; ecosystem still catching up Huawei phone users who want Super Device multi-device flow

    How to choose

    Follow your phone: iPhone → HomeKit first. Huawei → HiLink first. Other Android → Mi Home is easiest. With Matter, devices from different ecosystems can still be controlled by the same phone — no need to pick sides all at once.

    3. Your phone as the home hub

    In most starter setups, the phone is your "home hub" — control lights, AC, curtains, and security from an app, and build automations so the house "moves on its own":

    • Device control: Open HomeKit/Mi Home/Smart Life to toggle lights, change color temperature, set AC temperature, open/close curtains, and view cameras — locally or remotely.
    • Automation scenes: Combine "condition → action." Three favorites:
    • Away mode: Last person leaves (location leaves or door locks) → lights off + AC off + plugs off + cameras on + arm security.
    • Sleep mode: Every night 23:00 → main lights off + curtains close + AC to 26°C + night light on.
  • NFC tap: Stick an NFC tag by the door; tap the phone to trigger a scene (tap once for entry lights, twice for sleep). On iPhone use Shortcuts automation; on Android use Wallet or the brand app to write the tag.

    • Try it: Build a "Coming home" scene

    In your smart home app's "Automation," create one: trigger "arrive at place" (home), actions "entry light on," "AC to 26°C," "curtains close." Save it, go out for a walk, and see if the lights turn on when you return — that first success feels better than ordering new gear.

    4. Starter kit picks

    You don't need everything at once. These four cover about 80% of daily needs:

    • Smart speaker: Xiao AI (Mi Home, great value) / HomePod mini (Apple, also a Thread border router) / Alexa (broad overseas ecosystem). Note: The speaker picks your voice ecosystem — decide the ecosystem before buying.
    • Smart bulbs: Yeelight (Mi Home/Matter, adjustable color temperature and brightness, cheap) / Philips Hue (great color and stability, but needs a Hue hub and costs more). Note: Check socket type (E27/B22) and whether you need color changing.
    • Smart plugs: Xiaomi Smart Plug (cheap, energy stats) / TP-Link Kasa (good Matter support overseas). Note: For high-power appliances (water heater, space heater), always check the rated wattage and don't overload.
    • Smart locks: Loock/Xiaomi (value and Mi Home integration) / Kaadas (traditional lock maker, solid mechanics). Note: Check Matter/your ecosystem support, battery life, and where the emergency keyhole is.

    Suggested buying order

    Smart speaker first (locks your ecosystem) → then bulbs and plugs (low barrier, instant feedback) → finally locks and cameras (security-related, choose carefully). Add one category at a time so you don't end up with gear you can't use.

    5. Safety basics

    More smart devices mean a bigger attack surface. These four lines are non-negotiable — check them one by one:

    1. Change default passwords: Factory passwords for cameras, routers, and locks are public online. First thing after unboxing: set a long, unique password.
    2. Update firmware promptly: Vendor updates often fix security holes. Turn on auto-update in the app, or check manually at least monthly.
    3. Network isolation: Put IoT devices on a separate Wi-Fi (or guest network) away from your phone and computer. If one device is compromised, it's harder to pivot to your important data.
    4. Privacy: Enable camera "privacy zones" (skip bedrooms and bathrooms), turn off 24/7 cloud recording, and don't leave home camera feeds open to third-party apps long-term.

    Don't step in these traps

    • Don't use remote unlock for strangers — prefer temporary passwords that expire.
    • Don't point cameras at beds or out the window — that's your own privacy leaking.
    • Don't buy no-name "white label" gear for a bargain — it often never gets firmware updates, basically a back door into your home.

    Chapter recap

    • Matter + Thread is the 2023–2026 direction — look for that label on new gear
    • Each ecosystem has a strength: Apple for privacy/experience, Mi Home for value, Huawei for multi-device flow
    • Your phone can be the hub — set up Coming home / Away / Sleep and the house runs itself
    • Starter four: smart speaker, bulbs, plugs, locks — add them in that order
    • Change default passwords, update firmware, isolate the network, privacy-mask cameras — four safety lines you can't skip

By 2026, AI coding had evolved into Agentic Engineering — "give AI a goal and it plans, works, and checks itself." Eleven chapters cover the five thinking principles, context and requirements engineering, tools and model choice, LLM API practice, three full projects, and a quality system — taking you from "I can use AI" to "I command an AI squad."
