    Chapter 37: The Paradigm Shift — From Writing Code to Directing AI

    Congratulations — by opening this book you're standing in the middle of a professional paradigm shift. It started with one programmer's social post in 2025. Dramatic? It really happened that way.

    1. The birth of Vibe Coding: A movement sparked by one sentence

    In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy — remember this name, you'll see it again — posted a tweet that got quoted over and over: "There's a new kind of coding called Vibe Coding, where you fully give in to the vibes, ignore the code details, and let AI handle everything. You say what you see, copy-paste, and basically it just works."

    That casual-sounding remark precisely named a paradigm shift already underway: humans no longer write code line by line. Instead, we describe intent in natural language and AI implements it. Karpathy's wording was playful, but the insight is deep: once AI code generation crossed a threshold, the bottleneck stopped being "can I write this line?" and became "can I think this through clearly?"

    Quick tip: What's a "vibe"?

    "Vibe" means mood or feel. Vibe Coding is "directing AI coding by feel" — you describe what you want, AI implements it. Remember the term; it's this movement's birth certificate.

    From that moment, "coding" split in two: classic coding turns designs into syntax; new coding turns intent into instructions. The first tests your fingers; the second tests your brain.

    Vibe Coding quickly moved from joke to serious engineering concept. By mid-2026 it had grown from a social-media meme into a full methodology covering requirements, context management, iterative validation, and quality assurance. People also realized "coding by vibes" is only the beginner stage — truly efficient AI coding needs a systematic way of thinking. That way of thinking is what this book gives you.

    2. 2026 status: The Agentic Engineering era

    By August 2026, AI coding had gone through several paradigm shifts. Vibe Coding was the first spark, but people soon found that pure vibes + chat produced wildly unstable code — brilliant sometimes, broken others. So the paradigm evolved: from casual chat coding toward structured agent engineering.

    Karpathy again — in early 2026 he proposed Agentic Engineering. Unlike Vibe Coding's "say it and it generates," Agentic Engineering means: give AI a goal and let it plan steps, call tools, verify results, and iterate. AI is no longer just a code generator; it's an agent that perceives its environment, makes decisions, and takes actions.

    This shift brought three key changes:

    1. Interaction changed: From "one question, one answer" to "set the goal, then delegate."
    2. Deliverables changed: From "a piece of code" to "a complete project."
    3. Your role changed: From "review every line" to "define boundaries and accept results."

    The numbers don't lie: In Cursor 3, released April 2026, Agent mode usage overtook Tab completion for the first time — a clear sign developers had shifted at scale. Claude Code, the terminal-native AI coding tool, hit a $2.5 billion annualized revenue run rate by mid-2026. The chart below shows that crossover moment:

    Figure 1: AI coding interaction-mode usage trends (estimated from industry research; Agent mode overtakes Tab completion in 2026 Q2)

    Honest truth: tools and models change, but successful AI coding practitioners follow the same underlying methodology whether they use Cursor or Claude Code, GPT-5 or Claude 4.5. That methodology is what this guide teaches.

    3. The core mindset shift: From Coder to Conductor

    Traditional coding education teaches you to be a Coder — understand syntax, memorize APIs, debug logic. In the AI coding era, that role is being redefined. You no longer need to type every line yourself. Instead, become a Conductor: define the battlefield, set rules, assign tasks, accept results.

    The shift isn't about "can you write code" — it's about "can you think clearly about what to build." A great conductor isn't necessarily the best soldier, but they know the objective, terrain, and troop placement best. Likewise, a great AI coding practitioner doesn't need every syntax detail memorized, but must be crystal clear on goals, architectural constraints, and quality standards.

    Worth reading twice — this table captures the whole role change:

    DimensionTraditional CoderAI Conductor
    Core skillsSyntax memory, API calls, debuggingRequirements definition, context management, acceptance judgment
    How you workWrite code line by lineDescribe intent, review output
    Quality controlYou know it because you wrote itVerify AI output with tests and review
    Knowledge neededDeep mastery of a language/frameworkBroad tech literacy, deep business logic understanding
    Where the bottleneck isTyping speed and syntax memoryClarity of thought and communication
    Where errors come fromSyntax bugs, logic gapsVague requirements, missing context

    Traditional Coder vs. AI Conductor — capability comparison

    This does NOT mean coding knowledge is obsolete. Far from it: you can only review and correct AI code if you can read it; you can only judge whether AI's design is sound if you understand data structures and algorithms. Knowledge sets your "conductor ceiling" — but its role shifts from "execution tool" to "judgment basis."

    4. Why methodology beats tools

    Tools iterate every three months; methodology evolves only every three years. Learn a tool's mechanics and it may be obsolete in three months; master a way of thinking and it still applies three years later.

    Many beginners ask first: "Which tool is best?" "Which model is strongest?" Those questions aren't unimportant — they're just the wrong priority. The 2026 tool landscape looks nothing like 2025: Trae and Qoder rose and fell, Cursor went from plugin to standalone IDE to Cursor 3, Claude Code went from experiment to terminal-coding mainstream. Yet behind all that churn, the thinking principles of successful practitioners barely changed.

    That's why this book won't waste pages on one tool's button-by-button walkthrough — those go stale the moment they're written. Instead, it focuses entirely on a proven thinking methodology: how to think about requirements, how to talk to AI, how to verify output, how to keep iterating. Master this and any tool is quick to pick up. Learn only tool steps and every new tool starts you from zero.

    Reassurance for absolute beginners

    If you're starting from zero, don't let "methodology" scare you. It's not abstract philosophy — it's an operator's manual for "how to think when something breaks." Like cooking: you can follow a recipe (tool steps), but a real chef understands "why season this way" and "how to control heat" (methodology). This book starts from the basics, pairs every principle with concrete examples, and makes sure you understand both "what" and "how."

    Hands-on: Take a "role photo" of yourself today

    On a piece of paper, answer three questions: ① How do you currently use AI to write code (if at all)? ② Are you more like the "Coder" or the "Conductor" in the table above? ③ How would you like to describe your workflow three months from now? Tuck it in the book and revisit after Chapter 47 — you'll be surprised how fast things change.

    • By 2026 it evolved into Agentic Engineering: set goals, delegate, AI plans and executes, humans accept results

    Chapter 38: Five Thinking Principles of AI Coding

    If this book makes you remember only one chapter, make it this one. The five thinking principles are the book's heart. Everything after — context, requirements, prompts, quality — expands these five in different scenarios. Don't worry: none are hard to grasp, but each deserves a few projects to sink into muscle memory.

    The story starts with a fun origin: when Andrej Karpathy open-sourced his project, he attached a 70-line CLAUDE.md summarizing four core principles for working with AI. That file earned 70,000+ GitHub Stars and became the most widely cited playbook for AI coding practitioners worldwide. These four principles aren't empty slogans — they're actionable thinking habits distilled from massive practice. This book adds a fifth — Iterate and Verify — completing the five-principle system.

    Why is a 70-line file so valuable?

    What do 70,000 Stars mean? Most GitHub projects never get close. That a 70-line text file earned them proves one thing: in the AI era the scarcest resource isn't code — it's the ability to "think clearly." Those 70 lines are a concentrated form of clarity.

    1. Principle 1: Think Before Coding

    This is the most counterintuitive of the five. If AI can write code for us, why think first? Simple: AI output quality tracks your input quality. If you haven't figured out what you want, AI's answers will trap you in endless revision loops — aka "AI getting lost with you."

    "Think first" means answering three questions before prompting AI — an inseparable "thinking triangle":

    1. What problem am I solving? (Goal)
    2. What should the result look like? (Acceptance criteria)
    3. What constraints must I respect? (Boundaries)
    Thinking dimensionVague input (bad)Clear input (good)
    Problem definitionMake me a websiteMake a personal tool site with entry cards for 3 small AI tools
    Expected resultMake it look niceResponsive layout, dark theme, hover animation on cards, works on mobile
    Constraints(Not stated)No frameworks, pure HTML+CSS+JS, single-file deploy, no backend

    Vague vs. clear input for the same request

    Note: Think first ≠ write a perfect spec first

    "Think first" doesn't mean "write a perfect PRD before starting." It's a quick but structured thinking pass — 30 seconds on those three questions beats 30 minutes of back-and-forth in chat. Small tasks need short answers; big projects can expand them into full requirement docs (see Chapter 40).

    2. Principle 2: Simplicity First

    The biggest trap in AI coding isn't "can't build it" — it's "builds too much." Ask AI for a "user management system" and it may generate auth, permissions, roles, audit logs, data export — when all you need is a simple login page. Overbuilding is the main cause of bloated AI code.

    "Simplicity First" means following the "minimum viable" rule every time you prompt: implement the core with the least code, solve the problem with the simplest design, validate the idea with the fewest features. Karpathy put it well: "If you need a discounted price, you don't need an e-commerce engine."

    In practice, Simplicity First means a few concrete habits:

    • Have AI implement one feature at a time, not the entire system in one prompt;
    • Prefer standard libraries and simple designs over heavy dependencies;
    • If 50 lines can solve it, don't let AI write 500;
    • When AI's output goes beyond scope, boldly tell it to cut the extras.
    ScenarioOverbuilt (avoid)Simple (recommended)
    Need to store dataSet up MySQL + ORMStart with JSON files or SQLite
    Need user loginOAuth2.0 + JWT + role permissionsStart with simple password auth
    Need a frontend frameworkReact + Redux + RouterTry plain HTML + vanilla JS first
    Need to deployDocker + CI/CD + K8sGet it running locally first

    Overbuilt vs. simple approaches for common scenarios

    3. Principle 3: Surgical Changes

    When iterating an existing project, every change should be surgical — touch only what must change. This matters especially in AI coding because AI loves to "tidy up while it's in there": you ask it to fix one bug and it refactors half a file.

    Surgical Changes means every prompt explicitly states the scope and boundaries: "Only modify the calculate_discount function," "don't touch anything else," "keep the existing code style." If AI goes beyond scope, immediately tell it to revert the extras.

    Karpathy illustrated this with a diff example. Say you ask AI to add "member pricing" to a cart discount function. Good output: only that function changes, a few lines added. Bad output: the whole file is refactored — the new code might look "cleaner," but you can't be sure it didn't introduce bugs. In AI coding, "looks better" is never a reason to ignore instructions.

    Bad prompt (vague scope)

    Help me optimize this project's discount logic

    Good prompt (precise scope)

    Only modify the calculate_discount function in cart.py: 1. Add member pricing on top of existing discounts 2. Members get an extra 10% off 3. Do not change the function signature or other functions 4. Keep the existing variable naming style

    4. Principle 4: Goal-Driven Execution

    This principle answers a key question: should you tell AI "how to do it" or "what to do"? Karpathy's answer is the latter. Instead of "create a class, then add methods, then write tests," say "I need a tool that parses a CSV and counts unique values per column." Let AI pick the implementation path; you accept the result.

    Goal-driven execution has a double payoff. AI gets room to choose the best path instead of being boxed in by your middle steps. You shift attention from "how" to "is the result right" — exactly what a conductor should do.

    Note: Goal-driven ≠ hands-off

    You still need strict acceptance after AI runs: Does the result meet the need? Are edge cases handled? Any obvious overengineering? If it's off, give specific feedback — not "redo it," but "this raises IndexError on empty list input; please add a null/empty check."

    Instruction styleExampleOutcome
    Imperative (how)"First create a Python class called DataParser, add a parse method that takes filename, use the csv module to read…"AI becomes a typist; your middle steps may not be optimal
    Goal-based (what)"I need a tool: read a CSV, count unique values per column, output JSON. Please implement it fully."AI picks the best path; you accept the result

    Imperative vs. goal-based instructions

    5. Principle 5: Iterate and Verify

    This is the fifth principle this book adds to Karpathy's four. Core belief: AI's first output is almost never final. Effective AI coding is a generate → verify → correct loop, not one-shot prompt → output.

    "Iterate and Verify" isn't passive "try again if wrong" — it's a structured validation flow. After each AI output, verify on three levels:

    • Level 1 · Functional: Does it run? Are inputs and outputs right?
    • Level 2 · Boundary: What about empty, oversized, or invalid inputs?
    • Level 3 · Architectural: Is the structure sound? Hardcoded values? Easy to extend later?
    Define the goal➜ AI generates code➜ Feature check
    Pass➜ Edge-case check➜ Pass➜ Architecture review➜ Passed — go to the next step
    Fail➜ Give specific feedback➜ Regenerate

    Figure 2: The iterative verification loop in AI coding

    The key step is "give specific feedback." When verification fails, don't say "wrong, redo." Say "the function raises IndexError on empty list input; please add an empty check on line 15." Specific feedback lets AI fix precisely; vague feedback just makes it re-guess your intent.

    6. Harness Engineering: Agent = Model + Harness

    In mid-2026, Harness Engineering started trending in the AI coding community. The core formula is simple:

    An agent's capability = model capability × harness quality

    Model capability is the brain's intelligence ceiling; the Harness is the "work environment" around it — context management, tool integration, workflow orchestration, memory systems, and more.

    This explains a common puzzle: with the same GPT-4 or Claude, why do some people ship stunning projects while others get mediocre code? The difference isn't the model — it's the harness. A good harness includes clear project spec files, sensible tool integration, organized conversation context, and solid verification flow. The model sets the ceiling; the harness decides how much of it you can use.

    The genius intern analogy

    Think of the model as a genius intern — sky-high IQ, but without project docs, tool guidance, deadlines, and acceptance criteria, they won't ship great work. Harness Engineering is the craft of "setting up a genius intern's workspace."

    The rest of this book is essentially about building a good harness: Chapter 39 teaches context management (project memory), Chapter 40 requirements (PRD), Chapter 43 conversation technique (prompt layering), Chapter 45 quality assurance (verification flow). Together, that's your harness.

    Hands-on: Break down your next idea with the "thinking triangle"

    Pick a small thing you've wanted to build but never started (a countdown page, a drink-water reminder script). Spend 3 minutes answering: ① What problem does it solve? ② What should it look like done? ③ What constraints (time, tech, environment)? Write the answers as one paragraph. Congratulations — you just did your first Think Before Coding. That paragraph is a solid high-quality prompt.

    Chapter recap

    • Five principles from Karpathy's 70-line CLAUDE.md (70K+ Stars); this book adds "Iterate and Verify"
    • Think Before Coding: Answer three questions first — what, what result, what constraints?
    • Simplicity First: AI's biggest trap is building too much — a discount doesn't need an e-commerce engine
    • Surgical Changes: Change with surgical precision; refuse AI's "while I'm in here" refactors
    • Goal-Driven Execution: Say what, not how — let AI choose the path
    • Iterate and Verify: Three-level checks (functional/boundary/architecture) + specific feedback, loop
    • Harness Engineering: Ability = Model × Harness — manage AI like a genius intern's workspace

    Chapter 39: Context Engineering — Make AI Understand You

    Ever open a new chat and watch AI forget everything about your project? It's not messing with you — it's just forgetful by design. This chapter teaches you to install a "long-term memory system" for AI, and introduces one of 2026's hottest development paradigms: Spec-Driven Development.

    1. Project memory files: AI's long-term memory

    AI models have a fundamental limit: their memory is short-term. At the start of every conversation, AI knows nothing about your project. You'd have to keep saying "we use React," "backend is Node.js," "database is PostgreSQL," "code style uses double quotes." That's inefficient and easy to miss — like onboarding a new colleague every single day.

    The fix is a project memory file — a plain text file in the project root that AI tools auto-read at the start of each conversation. Different tools use different names:

    ToolFile name
    Cursor.cursorrules
    Claude CodeCLAUDE.md
    GitHub Copilotcopilot-instructions.md
    Generic optionAGENTS.md

    Project memory file naming conventions by tool

    Names differ, but the idea is the same: write down what you want AI to always remember. A good project memory file includes: project overview (what this is), tech stack (what you're using), code conventions (naming, indentation, comments), directory layout (how code is organized), and development practices (branch strategy, commit style, testing). Karpathy's CLAUDE.md is only 70 lines but covers all key info — concise and complete.

    CLAUDE.md···
    # Project: personal finance tracker
## Overview
A full-stack personal finance tracker that helps users record daily income and expenses.
## Tech stack
- Frontend: React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS
- Backend: Node.js + Express + TypeScript
- Database: SQLite (dev) / PostgreSQL (production)
- Testing: Vitest
## Code style
- Use double quotes
- 2-space indentation
- Function names in camelCase
- Type definitions in PascalCase
- Every function must have a JSDoc comment
## Directory structure
/src
  /frontend  - frontend code
  /backend   - backend code
  /shared    - types shared by frontend and backend
  /tests     - test files
## Development conventions
- Commit messages in English
- New features must have tests written first
- APIs always return { success, data, error }

    Note: Don't turn it into a second requirements doc

    Watch the length — don't write a multi-page requirements document. The purpose is to help AI build background context quickly, not to describe every feature in detail. Keep it concise, structured, and limited to what AI needs to know.

    2. Spec-Driven Development (SDD)

    Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is a 2026-era paradigm with one core idea: write the spec first, then the code. Unlike classic TDD (test-driven development), SDD "specs" aren't just test cases — they include requirement descriptions, interface definitions, data models, and more. AI generates code from those specs; humans write and maintain the specs.

    SDD workflow in five steps:

    1. Describe the requirement spec in natural language (in a .md file);
    2. Define interfaces and data structures (in the spec file);
    3. Have AI generate code from the spec;
    4. Run tests to verify the output matches the spec;
    5. If it doesn't match, fix the spec or have AI fix the code.

    In this flow, the spec file is the single source of truth — code can be regenerated, but the spec must be right first.

    Write the spec file➜ Is the spec complete?
    Complete➜ AI generates code from the spec➜ Run tests to verify the output
    Incomplete / tests fail➜ Code problem → fix the code; spec problem → fix the spec➜ Back to verification
    All pass → deliver

    Figure 3: Spec-Driven Development (SDD) workflow

    SDD's advantage: specs are more stable than code. When models or tools change, your spec file stays valid — just have the new AI tool regenerate the code. That's why this book insists methodology beats tools: the spec file is the concrete carrier of your methodology.

    3. Context window management

    Even with a project memory file, you'll still hit "not enough context." AI context windows (how much info they can handle at once) are limited. When a chat gets too long or pulls in too many files, AI "forgets" early info and quality drops — like chatting with a friend for six hours and them forgetting the first thing you said.

    The core strategy for context windows is layered referencing:

    Context layerContentHow to manage
    Layer 1: Project memoryTech stack, conventions, directory structureWritten in CLAUDE.md etc., auto-loaded — no need to repeat
    Layer 2: File referencesCode files for the current taskReference precisely with @; don't paste entire files into chat
    Layer 3: Conversation contextChat history for the current taskStart a new chat after finishing a task to avoid context bloat
    Layer 4: Immediate instructionsSpecific requirements for the current stepClear, concise, targeted — avoid long-winded descriptions

    Layered context window management

    4. Practical tips for context engineering

    Context engineering isn't a one-time setup — it's ongoing tuning. Here are tips proven over and over in practice:

    1. Keep the memory file in sync with the project. When you add a new technology or change the architecture, update the memory file right away instead of explaining it ad hoc in chat.
    2. Prefer @ references over pasting whole files. Most AI coding tools support @file or @folder syntax and inject content in the background — more efficient and cleaner than manual paste.
    3. Keep chats short and focused. One conversation handles one task or one feature. Start a new chat for the next one. Long chats burn context and make AI "distracted."
    4. Show AI the result, don't just describe it. When you hit a bug, @-reference the raw error log instead of saying "there's some error." AI works better with original information than your paraphrase.
    5. Clean up and archive regularly. Finished chats and temp files clutter the workspace. Cleaning them keeps the project tidy and helps AI understand the structure faster.

    Hands-on: Write a 70-line memory file for your project

    Pick a project you're doing (or planning) and write a CLAUDE.md: project overview (2–3 sentences), tech stack (list it), code conventions (3–5 rules), directory structure (draw a tree), dev practices (2–3 items). Keep it under 70 lines — you'll find your own understanding of the project sharpens too.

    Chapter recap

    • AI memory is short-term: every new chat starts at zero project knowledge
    • Project memory files (CLAUDE.md etc.) are AI's long-term memory, auto-loaded each chat
    • Good memory file = overview + stack + conventions + layout + practices — 70 lines is plenty
    • SDD: spec first, then code. The spec is the single source of truth and more stable than code
    • Four context layers: project memory → @file references → chat history → immediate instructions
    • Five practical tips: keep in sync, use @, keep chats short, show raw info, clean up regularly

    Chapter 40: Requirements Engineering — Turn Ideas into AI-Ready Instructions

    If context engineering helps AI understand the background, requirements engineering helps AI know what to do this time. It's where people differ most in AI coding — same tools, same models, yet some ship stunning projects while others only make mediocre toys. The gap is rarely raw technical skill; it's the ability to express requirements.

    1. From fuzzy idea to structured requirements

    Every project starts as a fuzzy idea — "I want a budgeting app," "a personal website," "a to-do list." Nothing wrong with that, but toss it straight to AI and quality is pure luck. Requirements engineering turns that fuzzy idea into something AI can execute precisely.

    Good news: structured requirements don't need a multi-page PRD. Just answer five questions — the "five requirement elements":

    ElementQuestionExample: budgeting app
    WhoWho is it for?Personal use, tracking daily income and expenses
    WhatWhat does it do?An app that records transactions, summarizes monthly, and visualizes spending
    WhyWhy build it?To understand my spending structure and cut unnecessary expenses
    HowRoughly how?React frontend, data in browser localStorage, no backend or login yet
    ConstraintAny constraints?Solo developer, 2 weeks, no need to deploy publicly

    The five requirement elements with example

    You don't need a formal document for these five — even a quick mental pass is enough. The key is building the habit of "think clearly before you speak." Once you can answer these five clearly, your requirement descriptions naturally become structured.

    2. The art of layered requirement breakdown

    For bigger projects, one requirement description isn't enough. Break the big one into small, independently verifiable sub-requirements. This is "requirement breakdown." Core rule: each sub-requirement should be completable, verifiable, and deliverable on its own.

    For "build a personal budgeting app," a sensible breakdown:

    1. Implement basic transaction recording (add, view, delete entries);
    2. Add categories (tag entries as dining, transport, etc.);
    3. Implement monthly summaries (income and expenses by month);
    4. Add data visualization (charts for spending structure).

    Each step is a feature increment that runs and verifies on its own.

    The golden rule of breaking down requirements: after every step, the project should still be a "thing that works" — even if crudely. Never let the project sit in a state where "everything is half done but nothing works."

    Two benefits. First, you always see progress — every step adds a feature, and that positive feedback matters for long projects (humans need wins). Second, each AI task stays small, lowering the risk of misunderstanding — smaller tasks, clearer understanding, better output.

    3. PRD writing template and practice

    For larger projects (full-stack apps with frontend, backend, and multiple modules), the five elements may not be enough. You'll need a more formal PRD. One common misconception: a PRD is not for AI to read — it's for you, to clarify your thinking so you can give AI more precise instructions.

    A good PRD doesn't need to be long, but should cover six parts: project overview (one paragraph on what it is), feature list (each feature defined), technical plan (stack and rough architecture), data model (core structures), interface description (what main screens look like), and development plan (steps to finish).

    PRD.md···
    # Personal finance tracker PRD
## Project overview
A lightweight personal finance tracker supporting income/expense records, categories, monthly summaries and data visualization.
## Feature list
1. Record income/expenses: amount, type (income/expense), category, note, date
2. Category management: presets for food, transport, shopping, entertainment, other
3. Monthly summary: total income, total expenses and balance by month
4. Spending visualization: a pie chart of each category's share
5. Data export: export as CSV
## Technical approach
- Frontend: React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS
- Data storage: localStorage (no backend needed)
- Charts: Chart.js
- Build: Vite
## Data model
Record {
  id: string
  amount: number
  type: 'income' | 'expense'
  category: string
  note: string
  date: string  // YYYY-MM-DD
}
## Development plan
Step 1: basic record features (CRUD)
Step 2: category management
Step 3: monthly summaries
Step 4: data visualization
Step 5: data export

    Note the writing style: concise lists and structured formatting instead of long essays. Each feature has a clear definition; data models use simple type descriptions. This style is easy for you to read and easy for AI to understand precisely when you hand it over.

    4. Hands-on: full walkthrough from idea to plan

    Theory is boring — let's walk through a complete requirements engineering example. Suppose your idea is: "I want a study tracker that records what I learned each day."

    Step 1: Run through the five requirement elements.

    • Who: Personal use.
    • What: A tool that records daily study content, tracks study time, and reviews progress.
    • Why: Build a consistent study habit and see the accumulation.
    • How: Start with a web version, data in browser localStorage.
    • Constraint: Beginner developer, core features done in 1 week.

    Step 2: Break down the requirements.

    1. Step 1: Implement "record study entries" (date, content, duration);
    2. Step 2: Add "study time stats" (today, this week total);
    3. Step 3: Implement a "study calendar" view (like a GitHub contribution graph);
    4. Step 4: Add "study review" (randomly show a past day's entries for revision).

    Step 3: Write a short PRD. It doesn't need to be long — the breakdown above is already the PRD body. Organize it into a .md file in the project root as the shared reference for you and AI.

    Step 4: Start developing the first step. A prompt to AI could be:

    Prompt for the AI···
    I need the first feature of a learning tracker — logging learning entries.
The user can add a learning record with the date, what was studied and the duration in minutes.
Data is stored in localStorage.
The frontend uses React + TypeScript.
Please give a complete implementation.

    Notice the prompt's traits: it describes only the current step's goal (recording), without other features mixed in; it states technical constraints (React, TypeScript, localStorage); it gives enough info for AI to know "what" and "how roughly," while leaving implementation details to AI. That's a high-quality AI coding prompt after requirements engineering.

    Hands-on: Write a five-element card for your pet project

    Pick a small project you've been brewing and spend 5 minutes filling a card: Who / What / Why / How / Constraint, one sentence each. Then break it into 3–5 steps where each step is "usable on its own." You'll find that once written down, the idea turns from a daydream into a to-do list.

    Chapter recap

    • Five requirement elements: Who / What / Why / How / Constraint — think before you speak
    • Golden rule of breakdown: after every step the project is "something that works"
    • A PRD is for you: overview, features, technical plan, data model, UI, plan
    • Good prompt = only the current step + clear constraints + what, not how
    • Full walkthrough template: five elements → breakdown → PRD → prompt — four steps

    Chapter 41: The 2026 AI Coding Tools Landscape

    A heads-up first: this chapter is a snapshot of the August 2026 tool landscape. It'll be outdated in six months — and that's exactly the first lesson. The goal isn't "which tool to use," but a judgment framework for how to choose tools. Understand each tool's design philosophy and you can pick what fits anytime.

    1. Three schools and a choice framework

    In 2026, AI coding tools roughly fall into three schools, each with a different design philosophy. First, the panorama:

    SchoolRepresentative toolsDesign philosophyBest scenarios
    IDE-native AICursor 3, Trae, Windsurf, CodeBuddyDeeply integrate AI into the editorDaily development, code review, incremental enhancement
    Terminal agentsClaude Code, Codex CLI, AiderTerminal-first; AI operates files and commands directlyProject-wide operations, batch edits, CI/CD integration
    Cloud buildersv0, Bolt, Replit AgentCreate complete projects from scratch in the browserRapid prototypes, zero setup, instant preview

    Three schools of AI coding tools

    Choosing isn't about "which is best" but "which fits your current situation." Three practical dimensions:

    • How's your coding foundation? Beginners → cloud builders. Some experience → IDE-native AI. Advanced → terminal agents.
    • What stage is your project at? From scratch → cloud builders. Iterating → IDE-native AI. Maintenance/refactor → terminal agents.
    • What's your deployment need? Quick validation → cloud builders. Serious projects → IDE-native AI. Automated pipelines → terminal agents.

    2. IDE-native AI school

    IDE-native AI is the mainstream school: AI capabilities embedded in your code editor, keeping the classic coding experience while adding AI boosts. In 2026 the leaders are Cursor 3, Trae, Windsurf, and CodeBuddy.

    1. Cursor 3

    Cursor is the world's most widely used AI coding IDE. Cursor 3, released April 2026, marked a turning point: Agent mode usage overtook Tab completion — developers shifted from "AI completes my code" to "AI finishes my task." Key Cursor 3 features include multi-file editing (AI changes several files to complete a task), context awareness (understands project structure and dependencies), and deep terminal integration (AI runs commands and sees output right in the editor).

    2. Trae

    Trae is ByteDance's AI coding IDE with a strong user base in China. Its SOLO mode (also called Builder mode) is the classic "create a project from one sentence" — describe the need and AI handles init to code generation. Trae shines in Chinese support and domestic network adaptation; great for Chinese users to start fast.

    3. Other tools

    Windsurf (formerly Codeium) is known for smooth completions — great for developers who love "typing at the speed of thought." Tencent Cloud CodeBuddy, as a VS Code plugin, integrates well with Tencent Cloud and WeChat Mini Programs. Alibaba Tongyi Lingma and Baidu Comate offer similar IDE integrations, each tuned for Chinese scenarios.

    3. Terminal agent school

    Terminal agents are the fastest-growing school of 2026. Core idea: AI shouldn't be just an editor plugin — it should operate the whole development environment like a developer: read/write files, run commands, check output, install dependencies. Claude Code leads this school.

    1. Claude Code

    Claude Code is Anthropic's terminal AI coding tool, reaching $2.5 billion annualized revenue by mid-2026. It works completely differently from a classic IDE: describe the task in natural language in the terminal, and Claude Code reads files, edits code, runs tests, checks results, and iterates — without opening an editor.

    Claude Code's edge is full-project awareness: it isn't limited to editor windows and can browse the whole project tree and understand file dependencies. It also supports CLAUDE.md project memory files so AI knows the background at session start. For large refactors, batch edits, and test writing, terminal agents beat IDE plugins.

    2. Codex CLI and Aider

    OpenAI's Codex CLI offers a similar terminal experience and supports /import to bring in existing codebases for AI to understand. Aider is an open-source terminal AI coding tool supporting many models (GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and more) — great if you like switching models. Different flavors, same idea: give AI full development-environment control in the terminal.

    4. Cloud builder school

    Cloud builders are the most beginner-friendly school. No installs — open a browser, describe the need, and AI creates a full project in the cloud with instant preview.

    • v0 (by Vercel): Great at frontend UI components and pages — perfect for quick web prototypes.
    • Bolt: Creates full-stack apps from one sentence, including frontend, backend, and database.
    • Replit Agent: Works in Replit's cloud IDE — creates projects and can run and deploy in the cloud.

    Shared advantage: zero setup — open the browser and go. Limitation: when projects grow complex, cloud editing is less flexible than a local IDE. Best for the 0-to-1 prototype stage: validate ideas quickly in a cloud builder, then move to a local IDE for deeper development.

    5. Tools change; methodology doesn't

    If every AI coding tool disappeared tomorrow, three habits should remain: think it through before you act, take one small step at a time, and verify when done. Tools are amplifiers; methodology is the foundation. Amplifiers can be swapped out — the foundation must not shake.

    Look at 2024–2026: GitHub Copilot ruled 2024, Cursor took over in 2025, Claude Code surged in 2026. Every new tool brings "this time is different" claims, yet the people who use new tools well are the ones with solid methodology. They adapt in days; people who only memorized buttons start from scratch each time.

    Suggested path: start with any one tool, practice the five thinking principles, and once your methodology is solid, try tools from different schools to feel their design philosophies. Eventually you'll form your own combo — say Cursor for daily work, Claude Code for refactors and tests, v0 for quick prototypes. Combos vary by person; methodology is shared.

    Hands-on: Assemble your own tool kit

    Locate yourself on the three dimensions (coding foundation, project stage, deployment need). Beginner → try Bolt or v0 for a page. Some experience → use Cursor or Trae for an iteration task. Feeling ambitious → run Claude Code in the terminal. Then answer: which school fits your current stage best?

    Chapter recap

    • Three schools: IDE-native AI (daily work), terminal agents (project-scale ops), cloud builders (beginner prototypes)
    • Three questions when choosing: coding foundation? project stage? deployment need?
    • Cursor 3 Agent mode overtook Tab completion; Claude Code hit $2.5B annualized revenue
    • Cloud builders fit 0-to-1; after validation, move to a local IDE for depth
    • Tools iterate every three months: people with methodology adapt in days

    4. Getting Started with API Calls: Connecting to a Large Model from Scratch

    Many AI coding tutorials only teach you how to use the chat interface, but real 'AI programming' — having your application call a large model — goes through an API. An API (Application Programming Interface) is a communication protocol between programs. Through an API, your code can call on a large model's abilities as easily as calling a function.

    1. What Is a Token

    Before APIs, you must first understand the concept of a 'token.' A token is the basic billing unit for large models — think of it as the AI's unit of reading and writing. One token is roughly 0.75 English words (4 characters), or 0.5-1 Chinese characters. A 1,000-character Chinese passage consumes about 1,500-2,000 tokens.

    A token is not a word count, nor a character count. Large models use a dedicated tokenizer to split text into tokens. The same word can cost a different number of tokens in different models — 'artificial intelligence,' for instance, might be 3 tokens in GPT but 2 in DeepSeek. Most models' APIs return the actual number of tokens consumed, and you can check it in the API response.

    Quick Token Cost Estimates

    One million Chinese characters is roughly 1.5 million tokens. Processing 1 million characters of input plus 1 million characters of output with DeepSeek V4 Flash costs about $0.42 (around 3 yuan); the same volume with Claude Fable 5 costs about $60 (around 434 yuan). That is why your choice of model directly shapes your project's cost.

    2. Getting an API Key

    The first step in using a large model API is getting an API Key — a string used to verify your identity. Every model provider has its own API platform, where you register an account and create an API Key. Here are the API platform entry points for the mainstream models and the steps to get a key:

    Zhipu GLMopen.bigmodel.cnSign up → identity verification → create API KeyFree allowance for new users

    API platforms for mainstream models and how to get a key (August 2026)

    Security Note: Your API Key Is Your Wallet Password

    An API Key is the equivalent of your wallet password — anyone who gets hold of it can spend your quota calling the model. So: never write an API Key into your code (manage it with environment variables); never commit code containing a Key to a public Git repository; never share screenshots containing a Key on social media. If a Key leaks, delete it on the platform and create a new one immediately.

    3. Your First API Call

    Once you have an API Key, you can call a large model API from any programming language. Here is the simplest possible call, shown in Python — send one message to DeepSeek and get the reply back.

    PYTHON · Your first API call···
    # Install the SDK: pip install openai
# DeepSeek is compatible with the OpenAI SDK format — use it directly
from openai import OpenAI
import os

# 1. Create the client (the API key is read from an environment variable)
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com"
)

# 2. Send the request
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-chat",  # pick the model
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a Python coding assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Write a quicksort function."}
    ]
)

# 3. Get the reply
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

# 4. Check token usage
print(f"Input tokens: {response.usage.prompt_tokens}")
print(f"Output tokens: {response.usage.completion_tokens}")
print(f"Total tokens: {response.usage.total_tokens}")

    The core logic of this code: create a client (carrying the API Key and the model address) → build the message list (system sets the role, user is the human's input) → send the request → get the reply. This pattern works for nearly every OpenAI-compatible model — just swap the api_key and base_url to change models. That is why so many Chinese models choose to be OpenAI SDK compatible: developers can switch models by changing two lines of code, so the cost of migrating is almost nil.

    Here is what changes when you switch to another model — note that only two lines need to change:

    PYTHON · Switching models takes just two lines···
    # DeepSeek
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com"
)
# model="deepseek-chat"

# Qwen (Tongyi Qianwen, Bailian platform)
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("DASHSCOPE_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
)
# model="qwen-plus"

# Zhipu GLM
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("GLM_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://open.bigmodel.cn/api/paas/v4"
)
# model="glm-4"

# OpenAI GPT
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
    # the default base_url is fine
)
# model="gpt-5.6-terra"
    4. Streaming Responses

    In a real application, you usually don't want to wait for the AI to finish everything before displaying it in one lump — that makes users wait far too long. Streaming responses let the text appear word by word as the AI generates it, which vastly improves the user experience. Like a typewriter with letters popping out one at a time — it feels completely different to the user.

    PYTHON · Streaming responses···
    # Streaming: output one character at a time
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-chat",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Write a tutorial on bubble sort in Python"}
    ],
    stream=True  # enable streaming
)

# Receive chunk by chunk and print
for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content is not None:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="", flush=True)
# The output appears character by character, like a typewriter

    5. A Buyer's Guide to Token Plans

    Most model providers offer two billing methods: pay-as-you-go and subscription plans (Token Plans). Understanding the difference between the two can cut your costs dramatically.

    1. Pay-As-You-Go vs. Subscription Plans
    AspectPay-as-you-goSubscription plan
    Billing MethodPay only for the tokens you usePay a fixed amount up front and receive an allowance
    Best ForUnsteady usage, occasional callsSteady usage, frequent calls
    Price AdvantageStandard price20%-50% cheaper than pay-as-you-go
    FlexibilityAvailable anytime, no commitmentRequires prepayment; unused allowance may expire
    Going Over QuotaAutomatically billed as you goSwitches to pay-as-you-go once the allowance runs out
    Typical PlatformsEach model's official API platformOpenAI Plus/Pro, Claude Pro, Cursor Pro

    Comparing the Two Billing Methods

    For beginners, start with pay-as-you-go — no upfront cost, and you pay for exactly what you use. Once your monthly usage settles at a steady level (say, above 50 yuan a month), consider switching to a subscription plan for a lower unit price.

    Chinese models handle subscriptions a little differently. DeepSeek is mainly pay-as-you-go, with no monthly subscription plan — you top up and get charged based on actual usage. Qwen offers prepaid resource packages on the Bailian platform (buy a fixed amount of tokens at a discounted price). Doubao has similar prepaid options on Volcano Engine. For developers in China, the most economical combination is usually: DeepSeek pay-as-you-go (daily development) plus Doubao's free allowance (trying things out).

    3. API Aggregation Platforms

    If you need to use several models at once, an API aggregation platform is a hassle-free option. An aggregator gives you one unified API Key that can call dozens of models worldwide, with no need to register separately on each platform.

    PlatformFeaturesPrice AdvantageBest For
    OpenRouter (openrouter.ai)Overseas aggregator: one Key for models worldwideTransparent pricing with real-time comparisonFlexibly switching among many overseas models
    SiliconFlow (siliconflow.cn)China-based aggregator offering APIs for many Chinese models20%-30% below official pricesDevelopers in China comparing model prices

    Watch Out: Don't Buy 'Shared Keys'

    Do not buy so-called 'shared API Keys' on Taobao, Xianyu, or similar platforms — these Keys usually come from unclear sources, can be banned at any moment, and carry the risk of data leaks. Always get API Keys through official platforms or reputable aggregators.

    4. Cost Optimization Strategies

    Picking the right model is only the first step — knowing how to 'use it frugally' matters just as much. Here are a few cost optimization strategies proven in practice:

    1. Make the most of cache hits. Many models offer 'caching' — when your request includes content that has been processed before (such as a system prompt), that portion is billed at a tiny fraction of the normal price. DeepSeek charges just 1/60 of the regular price for cache hits. Putting your fixed system prompt at the start of the message list maximizes cache hits.
    2. Tiered routing — use a cheap model for simple tasks and an expensive one for complex tasks. For example, DeepSeek V4 Flash for text classification (2 yuan per 1M output tokens) and Claude for architecture design (181 yuan per 1M output tokens). In a typical project, 80% of calls can go to the cheap model.
    3. Cap your output length. APIs bill by output tokens, so longer output costs more. In scenarios that don't call for long-winded answers, set the max_tokens parameter to limit output length and keep the AI from 'rambling on.'
    4. Use the Batch API for non-real-time tasks. If you have lots of tasks that don't need instant responses (such as bulk data labeling or document summarization), the Batch API earns you a 50% discount. Both OpenAI and Azure offer this feature.
    5. Monitor your token usage. Most API platforms provide a usage dashboard. Check the usage breakdown regularly, find the calls that burn the most tokens, and optimize them specifically. One small prompt tweak (say, changing 'please explain in detail' to 'please explain in 3 sentences') can save 50% of your tokens.
    StrategySavingsDifficultyNotes
    Cache hitsUp to 98%LowPut fixed content at the start of your messages
    Tiered routing50%-80%MidUse a cheap model for simple tasks
    Cap output length30%-60%LowSet the max_tokens parameter
    Batch API50%LowUse batch processing for non-real-time tasks
    Prompt optimization20%-50%MidStreamline prompts and trim redundancy

    Cost optimization strategies and their impact (August 2026)

    6. Hands-On: Wiring a Large Model API into a Project

    Let's wrap up the chapter with a complete hands-on exercise — building an 'AI Summarizer': the user pastes in a long piece of text, and the app calls a large model API to produce a summary. This exercise walks through the full API workflow: environment setup, the API call, error handling, and cost control.

    PYTHON · ai_summarizer.py···
    # ai_summarizer.py - AI summarizer
import os
from openai import OpenAI

# 1. Configure (the API key is read from an environment variable — never hard-code it)
client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com"
)

def summarize(text: str, max_length: int = 200) -> dict:
    """Summarize a text

    Args:
        text: the original text to summarize
        max_length: maximum summary length (in tokens)

    Returns:
        dict: the summary plus token-usage info
    """
    try:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="deepseek-chat",
            messages=[
                {
                    "role": "system",
                    "content": "You are a summarizer."
                               "Summarize the user's text concisely."
                               "Keep the summary to 3 sentences at most."
                },
                {
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": f"Summarize the following text:\n\n{text}"
                }
            ],
            max_tokens=max_length,  # cap the output length
            temperature=0.3  # low temperature = more stable
        )

        return {
            "success": True,
            "summary": response.choices[0].message.content,
            "input_tokens": response.usage.prompt_tokens,
            "output_tokens": response.usage.completion_tokens,
            "total_tokens": response.usage.total_tokens
        }

    except Exception as e:
        return {
            "success": False,
            "error": str(e)
        }

# 2. Usage example
if __name__ == "__main__":
    long_text = """
    (paste a long text here...)
    """

    result = summarize(long_text)

    if result["success"]:
        print(f"Summary: {result['summary']}")
        print(f"Tokens used: {result['total_tokens']}")
        # estimate the cost: DeepSeek V4 Flash
        cost = result['total_tokens'] * 0.000004  # about 0.4 fen per 1,000 tokens
        print(f"Estimated cost: {cost:.4f} yuan")
    else:
        print(f"Something went wrong: {result['error']}")

    This code embodies several API best practices: the API Key is read from an environment variable and never hardcoded; the function has clear documentation and type hints; max_tokens is set to cap the output length; temperature is set low (0.3) for more stable output; error handling is complete; and token consumption is returned for cost tracking. When you have the AI write this code, you can simply tell it these requirements — it is fully capable of implementing them.

    The final lesson of this chapter: models are the "ammunition," methodology is the "tactics." The right ammunition makes the battle smoother, but without good tactics even the best ammo loses the war. Now that you know each model's strengths and how to use the APIs, you have a well-stocked arsenal — but how you fight the battle still depends on the thinking methods from the earlier chapters.

    Try It Yourself: Get Your First API Call Running

    Register on a Chinese model platform (we recommend DeepSeek or Zhipu — both give new users a free allowance), create an API Key, put it into your system environment variables (not into your code!), and then run the 'first API call' code above. The moment you see the AI's reply print out, you have crossed the line between 'using AI' and 'building AI applications.'

    Chapter 43: Conversation Engineering — How to Talk with AI Effectively

    Conversation is the core mode of interaction in AI coding. But note: 'conversation' is not the same as 'chatting' — an effective AI coding conversation is a structured communication technique, which we call 'conversation engineering.' It studies how to get the highest-quality code output in the fewest rounds of dialogue. Plainly put, this chapter teaches you how to 'make yourself clear' to the AI.

    1. Prompt Layering

    A conversation with the AI can be split into three layers, each with its own job. Once you understand these three layers, you can stack them like building blocks to assemble highly effective prompts.

    LayerPurposeExampleFrequency
    System layerSets the AI's role and the global constraints"You are a React expert; all code must be written in TypeScript"Set once at the start of the project
    Task layerDescribes the specific task at hand"Build a form component with username and password fields"Given at the start of each task
    Feedback layerEvaluates and corrects the AI's output"The password field is missing a show/hide toggle — please add it"Given based on the quality of the output

    The Three Layers of a Conversation Prompt

    The system-layer prompt usually lives in the project memory file (such as CLAUDE.md) and doesn't need to be repeated in every conversation. The task layer is what you'll use most in conversation — it should contain three elements: 'what to do,' 'what technology to use,' and 'what constraints apply.' The feedback layer is where real skill shows — good feedback lets the AI make precise corrections, while bad feedback only makes it guess again.

    Tip: The Three-Part Feedback Formula

    A practical feedback template is 'point out the problem + state the expectation + provide context.' For example: 'The error handling on line 25 only uses console.log (point out the problem); production should use the unified error handler and return a user-friendly message (state the expectation); there is a handleError function in the project you can use (provide context).' Feedback like this is ten times more effective than 'fix the error handling.'

    2. Debug Conversations: Describing Errors So the AI Can Pinpoint Them Fast

    Debugging is one of the most frequent scenarios in AI coding. When you hit a bug, how you describe the problem to the AI directly determines how quickly it can locate and fix it. Here are the four keys to a good debugging conversation:

    1. Let the AI 'see' the raw information, not your paraphrase of it. Reference the error logs, exception stack traces, and relevant code directly with @, rather than describing it as 'there seems to be some kind of error.' The AI reading the raw information is more accurate than the AI reading your interpretation.
    2. Describe the gap between 'expected behavior' and 'actual behavior.' 'I expect clicking the button to take me to the home page (expected), but when I actually click it, nothing happens (actual)' — that is far more useful than 'the button is broken.'
    3. Provide reproduction steps. 'First I enter the username, then I click the login button, and this error appears' — reproduction steps let the AI retrace your path, which makes the problem easier to pinpoint.
    4. Be clear about what you have already tried. 'I already checked the network request — it returns 200 and the data is fine' — this helps the AI rule out the directions you have already verified, instead of wasting time rechecking them.

    A Poor Debugging Description

    The button doesn't do anything when I click it, take a look

    A Good Debugging Description

    Clicking the login button does nothing. Expected behavior: clicking it should navigate to the /home page Actual behavior: nothing happens at all, and the console shows no errors Reproduction steps: 1. On the login page, enter username admin and password 123456 2. Click the "Log In" button 3. Nothing happens on the page Already ruled out: - Network requests are fine, returning 200 - The onClick event is bound - Reviewed the LoginButton component code Related files: @src/components/LoginButton.tsx @src/pages/Login.tsx

    3. Iteration Strategy: Small Quick Steps vs. Big Refactors

    Iteration in AI coding has two basic strategies, each suited to different situations. Understanding the difference helps you make the right choice in each case.

    The 'small quick steps' strategy suits feature development and bug fixes. Its core: have the AI make one small change at a time, and only move on to the next after verifying it. The advantage is that every step can be verified and rolled back, so risk stays under control; the drawback is that it is slower and takes frequent back-and-forth. Good for: developing new features, exploring when you are not sure of the best approach, and careful iteration whenever you are not fully confident in the AI's output.

    The 'big refactor' strategy suits large-scale changes where the goal is clear. Its core: describe the complete goal in one go and let the AI plan and carry out the entire change on its own. The advantage is speed — the AI sees the whole picture and can make better architectural decisions; the drawback is high risk — if the AI misunderstands, correcting it is costly. Good for: clear-cut architecture upgrades, large code migrations, and refactors protected by thorough tests.

    AspectSmall quick stepsBig refactor
    Change SizeOne feature or one bugOne module or one architectural layer
    Verification FrequencyVerify right after every changeVerify everything together once all changes are done
    Conversation RoundsMany (5-10 rounds per feature)Few (1-3 rounds per module)
    RiskLow — every step can be rolled backHigh — fixing a misunderstanding is costly
    Best ForNew features, exploratory developmentRefactors and migrations with a clear goal
    PrerequisitesNone in particularNeeds test coverage

    Comparing the Two Iteration Strategies

    In practice, the two strategies are often combined. For example, when refactoring a module, first use the 'big refactor' approach to have the AI produce an overall plan; after you review the plan, execute it step by step with 'small quick steps.' That way you keep the big-picture view while keeping execution risk under control.

    4. Context Management for Multi-Turn Conversations

    As the number of turns grows, you need to actively manage the conversation's context to avoid the 'the AI forgot what we said earlier' problem. Here are a few practical context management techniques.

    First, 'anchor' key information. At the start of a conversation, spell out the key constraints, and restate them when the time comes. For example, 'Remember, our data lives in localStorage — we can't use a database.' Repeat that constraint in the relevant change requests so the AI doesn't forget.

    Second, use the 'summarize and continue' technique. When a conversation gets very long, ask the AI to 'summarize the progress so far and what is left to do,' then open a new conversation and use that summary as the starting point. That preserves the key context while sidestepping the decay of a long conversation.

    Third, 'one conversation, one task.' This is the simplest and most effective context management strategy. Each conversation handles just one task or one feature; when it is done, open a new conversation for the next one. This naturally caps the conversation length and keeps the context clean.

    Fourth, use your tool's context management features. Most AI coding tools have a 'clear context' or 'new session' button — when you sense the quality of the AI's answers slipping, don't hesitate: open a new session. Losing a bit of conversation history beats struggling on inside a degraded context.

    Try It Yourself: Play 'Patient' for Your AI

    Deliberately build a small page in the browser with a planted bug (say, a button that does nothing). Then, following the 'good debugging description' format from this chapter, give the AI one complete description: raw information, expected vs. actual, reproduction steps, and what you have already ruled out. Feel the difference in how fast the AI pins down the problem — you will understand why 'describing the problem' is a craft of its own.

    Chapter Recap

    • Three prompt layers: system layer (kept in the memory file), task layer (what to do + technology + constraints), feedback layer (problem + expectation + context)
    • Four debugging essentials: give the raw information, expected vs. actual, reproduction steps, and what you have already ruled out
    • Small quick steps: low risk, many rounds, good for new features; big refactor: high risk, few rounds, needs test coverage
    • Four context management moves: anchor key information, summarize-and-continue, one conversation per task, and open a new session without hesitation

    Chapter 44: From 0 to 1 — A Complete Project, End to End

    The theory is done; now it is time to get your hands dirty. This chapter is not a simple 'type along' tutorial but a practical methodology covering how to think, how to ask, and how to verify. Using three projects of rising difficulty, we will show the complete thought process from requirements to finished product. No matter which tool you use, this workflow applies.

    1. Project 1: A Minimal Personal Tools Site (Beginner)

    1. Thinking Through the Requirements

    Goal: build a personal tools page that shows entry points to 3-4 handy little tools. This is a pure front-end project — no back end and no database needed. The point is not how fancy the tools are but experiencing the full 'from requirements to finished product' process.

    Applying the five requirement elements: Who — personal use. What — a web page showing tool entry points. Why — gather your frequently used tools on one page for easy access. How — a single-file HTML+CSS+JS build with no frameworks. Constraint — finish within 30 minutes, no deployment needed.

    2. Giving the Instruction

    Following the Think Before Coding principle, your instruction should carry enough information for the AI to understand the goal, without specifying every implementation detail:

    Prompt for the AI···
    Please create a personal toolbox web page with these requirements:
1. Single-file HTML (inline CSS and JS), no frameworks
2. Dark theme, modern minimalist style
3. Show 4 tool entry cards:
   - Text summarizer
   - Word counter
   - Color picker
   - QR code generator
4. Each card has an icon, a title and a short description
5. Cards have a hover animation
6. Responsive layout, usable on phones
7. A title bar at the top
Please give the complete HTML file directly.
    3. Acceptance and Iteration

    Once the AI hands over code, accept it using the three-layer check from iterative verification. First layer, functional check: does the file open in the browser? Do all 4 cards display? Do the hover animations work? Second layer, edge-case check: does the layout hold up at phone screen sizes? Do the cards wrap when the window gets narrow? Third layer, architecture check: is the code readable? Is the CSS inlined in a single style tag? Is there obvious redundancy?

    If you want one of the tool cards to actually work (rather than just be an entry point), add it gradually — implement one tool's functionality, verify it, then add the next. That is the 'small quick steps' strategy in action.

    2. Project 2: A Full-Stack Expense Tracker (Intermediate)

    1. Requirements Thinking and the PRD

    Goal: a full-stack expense-tracking app with a front end, a back end, and a database. This project is far more complex than the first and calls for the requirements engineering method from Chapter 40.

    Start by writing the PRD. Following the template from Section 3 of Chapter 40, lay out the project overview, feature list, technical plan, data model, and development plan. When choosing the tech stack, apply the Simplicity First principle — React on the front end but no complex state management like Redux; Node.js on the back end but no microservices; SQLite instead of PostgreSQL for the database (during development).

    Break the development plan into 5 steps: Step 1, the back-end API skeleton (an Express server + SQLite + CRUD endpoints); Step 2, the basic front-end pages (a records list + an add form); Step 3, hooking the front end to the back end (API calls + data display); Step 4, categories and filtering; Step 5, monthly summaries and simple charts. After every step you have 'something that works.'

    2. Setting Up the Project Memory File

    Before any coding begins, create the project memory file. This is a core context engineering practice — it gives the AI the project background at the start of every conversation.

    CLAUDE.md···
    # Project: full-stack finance tracker
## Overview
A personal finance tracker with income/expense records, categories and monthly summaries.
## Tech stack
- Frontend: React + TypeScript + Vite
- Backend: Node.js + Express + TypeScript
- Database: SQLite (via better-sqlite3)
- Shared type definitions for frontend and backend
## API conventions
- Base path: /api
- Response format:{ success: boolean, data: any, error: string }
- RESTful style
## Data model
Record { id, amount, type, category, note, date }
## Code style
- TypeScript strict mode
- 2-space indentation
- Functions have JSDoc comments
- Comments and commit messages in English
    3. Building It Step by Step

    Follow the development plan, completing each step in its own separate conversation. Here is a sample instruction for the first step:

    Prompt for the AI (Step 1)···
    I need a backend API skeleton.
Requirements:
1. Express server, port 3001
2. SQLite database, table name records
3. Fields of the records table:
   id (TEXT PRIMARY KEY)
   amount (REAL)
   type (TEXT: 'income'|'expense')
   category (TEXT)
   note (TEXT)
   date (TEXT: YYYY-MM-DD)
4. CRUD endpoints:
   GET /api/records - get all records
   POST /api/records - add a record
   PUT /api/records/:id - update a record
   DELETE /api/records/:id - delete a record
5. Error-handling middleware
Please give the complete backend code structure.

    Notice what makes this instruction work: it describes only the current step (the back-end skeleton) without mixing in front-end requirements; it explicitly lists the fields and endpoints (giving the AI firm constraints) while leaving the concrete implementation to the AI; and it follows the Goal-Driven Execution principle — saying 'what to do' rather than 'how to do it.'

    As soon as the AI hands over code, verify it immediately: run the server and test each endpoint with curl or Postman. Once everything checks out, open a new conversation for Step 2 (the basic front-end pages). Every step follows the 'instruct - verify - new conversation' loop.

    3. Project 3: An AI-Powered App (Advanced)

    1. Conceiving the Project

    Goal: an app that connects to a large model API — say, an 'AI Study Assistant' where the user enters study material and the AI generates a summary, links related concepts, and recommends learning resources. What makes this project special: your application itself is calling the AI, so you have to handle new problems like API calls, prompt engineering, and error handling.

    The most important lesson this project teaches: when you 'use AI to write code that calls AI,' you must pay extra attention to prompt engineering. The prompt your app sends to the large model API also needs to follow the principles discussed in this guide — clear, concise, and goal-driven.

    2. Key Technical Points

    This project involves a few technical points you did not meet in the first two projects:

    • API key management: keys must never be hardcoded in the code; manage them with environment variables;
    • Streaming response handling: large model replies usually arrive as a stream and need to be displayed bit by bit;
    • Token usage control: large models bill by the token, so usage must be controlled at the application level;
    • Prompt template management: different features use different prompt templates, which need to be managed in a structured way.

    The AI can help you implement all of these technical points, but you need to understand the 'why' behind each one — why can't keys be hardcoded? Why are streaming responses needed? Why must token usage be controlled? Only once you understand the 'why' can you judge whether the AI's solution makes sense.

    4. The Universal Hands-On Checklist

    Whatever the size of the project, here is a universal AI coding workflow checklist. Run through it every time you start a new project to make sure no key step slips through.

    StageWhat to DoPrinciple Applied
    1. Requirements thinkingGo through the five requirement elements and get clear on what to buildThink Before Coding
    2. Breaking down requirementsSplit big requirements into small, independently verifiable stepsSimplicity First
    3. Writing the PRDOrganize it into a structured document for referenceGoal-Driven
    4. Setting up the memory fileCreate CLAUDE.md or a similar fileHarness Engineering
    5. Building step by stepOne conversation per step: instruct - verify - nextSurgical Changes
    6. Testing and verifyingTest that each step works correctly right after finishing itIterate & Verify
    7. Reviewing the codeCheck architecture soundness, security, and maintainabilityIterate & Verify
    8. Iterating and improvingIterate based on the test and review resultsIterate & Verify

    The Universal AI Coding Workflow Checklist

    Try It Yourself: Finish 'Project 1' This Week

    Treat the 'personal tools site' from Section 1 of Chapter 44 as your first AI coding assignment: spend 5 minutes on the five elements, send the instruction to the AI (any tool will do), then accept the result with the three-layer verification. Finish it within 30 minutes — and your first AI coding creation is born. When you are done, save it somewhere safe; it is the keepsake of your move from 'reader' to 'practitioner.'

    Chapter Recap

    • Project 1 (beginner): a pure front-end tools site — experience the full workflow, done in 30 minutes
    • Project 2 (intermediate): a full-stack expense tracker — PRD + memory file + 5 steps, with something that 'works' at every step
    • Project 3 (advanced): an AI study assistant — use AI to write code that calls AI, with attention to prompt engineering
