    Chapter 45: Quality Assurance — Making AI-Written Code Reliable

    AI-written code has a telltale trait: it usually 'looks right' — tidy variable names, thorough comments, clear logic. But 'looking right' is not the same as 'being right.' Hidden problems in AI code are often harder to catch than in hand-written code, precisely because its surface quality is so high that it lulls you into lowering your guard. This chapter shows you how to build an effective quality assurance system for AI code — three lines of defense (testing, review, and version control) to turn 'looks right' into 'is right.'

    1. Test-Driven: Have the AI Write the Tests

    Testing is the first line of defense for quality in AI coding. The good news: having the AI write tests is easier and more reliable than having it write feature code — because a test's expected behavior is well defined, it rarely produces code that 'looks right but isn't.'

    The test-driven AI coding flow: first have the AI write the feature code; once the basic functionality passes, immediately have it write test cases. The test cases should cover the normal path, boundary cases, and error cases. Then have the AI fix the feature code based on the test feedback. The beauty of this flow: once the tests are written, they become a standing verification tool — any later change can be checked by running the tests to confirm no regressions slipped in.

    Prompt for the AI: write tests···
    Write unit tests for the calculate_discount function.
The test cases should cover:
1. Happy path:
   - 100-yuan item at 20% off -> 80
   - 200-yuan item at 50% off -> 100
2. Edge cases:
   - 0-yuan item at 20% off -> 0
   - 100-yuan item at 0% off -> 100 (no discount)
   - 100-yuan item at 10% off -> 100 (full price)
3. Error cases:
   - negative price -> should throw an error
   - discount rate > 1 -> should throw an error
   - non-numeric input -> should throw an error
Use the Vitest framework and give the complete test file.

    Notice what makes this instruction work: it explicitly lists the three categories of test cases (normal, boundary, and error), leaving the AI no room to 'test selectively.' Sometimes an AI will write only happy-path tests to 'get it done fast' — spelling out every category prevents that.

    2. Code Review Techniques

    Even with test coverage, you still need to review the AI's code yourself. Code review does not mean reading line by line — that is too slow and too dependent on your own coding skill. Effective AI code review focuses on these key dimensions:

    Review DimensionWhat to Look ForCommon Problems
    SecurityInput validation, key handling, SQL injection protectionThe AI often forgets to validate input and hardcodes keys in the code
    Error HandlingAre exceptions caught, and are the error messages sensibleThe AI loves empty catch blocks, or just a console.log
    PerformanceAny obvious performance problems, like N+1 queries or infinite loopsThe AI sometimes writes O(n²) algorithms
    MaintainabilityIs the code structure clear, and do the names make senseAI occasionally generates overly abstract code
    Dependency managementWhether the dependencies brought in are actually needed and their versions are explicitAI tends to pull in unnecessary libraries

    Key dimensions for reviewing AI code

    When reviewing, you don't have to check everything one by one yourself — you can have the AI do the first pass. An instruction like: "Please review this code for security, error handling, and performance, and point out potential issues." AI's self-review ability keeps improving; it can't fully replace human review, but it helps you filter out most of the obvious problems.

    III. Version Control: Git's Role in AI Coding

    Git plays an even bigger role in AI coding than in traditional programming. Because every change the AI makes can introduce unpredictable shifts, you need a reliable way to undo mistakes — and version control is exactly that.

    The best Git practice in AI coding is "commit often, move in small steps." Every time you finish one verifiable piece of functionality, make a commit. That way, when one of the AI's changes goes wrong, you can roll back precisely to the last working state instead of throwing away all your work.

    Another handy trick is "branch isolation." For AI changes with uncertain results (like a big refactor), create a new branch first and do the work there. If you like the result, merge it back into the main branch; if not, just delete the branch and the main branch stays untouched. This is far safer than making repeated changes on the main branch.

    1. Before each AI change, make sure the working area is clean (no uncommitted changes). That way, if you don't like what the AI did, you can quickly roll back with git checkout .
    2. After each AI change, once it passes verification, commit right away. The commit message should describe what the change does, like "feat: add user registration".
    3. For big refactors, create a branch first: git checkout -b refactor/auth-system. Finish the changes on the branch, and merge only after the tests pass.
    4. Build the habit of looking at the diff. After every AI change, use git diff to see exactly what changed. This not only helps you spot problems, it also helps you learn the code.

    IV. Common Pitfalls and How to Dodge Them

    A few pitfalls show up again and again in AI coding, and almost every beginner steps into them. Knowing them in advance saves you a lot of detours.

    1. Pitfall One: The Trust Trap

    "Code written by AI looks so professional — it must be fine, right?" This is the most dangerous trap. AI-generated code is very tidy on the surface — proper naming, complete comments, clear structure — and that "surface polish" makes people lower their guard. But a tidy surface doesn't mean the logic is correct. The antidote: always verify through testing, never judge by "does it look right."

    2. Pitfall Two: The Bloat Trap

    "Since AI can write my code, why not make the features more complete?" That leads to code bloat. AI is great at "giving extra": ask it for a login page and it hands you a full user management system. Extra features don't just add complexity — they raise the odds of bugs too. The antidote: strictly follow the Simplicity First principle and tell the AI explicitly to "build only this feature, add nothing extra."

    3. Pitfall Three: The Understanding Trap

    "The AI should understand what I mean, right?" Not necessarily. AI's comprehension is strong, but for vague requirements it still has to "guess." When it guesses wrong, the code it produces is wrong. Worse, code built on a wrong guess usually "looks reasonable," making you believe it understood. The antidote: put enough specific detail in your instructions to shrink the space the AI has to "guess" in.

    4. Pitfall Four: The Context Trap

    "I said this earlier in the conversation — the AI should still remember, right?" It very likely doesn't. As conversations get longer or you start new sessions, the AI loses earlier context. If a key constraint isn't written into the project memory file, it will very likely be ignored in later changes. The antidote: write key constraints into the project memory file instead of relying on conversational memory.

    The Four Traps at a Glance

    Trust trap — don't trust "it looks right"; Bloat trap — AI loves to "give extra"; Understanding trap — vague requirements make it "guess"; Context trap — conversational memory "forgets." The matching antidotes: verify with tests, cut the extras, give full details, write to the memory file.

    Hands-On: Build Three Lines of Defense for Your Project

    If you've already started Project One (the tool site): ① have the AI write the three types of test cases for your core functions; ② review the code against all five dimensions (security / error handling / performance / maintainability / dependencies); ③ initialize the project with git and make your first commit. With all three lines of defense in place, your project truly belongs to you.

    Chapter Summary

    • AI code that "looks right" ≠ "is right" — when the surface looks too good, it's easy to lower your guard
    • Have the AI write tests: explicitly list the three case types (normal / boundary / error) to prevent "selective testing"
    • Five review dimensions: security, error handling, performance, maintainability, dependency management
    • Git is your "undo button": commit often, move in small steps, isolate with branches, check the diff often
    • The four traps: Trust (verify with tests), Bloat (cut the extras), Understanding (give full details), Context (write to the memory file)

    Chapter 46: The Road Ahead — From User to Architect

    Once you've mastered the methodology of Chapters 37 through 44 and can use AI to finish projects with confidence, what comes next? This chapter explores the path from "AI tool user" to "AI system architect." At this stage the focus is no longer "how do I get the AI to write good code" but "how do I fit AI better into the whole development process."

    I. The MCP Protocol and Tool Extensions

    MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that appeared in 2025 and spread gradually through 2026. It defines a communication standard between AI models and external tools. Simply put, MCP lets an AI "use tools" — not just generate code, but also run commands, query databases, call APIs, and work with the file system.

    Before MCP, every AI tool had its own way of integrating tools, and none were compatible. The arrival of MCP means: a tool that follows the MCP standard can be used by any AI tool that supports MCP. That sharply lowers the cost of tool integration, and it stretches AI's capability from "generating text" to "taking actions."

    For advanced users, MCP means you can build custom tool capabilities for your AI. For example, if your team has an internal deployment system, you can write an MCP tool that lets the AI call the deployment system directly, with no human switching to the terminal. This "AI calling tools" capability is the infrastructure of Agentic Engineering.

    II. Custom Workflows and Skills

    When you keep repeating certain fixed AI coding routines, you can solidify them into "custom workflows" or "Skills." For example, your team may have a standard code review process — check security first, then performance, then maintainability. You can write that process as a Skill so the AI automatically follows it every time it reviews code.

    The core value of custom workflows is "consistency" — they make sure every run follows the same standard, without drifting because the conversation ran long or the context differs. This matters especially for team collaboration: when every member uses the same workflow, the style and quality standards of the code they produce converge.

    How you build a custom workflow varies by tool. Cursor supports Rules and Custom Instructions, Claude Code supports custom commands, and Replit supports Runme. But the core idea is the same: "encode" your best practices into instruction templates the AI can execute.

    III. Multi-Agent Collaboration Patterns

    By 2026, multi-agent collaboration has become a hot topic. The core idea: instead of using one AI to finish a task, use several AIs with different roles working together. For example, one AI writes the code, one writes the tests, one reviews the code — each does its own job and checks the others.

    The strengths of multi-agent collaboration are "division of labor" and "cross-validation": each agent focuses on its own domain and produces higher-quality output, and agents cross-checking one another catch problems any single one might miss. But the drawbacks are just as clear: coordination is costly, communication overhead is large, and debugging gets more complicated.

    Tip: You Can Play "Multi-Agent" Solo

    As an individual developer, you don't need to set up a complicated multi-agent system — you can "play" the different roles yourself to simulate multi-agent collaboration. For example: first have the AI write feature code in one conversation; then open a new conversation (with the CLAUDE.md context provided) and ask the AI to "review this code as a code reviewer"; finally open another conversation and ask the AI to "revise the code based on the review comments." This "one person, many roles" approach captures most of the benefits of multi-agent collaboration without any complicated infrastructure.

    IV. The Continuous Learning Path

    AI coding is a fast-moving field. Today's best practices may need updating tomorrow. Here are a few suggestions for continuous learning:

    First, follow the source, not secondhand takes. Andrej Karpathy's original tweets and CLAUDE.md, the official documentation from Anthropic and OpenAI, the changelogs of the major tools — these are first-hand information. Community articles and tutorials are interpretations and summaries of that information; they're valuable but can be distorted. Build the habit of reading primary sources.

    Second, let practice drive learning. Don't "learn first, then do" — "do and learn along the way." Every time you meet a new kind of problem (say, handling file uploads for the first time, or connecting to a third-party API for the first time), take it as a chance to learn the relevant knowledge. Learning in practice is far more efficient than book theory detached from real scenarios.

    Third, stay aware of tools without chasing every new release. Every month or two, spend half a day catching up on the latest tools and trends — but don't switch every time something new appears. The test is simple: does the new tool meaningfully relieve one of your bottlenecks? If not, your current setup is enough.

    Fourth, build a personal knowledge base. Write down every conversation where you solved a hard problem, every lesson from a stumble, every method that worked. You don't have to publish it — it's your own "methodology notebook." As it accumulates, it becomes your most valuable asset.

    Hands-On: Start a "Lessons Learned" Notebook

    Create a document today (a notes app or a .md file both work) and write down the three AI coding lessons you most want to remember so far — even if it's just "think it through before asking." From now on, every time you hit a pitfall or learn a new trick, add an entry. Half a year from now, you'll thank today's you.

    Chapter Summary

    • MCP is the communication standard between AI and tools: it lets AI run commands, query databases, and call APIs
    • The core value of custom workflows/Skills is "consistency": encode best practices into instruction templates
    • Multi-agent = division of labor + cross-validation; solo developers can simulate it with "one person, many roles"
    • Four habits for continuous learning: read the source, learn by doing, don't chase every new thing, build a personal knowledge base

    II. The Tool-Choice Decision Tree

    When you need to pick an AI coding tool, follow the decision path below. Note: this isn't a ranking of "which is best" — it's a framework for judging "which is best for you."

    III. FAQ: Common Questions

    Q1: I don't know how to program at all — can I still do AI coding?

    Yes. AI coding tools in 2026 are strong enough that you can describe what you want in plain language and have the AI generate the code. Two suggestions: first, start with cloud Builder tools (like v0 and Bolt), which need no development environment setup; second, learn basic concepts as you go — you don't need to master the syntax, but you do need to "read" the general meaning of the code the AI writes, so you can check its work effectively.

    Q2: Which programming language should I learn?

    It depends on what you want to build. Website front end — JavaScript/TypeScript; data processing or AI — Python; enterprise back end — Java or Go. But more importantly: in the AI coding era, the importance of "which language" is falling. AI can handle the syntax details for you; what you need to understand is "the structure of programs" — what a function is, what a loop is, what a data structure is. These concepts carry across languages, and once you understand them, picking up any language is fast.

    Q3: Is there a copyright issue with AI-written code?

    As of August 2026 this is still a contested legal question. Generally speaking, AI-generated code isn't considered to have a clear copyright owner in most jurisdictions. But if you're using it in a commercial project, it's wise to: ① check the intellectual property terms in the terms of service of the AI tool you use; ② review and modify key code yourself so it carries your own creative input; ③ avoid having the AI directly copy open-source code that may be copyrighted.

    Q4: Will AI replace programmers?

    Not in the short term. What AI replaces isn't the "programmer" as a profession but the task of "coding line by line." Just as the calculator didn't replace mathematicians — it freed them from tedious hand computation. AI coding tools shift programmers from "writing code" to "thinking through problems" — which actually raises the ceiling on a programmer's value. Future competitiveness won't lie in "how many lines of code you can write" but in "how complex a problem you can solve."

    Q5: How do I judge whether the AI's output is correct?

    Use the three-layer verification method. Layer one: functional verification — does it run? Are the inputs and outputs right? This is the most basic. Layer two: boundary verification — what happens with empty input, extra-long input, weird input? This surfaces hidden problems. Layer three: architecture verification — is the code structure sound? Any hard-coded values? Is it easy to extend? This takes some technical judgment of your own. If you can't judge layer three, at least do the first two — running fine with sane boundaries already puts you ahead of most beginners.

    V. Closing Thoughts: Tools in Hand, Methodology in Mind

    Let's come back to this book's core belief: tools iterate every three months; methodology evolves only every three years. Today, in August 2026, AI coding tools are astonishingly powerful — you can create a website with one sentence, generate a full-stack app from a short description, finish a complex refactor with a single instruction. But the more powerful the tools, the more methodology stands out — because powerful tools amplify every one of your decisions.

    If your requirements are clear, AI helps you build them efficiently; if they're vague, AI efficiently builds the wrong thing. If you follow Simplicity First, AI helps you validate ideas quickly; if you want everything at once, AI quickly piles up technical debt for you. If you make precise changes, AI optimizes your code with surgical precision; if your instructions are fuzzy, AI boldly introduces bugs for you.

    That's why this book spent most of its pages on methodology rather than tool operations. Not because tools don't matter, but because methodology is the tool's "multiplier" — the better your methodology, the more your tools are worth; with zero methodology, even the strongest tool is just zero times anything.

    You're no longer coding alone. You are the commander and AI is your army; the quality of your thinking determines your army's fighting power. From today, arm your mind with methodology and amplify your ability with tools — that's the whole secret of AI coding.

    Chapter 48: Getting to Know Android — From Operating System to Development Ecosystem

    Congratulations on making this decision — going from "someone who plays with phones" to "someone who makes phone apps." Before we start, let's spread out the map: where did Android come from? Why are developers all over the world writing apps for it? And from the moment your fingers hit the keyboard to when an app lands on a user's phone, what happens in between?

    I. Android's Origin Story: From "Little Robot" to "The World's Biggest System"

    Android's story begins in 2003 — an engineer named Andy Rubin founded Android Inc., with a modest goal: build a smart operating system that "understood cameras better." Google acquired it in 2005, and in 2007 joined dozens of manufacturers to form the Open Handset Alliance (OHA). In September 2008, the first Android phone, the HTC Dream (G1), went on sale.

    You know the rest of the story: by 2026, Android is the world's largest mobile operating system by market share, with active devices in the billions. Your phone, TV box, car dashboard screen, and smartwatch are very likely all running Android. What does that mean? It means every line of code you write has a chance to be used by the largest number of people on Earth.

    Tip: Android's Open-Source DNA

    Android's core code (AOSP, the Android Open Source Project) is open source — any manufacturer can take it and customize it. That's why Xiaomi has MIUI (now called HyperOS), Huawei has its HarmonyOS compatibility layer, and Samsung has One UI. That's good news for developers: what you learn is "Android development," not "development for one brand" — one skill set that works on every device.

    The version numbers are fun too: starting with 1.5 Cupcake, every major release was named after a dessert — Donut, Eclair, Froyo, Gingerbread... until Android 10 in 2019 switched to plain numbers. As of August 2026, the latest official release is Android 17, and the "minimum supported version" you actually need to care about in development is usually set by mainstream apps somewhere between Android 8 (API 26) and Android 10 (API 29) — support devices from a few years back and your potential user base is big enough.

    VersionCodename / YearWhat Matters for Developers
    Android 8 (API 26)Oreo · 2017Notification channels and background limits — the minimum line for many older devices
    Android 10 (API 29)2019Scoped storage arrives; the rules for file access get a major overhaul
    Android 12 (API 31)2021Material You dynamic color; a big upgrade in look and feel
    Android 13 (API 33)2022Runtime notification permission — a popup asks whether to allow notifications
    Android 14-15 (API 34-35)2023-2024Predictive back, 16KB pages, privacy tightened further
    Android 16-17 (API 36-37)2025-2026Faster minor-release cadence, AI capability integration (like Gemini extensions)

    A Brief History of Android Versions (as of August 2026 — key items for development)

    II. Which Language to Write In: Java or Kotlin?

    Two mainstream languages have appeared over Android's history. Java is the "founding elder" — Android used it from day one. Kotlin was named a "first-class citizen" by Google in 2017, and from 2019 the official stance has been "Kotlin-first." By 2026, nearly all new projects use Kotlin, and most older projects are gradually migrating too.

    Let's be honest: if you're a complete beginner, learn Kotlin directly and don't look back at Java. Three reasons: first, Kotlin takes 30%-40% less code than Java (same features, shorter and clearer); second, it's natively protected against "null pointers," a beginner's nightmare; third, all modern tutorials, official docs, and AI coding tools (remember our AI coding book?) are Kotlin-based. You'll only run into Java when maintaining old projects or reading old code.

    Java style (the wordy version)

    public class MainActivity extends Activity {
      @Override
      protected void onCreate(Bundle b) {
        super.onCreate(b);
        setContentView(R.layout.activity);
      }
    }

    Kotlin style (the clean version)

    class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
      override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        setContent { App() }
      }
    }

    Same task, but Kotlin drops a pile of curly braces and boilerplate. We'll learn it properly in Chapter 50; for now you only need to remember: the "common language" of Android development is called Kotlin.

    III. How Is an App Born?

    Many people think "developing an app" means opening the computer and furiously writing code. In reality, an app goes through roughly this pipeline from idea to a user's phone:

    Idea➜ 📐 Design (UI + features)➜ Write code
    Compile and package (APK/AAB)➜ Test (emulator + real device)➜ Release (store/installer)

    Figure 1: The full journey of an Android app from idea to the store

    Two concepts from this pipeline you need to know right now:

    • APK: the installation package format for Android apps (.apk). Like a Windows .exe, it installs onto a phone with a tap. Use it for your own testing or for sharing with friends to try.
    • AAB: Android App Bundle (.aab), the "advanced packaging format" used to publish on Google Play. The store dynamically trims the package to match each user's phone model, so everyone downloads a smaller file. You can't install it yourself — it only goes through the store.

    Another term you'll hear constantly: SDK (Software Development Kit). It's the full set of "development gear" provided officially by Android — the API libraries for each version, debugging tools, emulator images, and more. Classes like Activity and Button that you call in your code all come from the SDK.

    IV. The Android Tech Stack at a Glance: Your "Weapon List"

    Before we formally start learning, meet the standard configuration of a mainstream Android project in 2026 — it's fine if this list makes no sense yet; come back after you finish the book and it will all click:

    LayerMainstream Choice (2026)What It's For

    UIJetpack Compose + Material 3Draws the UI in code (the main thread of this book)
    ArchitectureMVVM + ViewModelKeeps UI and logic separate so the code stays tidy
    Data StorageRoom (database) + DataStore (settings)Saves data on the phone
    NetworkingRetrofit + OkHttp + Kotlin coroutinesTalks to the server
    Build ToolGradle + Kotlin DSLTurns code into an installable package
    Development EnvironmentAndroid StudioGoogle's official all-in-one IDE

    Don't be intimidated by all that English. These are just the pots and pans in the kitchen — right now you only need to know that "cooking means entering the kitchen"; how each tool works will be unpacked for you chapter by chapter. And here's the good news: when Android Studio creates a new project, it sets up this whole stack for you automatically. You just get cooking.
