    Chapter 59: Getting to Know iOS — Apple's Ecosystem and Developer Ecosystem

    Congratulations on this decision — going from "someone who uses an iPhone" to "someone who writes apps for the iPhone." Before you start, let's spread the map out flat: where did iOS come from? What does Apple's "walled garden" mean for developers? What happens between your fingers hitting the keyboard and an app landing on a user's phone?

    1. iOS's Origin Story: One Phone Changed an Industry

    In January 2007, Jobs pulled the first-generation iPhone out on stage. At the time it didn't even support third-party apps — not until 2008, when Apple launched the App Store and the iPhone SDK, letting developers worldwide write software for the iPhone. That was the moment the "app economy" was born: today, the App Store hosts millions of apps and has paid developers a cumulative total of hundreds of billions of dollars.

    The system itself has evolved too: it was first called iPhone OS and renamed iOS in 2010; the version number marched up to iOS 17 (2023), and then in 2025 Apple switched to year-based naming — iOS 26 shipped in 2025, and as of August 2026 the current version is iOS 27. The naming changes, but one thing never has: iOS users' willingness to pay and the platform's reputation for software quality are widely considered the best in mobile — the same app usually earns noticeably more on iOS than on Android.

    MilestoneYearWhat mattered to developers
    App Store launches2008Third-party development opens up
    Swift is released2014The modern language for iOS development arrives
    SwiftUI is released2019Declarative UI framework; the main line of this book
    iOS 26 (the year of the renaming)2025Naming follows the year; Apple Intelligence fully integrated
    iOS 272026Current latest version (this book's baseline)

    A timeline of iOS development (as of August 2026)

    2. The Walled Garden: The Apple Ecosystem's "Rules" and "Rewards"

    The Apple ecosystem is often described as a "walled garden"—lots of rules, tightly enforced: apps must pass review before they can be listed, development requires a Mac and Xcode, and distribution goes mainly through the App Store. Sounds stifling? But for developers, those rules buy rewards worth real money:

    • Almost no device fragmentation: there are only a handful of iPhone models, and screen sizes and system versions are highly uniform—adapt to just 5 models and you cover 95% of users (on Android you might have to cover dozens);
    • Extremely high system adoption: within a few weeks of a new release, 70–80% of users have upgraded, so you can confidently use new APIs without worrying about "systems from five years ago";
    • Users are happy to pay: App Store users are more willing to spend money on apps and in-app purchases;
    • Strict review, but a clean store: knockoffs and junk apps are rare, so good products are easier to get seen.

    Note: Let's Be Clear About the Cost First

    iOS development has hard requirements: you must have a Mac (Xcode runs only on macOS), and publishing requires a $99/year developer account (a free personal developer account lets you test on a real device locally, but you can't publish to the store). Think through that investment before you set off—the good news is that a free account is completely enough for the learning stage, as Chapter 60 will cover.

    3. Which Language to Write In: Objective-C or Swift?

    iOS development history has two "lead actors" as well. Objective-C was the founding veteran—used from 2008 to 2014; Swift is the new language Apple released in 2014, and it has evolved all the way to Swift 6 (released in 2024, bringing strict concurrency checking). By 2026, nearly all new projects use Swift.

    A bit of honest advice for absolute beginners: go straight to Swift and don't even look at Objective-C—unless your future job means maintaining legacy code from ten years ago. Swift's advantages: clean syntax (none of the C-era baggage of semicolons and header files), an Optional mechanism that wipes out "null pointer crashes" at the language level, seamless integration with SwiftUI, and Swift Playgrounds on the iPad for learning while you play.

    Objective-C style (ancient relic)

    NSString *name = @"Tom"; [name stringByAppendingString:@"Hello"]; // The classic trio: square brackets + pointers + semicolons

    Swift style (modern and clean)

    var name = "Tom" name += "Hello" // As plain as everyday language

    4. How Is an App Born?

    Like every platform, iOS apps come off an assembly line. But the Apple version adds two extra "security checks":

    Idea➜ 📐 Design (UI + features)➜ Write code (Swift + SwiftUI)
    Compile and sign➜ Test (emulator + real device)➜ Apple review➜ Published on the App Store

    Figure 1: The full journey of an iOS app from idea to the App Store (note the extra "review" step)

    Key concepts in the pipeline:

    • Signing: every iOS app must be "signed" before it can be installed—proof that "this package came from you and hasn't been tampered with." During the learning stage, Xcode signs automatically with your Apple ID; publishing uses a developer certificate. Chapter 67 covers the details.
    • Simulator: an iPhone virtualized on your Mac—the main arena for development and debugging. It runs on the Mac's CPU, so it's remarkably smooth—a big step up from Android emulators.
    • TestFlight: Apple's official "beta distribution" tool—before release, you send test builds to up to 10,000 testers, who install and try them with the TestFlight app. It's an elegance unique to the iOS ecosystem.

    5. The Full iOS Tech Stack: Your "Weapon List"

    LayerMainstream choice (2026)What it's for
    LanguageSwift 6The language for writing logic
    InterfaceSwiftUI + Apple's design guidelines (HIG)Drawing interfaces in code (the main line of this book)
    ArchitectureMVVM + @ObservableKeeping interface and logic apart
    Data storageSwiftData (database) + UserDefaults (settings)Saving data on the phone
    NetworkingURLSession + async/await + CodableTalking to servers
    Build toolsXcode Build System / xcodebuildTurning code into an installable package
    Development environmentXcode (macOS only)Apple's official IDE

    The mainstream iOS tech stack at a glance (2026)

    Notice anything? This list is quite a bit shorter than Android's—because Apple "takes care of" a lot of things for you. The closed ecosystem costs you freedom and pays you back in peace of mind: no agonizing over which networking library or which database to pick—the official option is usually the best answer.

    Hands-on: Look Up Your Phone's Apple Profile

    On your iPhone, open [Settings] > [General] > [About] and jot down three things: the iOS version, the model name, and the available storage. Then wander around the "Today" tab of the App Store and pay attention to the screenshots and copy of the featured apps—starting today, you're browsing the store with a "developer's" eyes instead of a "user's".

    Chapter summary

    • 2008: the App Store launches and the "app economy" is born; as of 2026 the current version is iOS 27
    • The walled garden's ledger: plenty of rules, but fewer devices, fresher systems, paying users, and a clean store
    • Hard requirements: a Mac is a must; publishing needs a $99/year developer account; a free account is enough for the learning stage
    • Go straight to Swift for the language; Objective-C belongs to legacy code only
    • The pipeline has one extra stop compared to Android: Apple's review; TestFlight is the go-to tool for beta distribution
    • The standard 2026 stack: Swift 6 + SwiftUI + MVVM + SwiftData + URLSession + Xcode

    Chapter 60: Setting Up Your Development Environment—Xcode and Your First Project

    A craftsman is only as good as their tools. In this chapter we'll set up the "kitchen": install Xcode, get the simulator running, create the first iOS project of your life, and then take the project structure apart so you understand every piece. Once the environment is ready, you'll see your own code turn into a button you can tap for the very first time—a moment many people remember for the rest of their lives.

    1. Getting a Mac Ready

    First, the entry requirement: iOS development must happen on macOS. If you don't have a Mac, you have three options: buy one (even a used Mac mini or MacBook Air is enough), rent a cloud Mac for the short term, or read Part 8, "Hands-On Android Development," first (you can do that on Windows).

    Tip: You Can Start Learning the Language Without a Mac

    The free Swift Playgrounds app on the iPad teaches the basics of the Swift language (no Mac needed); you can even install it on the iPhone. Get comfortable with the Chapter 61 language material in Playgrounds first, and you'll take off the moment you get a Mac. This is the classic "sharpen the axe before you chop" principle.

    2. Installing Xcode

    Xcode is Apple's official integrated development environment, and it's free. Three steps to install:

    1. On your Mac, open the App Store, search for "Xcode," and click Install—heads up, it's several GB, so pick a time when your connection is fast;
    2. On first launch after installing, accept the agreement and let the components install (it happens automatically);
    3. In the menu bar, go to Xcode > Settings > Locations and make sure Command Line Tools is selected—the command line tools are a prerequisite for many scripts and third-party tools.

    Note: The Version and System "Matching Game"

    A new Xcode usually demands the latest macOS, while older Macs get stuck on older versions. When you publish to the App Store, Apple requires building with a relatively recent Xcode (usually with a grace period). So don't put off system updates too long—iOS developers are among the busiest "new version chasers" out there.

    3. Creating Your First Project

    Open Xcode > Create New Project > choose iOS > the App template, then fill in:

    SettingWhat to enterDescription
    Product NameMyFirstAppApp name
    TeamYour Apple ID (free)Used for signing; a personal account is fine
    Organization Identifiercom.exampleCombined with the Product Name to form the bundle identifier
    InterfaceSwiftUIThe main framework used in this book
    LanguageSwiftNo explanation needed

    The five things to fill in when creating a project

    After you click Create, Xcode generates a project that runs right away. Pick a simulator in the top-left corner (say, iPhone 17) and click ▶ to run—a few seconds later, a window saying "Hello, world!" appears on the simulator's screen. Your first iOS app has been born.

    On the left is the project navigator—as a beginner, you only need to know these:

    • ContentView.swift: the main screen view—everything you're looking at right now lives here;
    • Assets.xcassets: the resource warehouse—icons, images, and colors all go here;
    • Target settings: click the blue project icon on the left to get in. The version number, the minimum iOS version, and signing are all in there. The app's display name and icon are configured here too.

    Get fluent with these and you'll look "very professional":

    6. Testing on a Real Device: Install the App on Your iPhone

    The simulator is nice, but a real device is the destination. You can test on a real device even with a free Apple ID:

    1. Connect your iPhone with a cable (or debug wirelessly over the same Wi-Fi);
    2. Pick your phone from the device list at the top of Xcode; the first time, you'll be asked to sign in with your Apple ID and signing gets configured automatically;
    3. On the iPhone, go to [Settings] > [General] > [VPN & Device Management] and trust your developer certificate;
    4. Click ▶, and the app lands on your real device.

    Note: The Free Account's "Seven-Day Limit"

    An app signed with a free Apple ID stops working after 7 days (just run it again to renew). This is Apple's anti-abuse mechanism, and it's completely fine for the learning stage; a paid developer account ($99/year) has no such limit—Chapter 67 has the details.

    Chapter 61: Swift Quick Start—Apple's Top Development Language

    In this chapter we officially start learning the language. Don't worry—Swift is famous for being "beginner-friendly," and you don't need to memorize a grammar book: once you've mastered 20% of the syntax, you can read and write 80% of everyday code. Look up the rest as you go, while working on projects. Remember our learning principle: understanding beats memorizing, and being able to use it beats being an expert.

    1. Variables and Types: Giving Data a Name

    A program is just "data + logic." A variable is simply a name you give to a piece of data so you can store it. Swift declares them with let and var:

    SWIFT · Variables···
    let name = "Alex"        // let: constant (the recommended default)
var age = 18             // var: variable (can change later)

age = 19                 //  var can change
// name = "Sam"         //  let can't be changed — compile error

let score: Int = 100     // you can also declare the type explicitly
let pi = 3.14            // omitted, it's still inferred automatically

print("Hello, \(name)")   // string interpolation: backslash + parentheses

    Memorize the common types with one table:

    TypeWhat it holdsExample
    IntWhole numbers42
    DoubleDecimals3.14
    StringText"Hello"
    BoolTrue/falsetrue / false
    [Int] (an array)A group of values[1, 2, 3]

    Common basic types in Swift

    Tip: The let-First Principle

    An iron rule of the Swift community: use let by default, and only use var when it's truly necessary. If you use var where let would do, Xcode will warn you with yellow text. This habit saves you from a whole family of "variable got changed by accident" bugs—the less your code changes, the easier it is to reason about.

    2. Optionals: Swift's "Anti-Crash Charm"

    This is the most important concept in Swift, bar none. In one sentence: when a value might "not exist," Swift forces you to deal with it—wiping out the industry's nightmare of "null pointer crashes" at the language level.

    SWIFT · Optionals···
    var name: String = Alex   // a regular type: never allowed to be nil
// name = nil                //  compile error — it stops you outright

var nickname: String? = nil  // add a question mark: nil is allowed (an optional)
nickname = "Al"

// To use an optional, you must "unwrap" it:
if let n = nickname {        // if let: safe unwrapping
    print("Hello, \(n)")
} else {
    print("No nickname yet")
}

let len = nickname?.count ?? 0   // ?? provides a default (the nil-coalescing operator)
print(len)

    Note: ! Is a "High-Risk Operation"

    Writing nickname! in code (force unwrapping) is like shouting at the compiler, "I guarantee it's not nil"—guess wrong once, and the app crashes on the spot. Beginner rule: use if let / ?? wherever possible, and never use !. When Xcode autocompletes your code it occasionally slips in a !—remember to swap it out.

    3. Functions and Closures: Packing Logic into "Buttons"

    A function is a named piece of logic, like a button on a remote control. A closure is a "function with no name," one you can hand to someone else on the spot:

    SWIFT · Functions and closures···
    // Functions: name first, then parameters and return type
func greet(name: String) -> String {
    return "Hello, \(name)!"
}
print(greet(name: "Alex"))     // the argument label is required at the call site

// Closures: defined inline, quick and direct
let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let doubled = numbers.map { $0 * 2 }   // $0 = the current element
// [2, 4, 6, 8]

let big = numbers.filter { $0 > 2 }    // filter
// [3, 4]

    Closures are everywhere in SwiftUI: the braces after Button("Tap me") { ... } are a closure. Please commit these "collection combo moves" to memory—map, filter, and sorted—because 90% of the list handling you'll ever do is just combinations of them.

    4. Structs and Protocols: Swift's "LEGO" System

    Swift's official preference is clear: prefer structs, and use classes only when you need inheritance. A struct is a "value type"—each copy lives its own separate life, which naturally cuts out a whole family of bugs:

    SWIFT · Structs and protocols···
    // A struct: a box for data
struct Record {
    var id = UUID()
    var amount: Double
    var category: String
    var date: Date

    // Structs come with a built-in "memberwise initializer": you can create one directly
}
let r = Record(amount: 25.5, category: "Food", date: Date())

// A protocol: a contract for "which abilities are required"
protocol Identifiable {
    var id: UUID { get }
}
struct Record: Identifiable { ... }   // conforming to a protocol = promising to fulfill its requirements

    Almost everything in SwiftUI is a struct (View is a protocol). It's fine if that sentence doesn't click yet—you'll run into it every day in Chapter 62. In the world of Swift, embrace the struct first.

    5. A Syntax Cheat Sheet for Absolute Beginners

    What you want to doHow to write it
    Define a constant/variablelet x = 1 / var x = 1
    String interpolation"Hello, \(name)"
    Define a functionfunc name(parameter: Type) -> ReturnType { ... }
    Making a decisionif condition { ... } else { ... }
    Looping through itemsfor x in array { ... }
    Safe unwrappingif let x = optionalValue { ... }
    Default valuex ?? defaultValue
    Define a structstruct X { var a: Int; var b: String }
    Closures{ $0 * 2 }

    Swift syntax cheat sheet (beginner edition)

    Hands-on: Play with Swift in Playgrounds for 15 Minutes

    If you have a Mac, open Xcode > Playground; if not, use Swift Playgrounds on the iPad or a web-based playground. Run every piece of code in this chapter, fiddle with the numbers and text, and deliberately create a few errors to see how Xcode reacts. These 15 minutes of "play first, learn after" will make starting Chapter 62 twice as easy.

    Chapter summary

    • let first, var with care; types are inferred automatically, but you can also declare them explicitly after a colon
    • Optionals are the soul of Swift: if a value might be missing, you must handle it—if let / ?? are your protective charm, and ! is a high-risk move
    • Function calls carry argument names; a closure = a function without a name, and they're everywhere in SwiftUI
    • Prefer structs and conform to protocols; almost everything in SwiftUI is a struct
    • 20% of the syntax does 80% of the work: learn to use it first, master it later

    Chapter 62: Building Interfaces—Getting Started with SwiftUI

    The interface is everything the user sees. SwiftUI is the declarative interface framework Apple launched in 2019—you only need to "declare" what the interface looks like, and the system automatically takes care of rendering, dark mode, and every kind of screen. By 2026, SwiftUI is the clear mainstream for new projects. In this chapter, we learn to "paint."

    1. The SwiftUI Idea: Declarative, Not Imperative

    Old-style interface development is "imperative": you give the system orders one step at a time—"create a button → place it at (20,30) → set the color." SwiftUI is "declarative": you simply describe "there's a red button on the screen that says 'Tap me'," and the system takes care of how to draw it and when to redraw it.

    SWIFT · Your first SwiftUI view···
    import SwiftUI

struct ContentView: View {
    var body: some View {      // body: describes "what the screen looks like"
        VStack {               // vertical stack
            Text("Hello, world!")
                .font(.largeTitle)      // modifier: large title
            Button("Tap me") {
                print("clicked")
            }
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)  // solid blue button
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

    Key point: a view = a struct that conforms to the View protocol, the body property describes the interface, and .modifier() chains "apply the makeup." That's the entire foundation of SwiftUI.

    2. The Basic Views: Text, Buttons, Text Fields, Images

    ViewWhat it doesExample
    TextDisplays textText("Hello")
    ButtonButtonButton("Tap me") { action }
    TextFieldText fieldTextField("Placeholder", text: $text)
    ImageDisplays an imageImage(systemName: "star.fill")

    SwiftUI's four basic views

    Notice Image(systemName:)—Apple ships a built-in icon library called SF Symbols (thousands of free icons); a name like "star.fill" instantly shows a solid star. This is a hidden perk of iOS development: you almost never have to hunt for icon assets.

    3. The Layout Trio: VStack, HStack, ZStack

    • VStack: lines things up vertically (like queuing for lunch);
    • HStack: lines things up horizontally (like sitting side by side);
    • ZStack: stacks things on top of each other (like a pile of playing cards—perfect for badges and overlays).
    SWIFT · The three layout stacks + common modifiers···
    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
    HStack {
        Text("Bill")
        Spacer()                 // flexible space: pushes the right side to the edge
        Text("-25.5 yuan").foregroundColor(.red)
    }
    Divider()                    // divider
    Text("Note: lunch")
}
.padding(16)                     // padding on all sides
.background(Color(.systemGray6)) // light gray background
.cornerRadius(12)                // rounded corners

// Modifier order matters: padding first, then background — the background excludes the padding

    Note: Modifier Order Matters

    padding(16).background(gray) and background(gray).padding(16) produce different results—the former "spaces first, then paints" (the background excludes the padding), the latter "paints first, then spaces" (the background includes the padding). This is the source of beginners' most common "mystery white edge." When in doubt, swap the order and the preview will tell you the answer instantly.

    4. State and Binding: Bringing the Interface to Life

    A static interface is dull. SwiftUI's rule: the interface always faithfully reflects the state—when the state changes, the interface redraws automatically.

    SWIFT · A @State counter···
    struct CounterView: View {
    @State private var count = 0   // @State: when this value changes, redraw

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("You tapped \(count) times")
            Button("Tap me +1") {
                count += 1          // change the state; the UI refreshes automatically
            }
        }
    }
}

    A text field needs "two-way binding"—the $ symbol hands over both the value and the right to change it:

    SWIFT · Two-way binding with @Binding···
    struct InputView: View {
    @State private var text = ""

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Type something", text: $text)  // $ = two-way binding
            .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
        Text("You typed: \(text)")   // updates live as you type
    }
}
    User action➜ State changes (count += 1)
    SwiftUI notices the change➜ UI redraws automatically (body recomputed)

    Figure 3: SwiftUI's one-way "state → interface" data flow

    5. Previews, Theming, and Animation: SwiftUI's "Power-Ups"

    • The #Preview macro: add #Preview { ContentView() } at the bottom of a file, and the canvas on the right renders in real time—change the code and see the result immediately;
    • Dark mode for free: use system colors (Color(.systemGray6), .primary) instead of hard-coded ones, and dark mode adapts automatically without a single extra line;
    • Animation in one line: withAnimation { count += 1 } or add .animation(.default, value: count) to a view—buttery-smooth transitions.
    SWIFT · Animations in ten minutes···
    struct AnimatedHeartView: View {
    @State private var liked = false

    var body: some View {
        Button {
            withAnimation(.spring(duration: 0.4)) {
                liked.toggle()
            }
        } label: {
            Image(systemName: liked ? "heart.fill" : "heart")
                .font(.system(size: 48))
                .foregroundColor(liked ? .red : .gray)
                .scaleEffect(liked ? 1.3 : 1.0)
        }
    }
}

    Tip: Function First, Animation Later

    A classic beginner mistake is "polishing animations before the interface even works." Get the functionality running first, then add motion at the end—animation is the icing, function is the cake. That's also our standing "simplicity first" principle.

    Hands-on: Build a "Mood Button"

    6. Common Modifiers Cheat Sheet: One Page in Hand, No Interface Worries

    What you want to doModifier
    Spacing.padding(16)
    Rounded corners.cornerRadius(12)
    Background color.background(Color(.systemGray6))
    Font and size.font(.title.bold()) / .font(.system(size: 20))
    Foreground color (text/icons).foregroundColor(.red)
    Fill the width.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
    Fixed size.frame(width: 100, height: 44)
    AlignmentVStack(alignment: .leading)
    Opacity.opacity(0.6)
    Shadow.shadow(radius: 5)
    Tap gesture.onTapGesture { ... }
    Keyboard type.keyboardType(.decimalPad)

    Common SwiftUI modifiers cheat sheet

    No need to memorize any of this—this page is for looking things up. The ones you'll use most are actually just the first four: padding, rounded corners, background, and font.

    Turn the template project into a mood switcher: one button that cycles through 😀 happy → 😢 sad → 😡 angry with each tap, while the text and background color change along with it. Hint: store the three pairs (text + color) in an array, keep the index in @State, and on each tap use (index + 1) % 3. Send it to a friend when you're done and collect your first round of "wow, you can make apps now."

    Chapter summary

    • SwiftUI is declarative: you describe "what it looks like," and the system handles drawing and redrawing
    • A view = a struct conforming to the View protocol; body describes the interface; modifiers chain on like "makeup"
    • The four basic views: Text / Button / TextField / Image; the SF Symbols icon library is free and all-you-can-eat
    • The layout trio: VStack stacks vertically, HStack horizontally, ZStack in layers; Spacer is flexible space
    • @State brings the interface to life; $ feeds two-way bindings into text fields
    • #Preview is WYSIWYG; system colors adapt to dark mode automatically; withAnimation adds motion in one line

    Chapter 63: Views, State, and Navigation

    You already know how to build a single-screen toy. This chapter tackles two "growing up" problems: how to hop between multiple screens (navigation) and how data flows between screens (state management). After this chapter, you'll be able to build the classic multi-screen app skeleton: "list → detail → edit."

    1. The Big Picture of State Management and Data Flow

    @State isn't the only state tool in SwiftUI. Start with this overview so you understand "which one to use when":

    ToolWhat it managesWho uses itTypical scenario
    @StatePrivate, temporary state for one screenThe current viewCounters, text field content
    @BindingBorrowing someone else's stateA child view changing a parent viewCustom components
    @StateObject / @ObservableLogic shared across screensThe view model (ViewModel)Data loading, business logic
    @EnvironmentObject / .environmentState shared across the whole appThe entire appLogin state, theme settings

    The SwiftUI state toolbox at a glance (2026, @Observable is now mainstream)

    SWIFT · The 2026 mainstream: @Observable view models···
    // The modern way on iOS 17+: the @Observable macro (recommended for new projects)
import Observation

@Observable
class CounterModel {                 // the view model
    var count = 0
    func increment() { count += 1 }
}

struct CounterView: View {
    @State private var model = CounterModel()   // holds the model

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("You tapped \(model.count) times")
            Button("Tap me") { model.increment() }
        }
    }
}

    Blunt advice for beginners: use @State for state private to one screen, and @Observable classes for anything shared across screens or involving logic. The @StateObject/@ObservableObject in older tutorials are the previous generation—being able to read them is enough; write new code the way described above.

    2. NavigationStack: The "Stack" Behind Screen Jumps

    Since iOS 16, multi-screen navigation uses NavigationStack—like a stack of plates: push one on, and pop them off one by one as you go back:

    SWIFT · Navigation with NavigationStack···
    struct HomeView: View {
    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List {
                NavigationLink("Alex's ledger") {
                    DetailView(name: "Alex's ledger")   // destination screen
                }
                NavigationLink("Sam's ledger") {
                    DetailView(name: "Sam's ledger")
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Ledger list")   // large title at the top
        }
    }
}

struct DetailView: View {
    let name: String
    var body: some View {
        Text("\(name) details")
            .navigationTitle(name)
            .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
    }
}

    NavigationLink is a "tappable link to another screen"; navigationTitle automatically generates the navigation bar title and the back button. When you need programmatic navigation (say, returning automatically after tapping "Save"), use @Environment(\.dismiss) to close the current screen—together, these two tricks cover 90% of your navigation needs.

    3. Pop-Ups and Bottom Tabs: sheet and TabView

    Besides "pushing screens," there are two more classic interactions:

    SWIFT · sheet dialogs + TabView tabs···
    // 1. Slides up half/full screen (the favorite for entry forms)
struct HomeView: View {
    @State private var showAdd = false
    var body: some View {
        Button("Add entry") { showAdd = true }
            .sheet(isPresented: $showAdd) {
                AddRecordView()     // the entry sheet
            }
    }
}

// 2. The bottom tab bar (the app's "skeleton")
struct MainTabView: View {
    var body: some View {
        TabView {
            RecordListView()
                .tabItem { Label("Ledger", systemImage: "book") }
            StatsView()
                .tabItem { Label("Stats", systemImage: "chart.pie") }
            SettingsView()
                .tabItem { Label("Settings", systemImage: "gear") }
        }
    }
}

    Tip: When Do You Use Which?

    Rules of thumb: use NavigationStack to push screens for the main flow (list → detail), use a sheet pop-up for temporary actions (adding, editing, confirming), and use TabView for several side-by-side sections (bottom tabs). Combine the three, and you have the skeleton of the vast majority of apps.

    4. List: iOS's Go-To List

    The most used—and most "Apple-flavored"—component on iOS is List: it comes with dividers, swipe-to-delete, and tap highlighting out of the box:

    SWIFT · List + swipe to delete···
    struct RecordListView: View {
    @State private var records = ["Lunch 25.5", "Metro 6.0", "Salary +8000"]

    var body: some View {
        List {
            ForEach(records, id: \.self) { r in
                Text(r)
            }
            .onDelete { indexSet in          // swipe left to delete
                records.remove(atOffsets: indexSet)
            }
        }
    }
}

    List + NavigationLink + sheet + TabView—put these four together, and you can already build a complete app skeleton: "ledger list → tap for details → tap + to open the entry sheet." The expense tracker project in the next chapter is built exactly this way.

    Hands-on: Build a "Three-Screen Skeleton"

    5. The App Lifecycle: Foreground and Background

    Much like Android's Activity lifecycle, iOS apps also move through "born, foreground, background, dead" state changes. In SwiftUI, watch them with the scenePhase environment value:

    SWIFT · Observing foreground/background switches···
    @main
struct MyApp: App {
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var phase

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        .onChange(of: phase) { _, newPhase in
            switch newPhase {
            case .active:    print("Back in the foreground, resuming refresh")
            case .inactive:  print("Transitioning (call / just backgrounded)")
            case .background: print("Went to background, saving draft")
            @unknown default: break
            }
        }
    }
}

    Typical uses: refresh data when coming back to the foreground, save drafts when heading to the background. iOS runs a tight ship on background activity—an ordinary app gets suspended (frozen) shortly after going to the background, so don't expect to secretly do heavy work back there; if you truly need scheduled tasks, use the local notifications from Chapter 68 instead of "staying alive in the background."

    Build a fake-data skeleton of the expense tracker: a TabView with three tabs (Ledger / Stats / Settings) → the Ledger screen shows fake data in a List, and tapping a row jumps to the details (NavigationStack) → the "+" button in the top-right opens the entry sheet. No saving, no internet—pure skeleton practice. Get this skeleton right, and filling it with real data in Chapter 65 will be a smooth ride.

    Chapter summary

    • The four state tools: @State (screen-private), @Binding (borrowed), @Observable (logic), .environment (global)
    • Use the @Observable macro for view models in new projects; being able to read the older @ObservableObject is enough
    • NavigationStack pushes screens; @Environment(\.dismiss) navigates back programmatically
    • Push screens for the main flow, pop up a sheet for temporary actions, and use TabView for side-by-side sections
    • List is the go-to list: dividers and swipe-to-delete work out of the box

    Chapter 64: Data Storage and Network Requests

    An app you can only "look at" is dead; an app that can store data and reach the network is alive. This chapter introduces the "three essentials" of the iOS data layer: UserDefaults (for small settings), SwiftData (for structured data), and URLSession (for talking to servers), plus Codable for parsing JSON and the modern async/await. After this chapter, you'll be able to write real apps that remember user preferences and update their content live.

    1. Choosing a Storage Option: Look at This Table First

    OptionWhat it's good forKey traitsWhere this book uses it
    UserDefaultsLoose settings (toggles, preferences)Key-value pairs, simple and directChapter 65 settings, Chapter 66 favorite cities
    SwiftDataStructured data (transactions, records)The official database wrapper, declared in one line with @ModelChapter 65 transaction records
    URLSessionServer data (not stored, fetched online)The built-in networking framework, no third-party dependenciesChapter 66 weather data

    The division of labor among the data trio

    Memorize this mantra: "small settings go into UserDefaults, batches of data go into SwiftData, and data from the outside travels over URLSession." Core Data from old tutorials still works (SwiftData is its modern incarnation), while hand-written SQLite is essentially a thing of the past—learn the new way directly and don't take the old road.

    2. UserDefaults: Storing a Few Small Settings

    SWIFT · UserDefaults example···
    // Write: store a value
UserDefaults.standard.set(true, forKey: "isDarkMode")
UserDefaults.standard.set("Beijing", forKey: "favoriteCity")

// Read: fetch it (falls back to the default)
let isDark = UserDefaults.standard.bool(forKey: "isDarkMode")
let city = UserDefaults.standard.string(forKey: "favoriteCity") ?? "Beijing"

// Delete: remove a key
UserDefaults.standard.removeObject(forKey: "isDarkMode")

    Keep in mind that it's only right for loose little settings—hand dozens or hundreds of records over to SwiftData, and don't use UserDefaults as a database (it slows down launch time and makes searching a pain).

    3. SwiftData: Giving Data a "Real Home"

    SwiftData is the official database solution starting with iOS 17, and it boils "creating tables, adding, deleting, updating, querying" down to the bare minimum—one @Model annotation turns a data class into a database table:

    SWIFT · SwiftData example···
    import SwiftData

// 1. @Model: this class automatically becomes a "table"
@Model
class Record {
    var amount: Double
    var category: String
    var note: String
    var date: Date

    init(amount: Double, category: String, note: String, date: Date) {
        self.amount = amount
        self.category = category
        self.note = note
        self.date = date
    }
}

// 2. Attach the container at the app's entry point
@main
struct MyApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        .modelContainer(for: Record.self)   // database ready
    }
}

// 3. In views, read with @Query and write via @Environment
struct RecordListView: View {
    @Query(sort: \Record.date, order: .reverse) var records: [Record]
    @Environment(\.modelContext) private var context

    var body: some View {
        List(records) { r in
            Text("\(r.category) \(r.amount) yuan")
        }
    }

    func add(amount: Double, category: String) {
        let r = Record(amount: amount, category: category, note: "", date: Date())
        context.insert(r)     // store
        try? context.save()   // persist to disk
    }
}

    This "@Model + modelContainer + @Query" template can be dropped into any of your projects as-is—just swap in your own field names. The moment the data changes, @Query refreshes the interface automatically. Simply delightful.

    4. Codable: A "Translator" for JSON

    Most of what servers send is JSON text. Swift's Codable protocol makes the "JSON ⇄ struct" conversion happen automatically—line up the field names, and the magic works:

    SWIFT · Parsing JSON with Codable···
    // JSON: {"name":"Beijing","main":{"temp":26.5},"weather":[{"description":"Sunny"}]}
struct WeatherResponse: Codable {
    let name: String
    let main: Main
    let weather: [Weather]
}
struct Main: Codable { let temp: Double }
struct Weather: Codable { let description: String }

// JSON string → struct
let decoder = JSONDecoder()
let data = jsonString.data(using: .utf8)!
let result = try decoder.decode(WeatherResponse.self, from: data)
print(result.weather[0].description)   // "Sunny"

    Iron rule: look at the JSON that actually comes back before you define your fields. Many "parse failed" bugs come from a misspelled field name or a wrongly guessed type (the server sends the string "26.5" and you declared a Double)—print out the raw JSON and compare, and you'll locate the problem in ten seconds.

    5. URLSession + async/await: Talking to Servers

    iOS networking uses the built-in URLSession, paired with Swift's async/await (asynchronous functions), so "waiting for the network" feels as natural as "waiting for a delivery":

    SWIFT · URLSession + async/await···
    struct WeatherService {
    // Async functions: async marks "I need to wait a moment," throws marks "this can fail"
    func fetchWeather(city: String) async throws -> WeatherResponse {
        let url = URL(string:
            "https://api.example.com/weather?city=\(city)")!
        let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)
        return try JSONDecoder().decode(WeatherResponse.self, from: data)
    }
}

// At the call site (inside .task):
.task {
    do {
        let weather = try await service.fetchWeather(city: "Beijing")
        // update the UI...
    } catch {
        print("Something went wrong: \(error)")
    }
}

    Pitfall Alert: Two Iron Rules of Networking

    1) Networking must use async/await and must never block the main thread—a frozen interface is a crash-level experience. Swift's structured concurrency makes this natural, but don't forget try await and do/catch. 2) ATS blocks plain-text HTTP by default: iOS requires HTTPS. While testing a local http:// service, you can temporarily allow an exception in Info.plist (NSAppTransportSecurity), but a production app must use HTTPS throughout—App Review keeps an eye on this too.

    Hands-on: Build a "Quote of the Day" Mini App

    6. "Grade" Your Network Errors Too: Don't Throw Every Error at the User

    No connection, timeout, 404, server 500... different errors deserve different messages for the user:

    SWIFT · Graded error handling···
    func friendlyMessage(_ error: Error) -> String {
    if let urlError = error as? URLError {
        switch urlError.code {
        case .notConnectedToInternet: return "Network is down — check your connection?"
        case .timedOut:               return "Request timed out — try again in a bit?"
        case .cannotFindHost:         return "Server not found"
        default:                      return "Network problem: \(urlError.code)"
        }
    }
    if let d = error as? DecodingError {
        return "Unexpected data format (the API may have changed)"
    }
    return "Something went wrong: \(error.localizedDescription)"
}

    Show the user "plain words," and save the "raw words" for the logs (print the full error). Don't fling the gibberish English of error.localizedDescription straight at the user—that feeling of a polished product hides in details like these.

    Find a free quotes API (something like hitokoto), use URLSession + async/await to fetch a "quote of the day," show it in the middle of the screen, and add a "New quote" button. Then use SwiftData to save your favorite quotes into a "favorites" list. This one exercise uses UserDefaults/SwiftData/Codable/URLSession all at once—finish it, and Chapters 7 and 8 will be a piece of cake.

    Chapter summary

    • The mantra: small settings into UserDefaults, batches of data into SwiftData, outside data over URLSession
    • SwiftData's three moves: @Model declares the table, modelContainer attaches the container, @Query reads and context.insert writes
    • Codable "translates" JSON automatically: line up the fields and the magic works
    • URLSession + async/await: networking feels like waiting for a delivery; do/catch handles failures
    • Two iron rules: never block the main thread; production apps must use HTTPS (ATS)

    Chapter 65: Project One—My Expense Tracker (Local Version)

    Welcome to your first "serious project." This expense tracker never touches the internet, but it's complete in every part: you can record a transaction, view the running history, see monthly totals, and edit or delete entries. Finishing it means you've walked the whole "data → logic → interface" path end to end. Don't rush to copy code—think it through first, then build. That's our standing principle.

    1. Thinking About Requirements: Ask Five Questions First

    ElementAnswer
    Who (who's it for)For yourself; family and friends too
    What (what it does)Record income and spending, view the history, monthly summaries, statistics by category
    Why (the reason)Practice + finding out where the money goes
    How (the approach)Swift + SwiftUI + SwiftData + MVVM, purely local, no backend
    Constraint (the limits)Done within one week; supports iOS 17 at minimum (the SwiftData requirement)

    The five requirement elements of the expense tracker

    Then break it into small steps where "every step is usable": 1) build the SwiftData data layer (can save a transaction); 2) the list screen (can view the history); 3) the entry sheet (can add a transaction); 4) deleting and editing; 5) the monthly summary card. After every step, the app is a "usable thing."

    2. The Data Layer: Giving Transactions a Home

    First, define what a transaction looks like—enough fields to do the job, but don't get greedy:

    SWIFT · Record.swift (the model)···
    import SwiftData

@Model
class Record {
    var type: String      // "income" = money in | "expense" = money out
    var amount: Double    // amount (in yuan)
    var category: String  // category: food, transport, salary...
    var note: String      // note (optional)
    var date: Date        // expense date

    init(type: String, amount: Double, category: String, note: String = "", date: Date = Date()) {
        self.type = type
        self.amount = amount
        self.category = category
        self.note = note
        self.date = date
    }
}

    Tip: Why Use Double for Amounts?

    Rigorous financial apps use Decimal (exact decimal arithmetic) to avoid floating-point errors (the old 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 problem). Double is plenty for a practice project; if you ever build a real financial product, remember to switch to Decimal or "an Int counted in cents"—a pitfall countless developers before you have stumbled into.

    3. MVVM: When Interface and Logic "Move Apart"

    Let the interface talk to the database directly? It runs, but the interface code becomes bloated and ugly. The MVVM architecture gives each part its own job: the View (interface) only draws, the ViewModel (logic hub) manages the data, and the Model (SwiftData) handles storage.

    View (the SwiftUI interface)⇄ ViewModel (the @Observable logic hub)⇄ Model (the SwiftData data layer)

    Figure 4: MVVM's three layers—data flows in one direction, and no layer oversteps its bounds

    SWIFT · RecordViewModel.swift (skeleton)···
    import Observation

@Observable
class RecordViewModel {
    var records: [Record] = []
    private let context: ModelContext

    init(context: ModelContext) { self.context = context }

    func load() {
        // filtering + sorting with SwiftData's #Predicate
        let descriptor = FetchDescriptor(
            sortBy: [SortDescriptor(\.date, order: .reverse)]
        )
        records = (try? context.fetch(descriptor)) ?? []
    }

    func add(type: String, amount: Double, category: String, note: String) {
        let r = Record(type: type, amount: amount, category: category, note: note)
        context.insert(r)
        try? context.save()
        load()                       // reload; the UI refreshes
    }

    func delete(_ record: Record) {
        context.delete(record)
        try? context.save()
        load()
    }
}

    In the interface, write @State private var vm = RecordViewModel(...), then render the list straight from vm.records—the moment the data changes, the interface refreshes automatically.

    4. The Interface: List Screen + Entry Sheet

    SWIFT · Expense list screen (core excerpt)···
    struct RecordListView: View {
    @State private var vm: RecordViewModel
    @State private var showAdd = false

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List {
                Section("This month's balance") {          // summary card
                    SummaryRow(records: vm.records)
                }
                Section("Transactions") {
                    ForEach(vm.records) { r in
                        RecordRow(record: r)
                    }
                    .onDelete { idx in
                        idx.forEach { vm.delete(vm.records[$0]) }
                    }
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("My expense tracker")
            .toolbar {
                Button { showAdd = true } label: {
                    Image(systemName: "plus")
                }
            }
            .sheet(isPresented: $showAdd) {
                AddRecordView(vm: vm)          // the entry dialog
            }
        }
    }
}

    Entry sheet essentials: use .keyboardType(.decimalPad) for the amount field (a number pad), a segmented control (Picker) for income/expense, a menu picker for the category, and on "Save," call vm.add(...) and dismiss() to close the sheet.

    Note: Don't Get Lazy with Input Validation

    Always validate the amount field: block empty values, negative numbers, and invalid input like "abc" (check with Double(text), which returns nil on failure). One of the most common reasons apps crash is "treating the user's input like a well-behaved child." Remember: treat everything the user types as hostile until proven otherwise.

    5. Editing, Deleting, and Summaries

    • Delete: List's .onDelete swipe-to-delete plus a confirmation dialog (accidental deletion is what users of expense apps hate most);
    • Edit: tapping a row opens an edit sheet pre-filled with the original values (fixing one word beats retyping everything);
    • Summaries: use filter + reduce to compute "this month's income / spending / balance," shown in a card at the top:
    SWIFT · Monthly totals calculation···
    func monthSummary(_ records: [Record]) -> (income: Double, expense: Double) {
    let cal = Calendar.current
    let monthRecords = records.filter {
        cal.isDate($0.date, equalTo: Date(), toGranularity: .month)
    }
    let income = monthRecords
        .filter { $0.type == "income" }
        .reduce(0) { $0 + $1.amount }
    let expense = monthRecords
        .filter { $0.type == "expense" }
        .reduce(0) { $0 + $1.amount }
    return (income, expense)
}

    6. Acceptance: A Three-Layer Check + Two Advanced Challenges

    When the project is done, run acceptance across three layers—"function → edge cases → architecture": can you record and delete, and does the data survive restarting the app (function); does entering 0 or a negative amount crash it (edge cases); are interface and data mixed together, and are any fields hard-coded (architecture)?

    Once the basic version passes acceptance, serve yourself two "advanced dishes":

    1. Category statistics: add a "Stats" tab and use Swift Charts to draw category spending as a pie chart or bar chart—Apple's official charting library, charts in just a few lines of code;
    2. iCloud sync: With SwiftData, turning on iCloud sync only takes a few settings—the ledger syncs automatically between iPhone and iPad, and instantly feels "pro."

    Get hands-on: finish it this week

    Work in the order "data layer → ViewModel → list page → entry sheet → summary card," one step a day. If you get stuck, paste the error message straight into a search engine or an AI (remember Part 7, "Hands-On AI Coding"? When describing a problem, clearly state the "expected behavior, actual behavior, and steps to reproduce"). Once it's done, use it to track a week of expenses—using an app you built yourself gives you a sense of accomplishment that will push you forward.

    Chapter summary

    • Five elements of a requirement → break it into small, "usable at every step" steps, then start building
    • Data layer: @Model models + the modelContainer container + FetchDescriptor queries
    • MVVM division of labor: the View only draws, the @Observable ViewModel handles logic, SwiftData handles storage
    • UI: List + Section + toolbar + a sheet for the entry dialog
    • Three-layer acceptance (features/edge cases/architecture) + advanced challenges (Swift Charts, iCloud sync)

    Chapter 66: Project 2—Weather App (the Networked Version)

    The expense tracker was "internal training"; the weather app is "seeing the world"—it has to deal with the internet. In this project you'll learn: how to apply for a free API, parse JSON, handle the three UI states of "loading/success/failure," and how to keep an API key safe. Once you finish it, you'll be able to build any "networked app"—news, exchange rates, translation—the pattern is exactly the same.

    1. Apply for a free weather API

    For personal practice, we recommend OpenWeatherMap or, in China, QWeather (HeFeng Weather)—both have free tiers you can use right after registering. Taking OpenWeatherMap as an example:

    1. Register an account → generate a Key (apikey) on the API keys page;
    2. The free tier can call the Current Weather endpoint: api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=beijing&appid=YOUR_KEY&units=metric;
    3. Try it in a browser first and see what the returned JSON looks like—this "preview" is a must before hooking up any API.

    Pitfall warning: never hard-code the key into your code

    An API key is like your "wallet password." Put it in code, commit it to GitHub, and crawlers will scan it up and abuse it within hours. The right way on iOS: put it in a Config.xcconfig (a config file that's already gitignored) and read it into your code via Info.plist. Search "iOS xcconfig manage keys" and follow along.

    2. The network layer: URLSession + Codable

    First define the model based on the JSON the API returns, then write the service:

    SWIFT · Data model + service···
    // JSON: {"weather":[{"description":"Sunny"}],"main":{"temp":26.5,"humidity":40},"name":"Beijing"}
struct WeatherResponse: Codable {
    let weather: [Weather]
    let main: Main
    let name: String
}
struct Weather: Codable { let description: String }
struct Main: Codable { let temp: Double; let humidity: Int }

struct WeatherService {
    let key: String   // read in from xcconfig

    func fetchWeather(city: String) async throws -> WeatherResponse {
        var comps = URLComponents(string: "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather")!
        comps.queryItems = [
            URLQueryItem(name: "q", value: city),
            URLQueryItem(name: "appid", value: key),
            URLQueryItem(name: "units", value: "metric"),
            URLQueryItem(name: "lang", value: "en")
        ]
        let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: comps.url!)
        return try JSONDecoder().decode(WeatherResponse.self, from: data)
    }
}

    3. Three UI states: loading / success / failure

    The soul of a networked app is "state management." Slow network, no connection, a misspelled city name... the UI needs to give the user an answer for every case. Express it elegantly with an enum + switch:

    SWIFT · UI state···
    enum LoadState {
    case loading                  // spinner showing
    case success(WeatherResponse) // success
    case error(String)            // failure
}

@Observable
class WeatherViewModel {
    var state: LoadState = .loading
    private let service = WeatherService(key: Config.apiKey)

    func search(city: String) async {
        state = .loading
        do {
            let data = try await service.fetchWeather(city: city)
            state = .success(data)
        } catch {
            state = .error("Can't find that city — try another name?")
        }
    }
}

// In the UI:
switch vm.state {
case .loading: ProgressView("Loading…")
case .success(let d): WeatherContent(data: d)
case .error(let msg): Text(msg).foregroundColor(.secondary)
}

    This loading/success/error three-part pattern is the "all-purpose template" for networked interfaces—memorize it first, and every networked app you build later can follow the same recipe.

    4. Hands-on UI code: drawing the weather

    SWIFT · Weather screen (core excerpt)···
    struct WeatherContent: View {
    let data: WeatherResponse

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 12) {
            Text(data.name)
                .font(.title.bold())
            Text("\(Int(data.main.temp))°C")
                .font(.system(size: 76, weight: .thin))
            Text(data.weather.first?.description ?? "Unknown")
                .font(.title3)
                .foregroundColor(.secondary)
            HStack(spacing: 24) {
                Label("Humidity \(data.main.humidity)%", systemImage: "humidity")
                Label("Feels like \(Int(data.main.temp))°C", systemImage: "thermometer")
            }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

    A few details worth learning: first? safely grabs the first element (the list may be empty), and ?? "Unknown" provides fallback text; a large temperature number in a thin font weight is a classic recipe for weather apps; Label is the official "icon + text" component, cleaner than hand-assembling an HStack.

    5. Interaction details and favorite cities

    • Search box: the .searchable modifier at the top gives you system-native search interaction; call vm.search on submit;
    • Favorite cities: store frequently viewed cities in UserDefaults, and they're looked up automatically the next time you open the app;
    • Pull to refresh: one line with .refreshable { await vm.search(...) } does it;
    • Weather icons: map descriptions with Image(systemName:) (sun.max / cloud.rain / snowflake) and the UI comes alive instantly.

    Tip: the quirk with Chinese city names

    OpenWeatherMap's support for Chinese city names is spotty—searching a Chinese name may return no results while "beijing" works fine. The production-grade approach is to bundle a "city name → English/coordinates" mapping table, or hook up a domestic weather service. At the practice stage, just support pinyin/English city names—don't fight it.

    Get hands-on: the weather app acceptance checklist

    6. How to debug network requests: printing, packet capture, and simulating a slow network

    When a networked app misbehaves, nine times out of ten it's "the request wasn't sent right" or "the response wasn't parsed right." Three debugging tools:

    1. Print the raw data: print String(data: data, encoding: .utf8) to see the raw JSON—field names and types at a glance, ten times faster than guessing;
    2. Packet capture tools: the free Proxyman on Mac, or the open-source Charles, can intercept all of the app's requests and responses, letting you see the network layer like an X-ray;
    3. Simulate a weak network: the Simulator menu's Features → Network Link Conditioner (download the tool from the developer website) can simulate 3G and high latency—surfacing those "spinner spins forever" experience problems.

    Tip: request blocked by ATS?

    If a request fails the moment it's sent with an "App Transport Security" error, you're probably using a plain-text http:// address. Production endpoints must use HTTPS; for local debugging you can temporarily add an exception (NSAllowsLocalNetworking in Info.plist), but remember to clean it up before release.

    ① Search for weather normally; ② disconnect the network and the app fails gracefully without crashing (turn off your Mac's network and test in the Simulator!); ③ enter a nonexistent city and get a friendly message; ④ favorite two cities and they're still there after restarting the app; ⑤ the UI looks good in Dark Mode. Only when all five pass does this project graduate.

    Chapter summary

    • Try the API in a browser and understand the JSON before writing code—"previewing" never hurts
    • Hide the API key in an xcconfig—never in the codebase
    • Codable models + URLSession async/await: match the fields and the JSON parses automatically
    • The loading/success/error three-state pattern is the Swiss Army knife of networked UIs
    • No connection, empty input, nonexistent city—error handling is the passing grade for a networked app

    Chapter 67: Polish and Ship—Testing, Debugging, and the App Store

    The app works—now what? This chapter covers the three things on the road from "it runs" to "it's deliverable": how to debug efficiently to find bugs, how to write tests to prevent regressions, and how to get your app onto the App Store for the whole world to download. Shipping isn't just ceremony—it's the dividing line between a project and a product.

    1. The three debugging essentials: print, breakpoints, and previews

    ToolWhat it doesHow to use it
    print + consoleView run logsIn code: print("value = \(x)"), and watch the output in the Xcode console at the bottom
    Breakpoint debuggingPause the program at a given line and inspect variable valuesClick next to a line number to place a blue marker; execution pauses there and you can step through
    SwiftUI previews + debuggerSee the UI and view hierarchy in real time#Preview canvas + the runtime View Hierarchy inspector

    The three debugging essentials

    Tip: how do you read a crash?

    When Swift crashes, the console prints "Fatal error" plus the reason, and Xcode stops on the offending line and highlights it. Historical crashes on real devices can be viewed in Xcode → Window → Organizer → Crashes (paid account required). When searching, prioritize "the first sentence of the error message + swiftui"—precise questions get precise answers.

    2. Testing: insurance for your code

    Manual testing can't be trusted—fix one feature and another quietly breaks. Tests are both the "undo button" and the "bulletproof vest." iOS uses the XCTest framework, in two flavors:

    LevelWhat it testsTargetSpeed
    Unit testsPure logic (calculations, validation)MyFirstAppTestsSeconds
    UI testsReal interface behaviorMyFirstAppUITestsMinutes
    Manual testingHuman feel and experience——Always needed

    iOS testing levels (the template project already includes two Test Targets)

    SWIFT · Unit test example···
    import XCTest

// Extract logic like "amount string to number" into a pure function
func parseAmount(_ input: String) -> Double? {
    guard let v = Double(input.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)),
          v > 0 else { return nil }
    return v
}

final class AmountTests: XCTestCase {
    func testEmptyInputReturnsNil() {
        XCTAssertNil(parseAmount(""))
    }
    func testNegativeReturnsNil() {
        XCTAssertNil(parseAmount("-5"))
    }
    func testNormalValueParses() {
        XCTAssertEqual(parseAmount("12.5"), 12.5)
    }
}

    Run tests with ⌘U. Change code only once everything is green, and you'll feel confident. The amount validation and summary calculations in the expense tracker should all be covered by unit tests.

    3. Signing and packaging: stamping your app

    Every iOS app must be signed before it can be installed—proof that "this package came from you and hasn't been tampered with." The hierarchy:

    • Learning stage: a free Apple ID + Xcode automatic signing (Personal Team) runs on a real device, renewed every 7 days;
    • Distribution stage: a paid developer account (99 USD/year) issues the certificates and provisioning profiles needed to ship and install long-term.

    Packaging: in Xcode, Product → Archive; once the build finishes, in Organizer choose Distribute App → App Store Connect → upload. Archiving must target the Generic iOS Device (not the Simulator)—a step beginners often forget.

    Pitfall warning: lose the certificate = updates cut off

    Once a signing certificate and its private key are lost, you can no longer push updates to your old app—users can only install it as a "brand-new" app. Back up your certificates carefully (export a .p12 from Keychain) and keep the password safe. Fortunately, Apple offers "automatic signing" and cloud certificate management (check Automatically manage signing in Xcode), which spares you most of the manual pitfalls.

    4. The full App Store submission process

    Register a developer account➜ Prepare store assets➜ Upload the build
    Fill in privacy and review info➜ Apple review (1-7 days)➜ Published

    Figure 5: Six steps to the App Store

    • Register: developer.apple.com, personal accounts 99 USD/year;
    • Assets: icon (1024×1024, no rounded corners—Apple does the rounding itself), screenshots (each iPhone size), description, privacy policy link;
    • Privacy questionnaire: honestly declare what data you collect—an offline expense tracker can declare "no data collected";
    • Review: the first submission often waits 1–7 days; if rejected, fix things one by one per the "review notes"—Apple's rejection reasons are usually written very specifically, so just follow them;
    • TestFlight: before release, send a beta build to friends for internal testing (up to 10,000 people), gather a round of feedback, then submit officially—very professional.

    5. Store assets: first impressions drive downloads

    The store page is the shop window users see while "browsing." Three assets decide the first impression:

    • Icon: 1024×1024, don't just make do with a screenshot. If you have no design skills, use an AI tool to generate a simple graphic; it only passes if it's still recognizable when shrunk down on a home screen;
    • Screenshots: at least 2 sets (mainstream iPhone sizes), showing your most core feature scenarios; give each one a plain-language caption ("Log an expense in one second" beats "An efficient expense-tracking solution" ten times over);
    • Description: the first sentence should make clear "what this is + who it's for." Don't pile on "the most professional, the most powerful"—sincerity works better than hype.

    Get hands-on: "ship" the expense tracker once

    6. A mini checklist for crash reporting and performance

    Before release, these two things are each worth half an hour:

    1. Crash monitoring

    Just because it didn't crash in your testing doesn't mean it won't on users' phones. Apple provides free crash reports in the Xcode Organizer (paid accounts can see real-device crash logs); an even more hassle-free option is a third-party SDK (such as Firebase Crashlytics). Shipping without crash monitoring is like driving with your eyes closed.

    2. Four performance self-checks
    1. Use LazyVStack / List for lists: don't lay out long lists with a plain VStack—lazy loading is lesson one of performance;
    2. Don't force in full-size images: use AsyncImage (for remote images) and the system cache; a 5MB original can bog down older phones badly;
    3. Don't do heavy work on the main thread: route network calls and large files through async/await;
    4. Measure with Instruments: Xcode's built-in profiler (Time Profiler, memory leak checks)—measure first, then optimize; don't go by feel.

    ① Add 3 unit tests for logic like parseAmount (green with ⌘U); ② use a breakpoint to catch a crash you created yourself and fix it; ③ build a package with Product → Archive and invite friends to test via TestFlight; ④ if you have the bandwidth, register a developer account and actually submit the expense tracker to the store. The first three steps can be done tonight.

    Chapter summary

    • The three debugging essentials: print logs, breakpoints, and SwiftUI previews with the view inspector
    • XCTest: unit tests (⌘U) + UI tests + manual testing, prebuilt in the template
    • Signing: free accounts get automatic signing (renewed every 7 days); distribution requires a paid account
    • Packaging: Generic iOS Device + Archive + Distribute; always back up your certificates
    • Six steps to release: register → assets → upload → privacy questionnaire → review → go live; beta test with TestFlight first

    Chapter 68: The Road Ahead—Permissions, Notifications, and Modern Architecture

    Being able to build an app is only the start. This chapter is about the hurdles between "can build" and "builds well": how to ask for permissions gracefully, how to send notifications without being annoying, how to lift your architecture another level, and—here in 2026—how to team up with AI to write iOS code. Every item is something you'll run into right away in a real project.

    1. Permissions: knock before you enter

    Camera, location, contacts, notifications... for these "sensitive zones," iOS requires the app to show a prompt asking the user at the moment of use. The rule is three steps: "declare + ask + degrade gracefully":

    SWIFT · Requesting permissions (location example)···
    // 1. Declare the usage text in Info.plist (without it, instant crash!)
// Privacy - Location When In Use Usage Description: "Used to look up the weather in your city"

// 2. Request it when you need it
import CoreLocation

@Observable
class LocationModel {
    private let manager = CLLocationManager()

    func request() {
        switch manager.authorizationStatus {
        case .notDetermined: manager.requestWhenInUseAuthorization()
        case .denied, .restricted: /* guide the user to Settings */
        default: /* already granted, go ahead */
        }
    }
}

// 3. Degrade gracefully after denial: show a hint + open Settings
// UIApplication.shared.open(URL(string: UIApplication.openSettingsURLString)!)

    Note: iOS permissions are "one-shot"

    The iOS permission prompt appears only once—once the user declines, it never pops up again. So: time the request for "the exact moment the user is about to use the feature" (not a pile of prompts at launch), and write the copy so it explains the purpose. Post-denial guidance ("go to Settings and turn on location") is standard equipment—don't leave users stuck in a dead end.

    2. Notifications: say something useful at the right time

    Notifications are the channel apps use to reach users, and also the feature most easily "blocked" by them. iOS uses the UserNotifications framework. Three rules for notifications: only send what's useful, let users turn them off, and never pester people in the middle of the night. Basic usage:

    SWIFT · Local notifications···
    import UserNotifications

// 1. Request notification permission (one-time dialog)
UNUserNotificationCenter.current()
    .requestAuthorization(options: [.alert, .sound, .badge]) { granted, _ in
        print(granted ? "granted" : "denied")
    }

// 2. Schedule a "daily 20:00 expense reminder"
func scheduleDailyReminder() {
    let content = UNMutableNotificationContent()
    content.title = "Expense reminder"
    content.body = "You haven't recorded today's expenses yet"
    content.sound = .default

    var comps = DateComponents()
    comps.hour = 20
    let trigger = UNCalendarNotificationTrigger(dateMatching: comps, repeats: true)

    let request = UNNotificationRequest(
        identifier: "daily-reminder",
        content: content,
        trigger: trigger
    )
    UNUserNotificationCenter.current().add(request)
}

    Note: the iOS notification permission is also "one prompt only," and users can switch it off anytime in system settings—so the sense of value in each notification matters a lot. One spam blast can lose a user forever.

    3. Architecture, going deeper: MVVM and testability

    Chapter 65 used MVVM; here are three advanced points to add:

    • Protocol abstraction: make the ViewModel depend on a protocol rather than a concrete class—then tests can inject a "fake data source." This is the cornerstone of testability;
    • Single responsibility: one ViewModel handles one thing only (the expense-tracking one doesn't handle weather); when features grow, split it up;
    • Don't over-engineer: for a solo small project, "an @Observable class + protocol abstraction" is plenty. Heavy architectures like VIPER or Clean Architecture can wait until team size and complexity come knocking—tools serve the goal; they're not for showing off.

    Tip: SwiftUI's "ecosystem dividend"

    The iOS ecosystem has two more "only-here" advanced tricks: widgets (WidgetKit) let users see information without opening the app (put the expense tracker's "spending this month" on the home screen), and Shortcuts (App Intents) let users invoke your features through Siri or automations. Both have official frameworks and are cheap to learn, yet they massively boost the user experience—worth unlocking early on the road to mastery.

    4. The 2026 twist: AI-assisted iOS development

    By 2026, AI is deeply embedded in Apple's development workflow. If you want to speed up, this combo is mature:

    StageHow AI helpsYour responsibility
    Writing codeXcode's built-in code completion + third-party AI plugins generate itDescribe requirements clearly, review the output
    Looking things upHand official docs and error messages to AI to interpretVerify key conclusions against the official docs
    Writing testsHave AI generate XCTest cases in the "normal/boundary/exception" categoriesConfirm the cases match the business meaning
    Fixing bugsPaste the crash log + relevant code, and AI locates and fixes itUnderstand the changes, run tests to verify

    Four scenarios for AI-assisted iOS development

    For the full methodology—how to give AI instructions, how to review its work, how to avoid pitfalls—the complete 11 chapters are in Part 7 of this book, "Hands-On AI Coding" (Chapters 37–47), which I strongly recommend reading alongside this one: leave the Swift syntax to this part, and the art of working with AI to Part 7.

    Get hands-on: add the "power trio" to the expense tracker

    5. Swift concurrency essentials: @MainActor and Task

    Swift 6's concurrency system has two rules every beginner must understand:

    • The UI can only be updated on the main thread: SwiftUI views are @MainActor by default, so bring network callbacks back to the main thread before changing state (await MainActor.run { ... }, or mark the ViewModel @MainActor);
    • Manage async work with Task: the .task { } modifier starts automatically when the view appears and cancels automatically when it disappears—that's the standard way to kick off async work in SwiftUI; don't scatter raw Tasks in body.
    SWIFT · The standard async pattern···
    struct WeatherScreen: View {
    @State private var vm = WeatherViewModel()

    var body: some View {
        Group {
            switch vm.state {
            case .loading: ProgressView()
            case .success(let d): WeatherContent(data: d)
            case .error(let m): Text(m)
            }
        }
        .task {                       // starts when it appears, cancels when it disappears
            await vm.search(city: "Beijing")
        }
    }
}

    Behind these two rules is Swift 6's "data-race safety" design—the compiler errors out the moment you get it wrong, instead of waiting for the app to crash to find out. The compiler's errors aren't nitpicking; they're taking a bullet for you.

    ① Add a "daily 8:00 PM expense reminder" to the tracker (notification permission + local notifications); ② switch the ViewModel's data source to a protocol abstraction and write a unit test that injects fake data; ③ add a "spending this month" home-screen widget. Finish the trio and your project starts to look like a regular army.

    Chapter summary

    • Permissions in three steps: declare in Info.plist (miss it and it crashes), ask at the moment of use, guide to Settings when denied
    • iOS permission prompts appear only once: pick the timing of "the moment they're about to use it," and write the purpose clearly
    • Three rules for notifications: only send useful ones, let users turn them off, don't pester; UserNotifications framework
    • MVVM advanced: protocol abstraction (testable), single responsibility, no over-engineering
    • Ecosystem dividends: WidgetKit widgets + App Intents Shortcuts

    2. Frequently asked questions (FAQ)

    Q1: Can I learn iOS development without a Mac?

    You can learn the language, but not do the full development. Swift Playgrounds on iPad/iPhone can cover everything in Chapter 61; but Xcode is macOS-only, so in the end you'll need a Mac. On a tight budget, you can rent a cloud Mac or buy a used Mac mini as a stopgap, then decide how much to invest after learning the language.

    Q2: How much does learning iOS development cost?

    Learning stage: 0 dollars (Xcode is free + a free Apple ID for on-device debugging). Release stage: a developer account at 99 USD/year (about 700 RMB). Add a Mac, and that's the entire cost. Compared with the payoff—even a small utility on the App Store has paying users—the math works out.

    Q3: SwiftUI or UIKit—which one first?

    SwiftUI. In 2026, new projects, new tutorials, and new job listings all center on SwiftUI, and this book uses it throughout. UIKit is the previous-generation framework, still used in many older projects—once you're comfortable with SwiftUI, pick up UIKit as needed (Apple has interop tutorials), and it will come quickly. Just don't reverse the order.

    Q4: Is iOS development easy to find work in?

    The 2026 job market: entry-level roles that amount to "can draw interfaces" are fiercely competitive, but developers who "know Swift + SwiftUI and have a shipped app" are still in demand. Median pay for iOS roles has ranked near the top among tech stacks for years. While you're learning, the best line on your resume is that app you made, sitting in the store.

    Q5: What if my app gets rejected in review?

    Don't panic—it's normal; first submissions get rejected at a decent rate. Apple's rejection reasons are usually written very specifically (which page, which guideline). Fix things one by one, reply with an explanation in App Store Connect, and resubmit. The three most common rejection reasons: permission purposes not clearly explained, buggy interfaces, and metadata (screenshots/description) that doesn't match the real thing. Self-check those three ahead of time and you'll save yourself a round of waiting.

    Tip: when builds act haunted, clean the cache first

    That spooky "it ran yesterday but not today" phenomenon is, six or seven times out of ten, a scrambled build cache. Clean with ⇧⌘K and rebuild, and it cures the majority of these hauntings. Still broken? Restart Xcode (and the Mac along with it), and if that fails, "delete the DerivedData folder"—the legendary ultimate trio, passed down among iOS developers.

    5. Closing: from your first app to your Nth app

    Looking back, you went from "having no idea what SwiftUI was" to installing Xcode, learning Swift, drawing interfaces with SwiftUI, hooking your app up to a database and the network, and on to testing, packaging, and shipping—on this road, you've already walked the hardest stretch of the journey from zero to one.

    The world of technology changes fast: frameworks upgrade, tools get replaced, and AI takes over more and more of the "typing" work. But one thing never goes out of date: your ability to take a fuzzy idea, break it into clear steps, and then build it one step at a time. Tools are the amplifier; the way you think is the foundation. The amplifier can be swapped out; the foundation must not shake.

    You're no longer just "someone who knows how to use a phone." You can turn the ideas in your head into real apps running on hundreds of millions of iPhones. From today, create with your keyboard — that's the romance of being an iOS developer.
